problem:
V OM - II - Task 3

Given: point $ A $, line $ p $, and circle $ k $. Construct triangle $ ABC $ with angles $ A = 60^\circ $, $ B = 90^\circ $, where vertex $ B $ lies on line $ p $, and vertex $ C $ lies on circle $ k $.
solution:
(method of geometric loci).
The task boils down to finding a point $ C $ that satisfies two conditions:
1° Point $ C $ lies on a given circle $ k $;
2° point $ C $ is a vertex of triangle $ ABC $ with a given vertex $ A $, whose vertex $ B $ lies on a given line $ p $ and in which $ \measuredangle A = 60^\circ $, $ \measuredangle B = 90^\circ $.
We will determine the geometric locus of the point satisfying condition 2°. We will distinguish two cases:
a) Point $ A $ does not lie on line $ p $. There are then two points $ M $ and $ N $ on line $ p $ of the desired geometric locus (fig. 30); they are the vertices of triangles $ ATM $ and $ ATN $, where $ AT $ is the distance from point $ A $ to line $ p $, and $ \measuredangle AMT = \measuredangle ANT = 30^\circ $.
Let $ C $ be a point satisfying condition 2° and let the angle $ ABC $ be oriented in the same direction as angle $ ATM $.
Point $ M $ then lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ ABC $. Indeed, point $ B $ either coincides with point $ M $, or lies on the ray $ MT $, in which case points $ M $ and $ C $ lie on the same side of line $ AB $ and $ \measuredangle AMB = \measuredangle ACB = 30^\circ $, or finally, point $ B $ lies on the extension of ray $ TM $ beyond point $ M $, in which case points $ M $ and $ C $ are on opposite sides of line $ AB $ and $ \measuredangle AMB + \measuredangle ACB = 180^\circ $, since $ \measuredangle AMB = 180^\circ - \measuredangle AMT = 150^\circ $, and $ \measuredangle ACB = 30^\circ $.
Since the diameter of the circumcircle of triangle $ ABC $ is $ AC $, then $ \measuredangle AMC = 90^\circ $. We have obtained the result that all points of the sought geometric locus, for which $ \measuredangle ABC $ is oriented in the same direction as angle $ ATM $, lie on a line perpendicular to line $ AM $ at point $ M $. Conversely, every point $ C $ of this perpendicular belongs to the geometric locus; if the circumcircle of triangle $ AMC $ passes through point $ B $ on line $ p $, then triangle $ ABC $ satisfies condition 2°, since $ \measuredangle ABC = \measuredangle AMC = 90^\circ $, and $ \measuredangle ACB = \measuredangle AMT = 30^\circ $.
Similarly, all points satisfying condition 2°, and such that angle $ ABC $ is oriented in the same direction as angle $ ATN $, form a line perpendicular to line $ AN $ at point $ N $.
We have proved that the sought geometric locus consists of two lines perpendicular to lines $ AM $ and $ AN $ at points $ M $ and $ N $, respectively.
b) Point $ A $ lies on line $ p $. In this case, we directly state that the sought geometric locus consists of all points of two lines passing through point $ A $ and forming angles of $ 60^\circ $ and $ 120^\circ $ with line $ p $, except for point $ A $ itself (fig. 31).
The solution to the given problem is obtained by finding the points of intersection of the given circle $ k $ with both lines of the determined geometric locus. Depending on the position of the circle relative to these lines, the number of solutions to the problem can be $ 4 $, $ 3 $, $ 2 $, $ 1 $, or $ 0 $.

problem:
IV OM - I - Problem 6

Prove that if a plane figure has two and only two axes of symmetry, then these axes are perpendicular.
solution:
The theorem will be proven when we show that if a plane figure has two axes of symmetry that are not perpendicular, then it has at least one more axis of symmetry.
Suppose that the plane figure $F$ has two axes of symmetry $k$ and $l$, which are not perpendicular. They can intersect (Fig. 26) or be parallel (Fig. 27). In both cases, the reasoning will be the same. Let $k'$ be the line symmetric to the line $k$ with respect to the line $l$. The line $k'$ is, of course, different from the line $k$ and different from the line $l$. We will prove that the line $k'$ is an axis of symmetry of the figure $F$.
If the figure $F$ contains some point $A$, then it also contains the point $B$ symmetric to the point $A$ with respect to the axis $l$, then the point $C$ symmetric to the point $B$ with respect to the axis $k$, and further the point $D$ symmetric to the point $C$ with respect to the axis $l$. Notice that the segment $AD$ is symmetric to the segment $BC$ with respect to the axis $l$, since points $A$ and $D$ are respectively symmetric to points $B$ and $C$ with respect to this axis. In this case, the perpendicular bisector of segment $AD$ is symmetric to the perpendicular bisector of segment $BC$ (i.e., to the line $k$) with respect to the axis $l$, which means that the perpendicular bisector of segment $AD$ is the line $k'$. We have proven that if the figure $F$ contains some point $A$, then it also contains the point $D$, symmetric to the point $A$ with respect to the line $k'$, i.e., that $k'$ is an axis of symmetry of the figure $F$.

problem:
III OM - II - Task 3

Are the statements true:
a) if four vertices of a rectangle lie on the four sides of a rhombus, then the sides of the rectangle are parallel to the diagonals of the rhombus;
b) if four vertices of a square lie on the four sides of a rhombus, which is not a square, then the sides of the square are parallel to the diagonals of the rhombus.
solution:
a) The first theorem is not true; to demonstrate this, it suffices to provide a counterexample, i.e., to show a figure contradicting the theorem.
From the center $ O $ of the rhombus $ ABCD $ (Fig. 28), draw a circle with a radius greater than the distance from the center of the rhombus to its side, but smaller than half the length of the shorter diagonal of the rhombus.
The entire figure is symmetric with respect to each of the lines $ AC $ and $ BD $, as well as with respect to the point $ O $. The drawn circle intersects each side of the rhombus at two points. Let $ M $ be one of the points of intersection of side $ AB $ with the circle, and let $ N $ be the point of intersection of side $ BC $ with the circle that is not symmetric to point $ M $ with respect to the line $ BD $. Let $ P $ and $ Q $ then be the points symmetric to points $ M $ and $ N $ with respect to point $ O $; segments $ MP $ and $ NQ $ are thus diameters of the circle; due to the symmetry of the figure with respect to point $ O $, points $ P $ and $ Q $ are points of intersection of sides $ CD $ and $ DA $ with the circle.
Quadrilateral $ MNPQ $ is a rectangle, as each of its angles is an inscribed angle in the drawn circle and subtends its diameter (e.g., angle $ MNP $ subtends diameter $ MP $). Side $ MN $ of this rectangle is not perpendicular to line $ BD $, as line $ MN $ does not pass through the point symmetric to point $ M $ with respect to line $ BD $; thus, side $ MN $ is not parallel to diagonal $ AC $. Side $ MN $ is also not parallel to diagonal $ BD $, as it connects points $ M $ and $ N $ lying on opposite sides of line $ BD $. The vertices $ M $, $ N $, $ P $, $ Q $ of rectangle $ MNPQ $ lie on the sides $ AB $, $ BC $, $ CD $, $ DA $ of the rhombus, respectively, but the sides of this rectangle are not parallel to the diagonals of the rhombus. Rectangle $ MNPQ $ thus serves as a counterexample refuting statement a).
b) We will prove that the second theorem is true.
Let $ MNPQ $ be a square inscribed in the rhombus $ ABCD $, with vertices $ M $, $ N $, $ P $, $ Q $ of the square lying on sides $ AB $, $ BC $, $ CD $, $ DA $ of the rhombus, respectively.
We will first prove that the center $ O $ of the square is also the center of the rhombus. Rotate the entire figure around point $ O $ by $ 180^\circ $. Vertex $ M $ of the square will end up in the opposite vertex $ P $ after the rotation (Fig. 29), line $ AB $ will become a line passing through point $ P $ and parallel to line $ AB $, i.e., it will coincide with line $ CD $. Since the same reasoning applies to each side of the rhombus, it follows that the rhombus will overlap with itself after the rotation, which means that the center of rotation $ O $ is the center of symmetry of the rhombus.
Now, rotate the entire figure around point $ O $ by $ 90^\circ $ so that ray $ OA $ coincides with ray $ OB $ (the direction of rotation is indicated by an arrow in Fig. 30). After the rotation, square $ MNPQ $ will transform into square $ NPQM $, i.e., it will overlap with itself; rhombus $ ABCD $ will transform into rhombus $ A'BC'D' $, which does not coincide with rhombus $ ABCD $, as the rhombus is not a square by assumption. If, for example, $ OA > OB $, then $ OA' > OB $ and $ OD' > OD $; thus, segments $ D'A' $ and $ AB $ intersect. The point of intersection of these segments is vertex $ M $ of the square, as point $ Q $ of segment $ AD $ will fall on this point after the rotation. Similarly, segments $ BC $ and $ A'D' $ intersect at vertex $ N $ of the square.
The figure composed of both rhombi is symmetric with respect to line $ BD $; in this symmetry, point $ M $ corresponds to point $ N $. Line $ MN $ is therefore perpendicular to the axis of symmetry $ BD $, i.e., it is parallel to line $ AC $, which was to be proved.
Note. If we were to discard the assumption that rhombus $ ABCD $ is not a square, the theorem would not be true, as an infinite number of squares can be inscribed in a square, of which only one has sides parallel to the diagonals of the given square.
From the proven theorem b), it follows that only one square can be inscribed in a rhombus that is not a square, such that each side of the rhombus contains one vertex of the square. A stronger theorem can be proven: there is only one square whose vertices lie on the perimeter of rhombus $ ABCD $ that is not a square. It suffices to show that there is no square whose two vertices lie on the same side of the rhombus, while the other vertices lie on other sides of the rhombus. We leave this as an exercise.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, which is not a parallelogram, the equality $AB=CD$ holds. Points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, respectively. Prove that the orthogonal projections of segments $AB$ and $CD$ onto line $MN$ are segments of equal length, equal to the length of segment $MN$.
solution:
Let point $E$ be the midpoint of side $AD$, and point $F$ be the midpoint of segment $MN$ (Fig. 1).
om58_1r_img_1.jpg
From the converse of Thales' theorem, it follows that $EM \parallel DC$ and $EM = \frac{1}{2}DC$. Similarly, we obtain the relationships $EN \parallel AB$ and $EN = \frac{1}{2}AB$. From the equality $DC = AB$, we get $EM = EN$. Therefore, triangle $MEN$ is isosceles, which means $EF \perp MN$. Consequently, the orthogonal projection of segment $EN$ onto line $MN$ is segment $FN$; and since segment $AB$ is parallel to segment $EN$ and has twice the length, the projection of segment $AB$ onto line $MN$ is a segment of length $2 \cdot FN = MN$.
Similarly, we prove that the orthogonal projection of segment $CD$ onto line $MN$ is a segment of length $MN$, which completes the solution of the problem.

problem:
XXVIII - I - Problem 10

Prove that in every tetrahedron there exists a vertex at which all three dihedral angles are acute.
solution:
The sum of the measures of the plane angles of any face of a tetrahedron is equal to $ \pi $. Therefore, the sum of the measures of all the plane angles of the tetrahedron is $ 4\pi $. It follows that there exists a vertex $ A $ of the tetrahedron such that the sum of the measures of the plane angles at this vertex does not exceed $ \pi $.
On the other hand, it is known (see the solution to problem 17(5) of the XXIV Mathematical Olympiad), that the sum of the measures of two plane angles at a vertex of a tetrahedron is greater than the measure of the third plane angle at that vertex. If, therefore, one of the plane angles at a vertex of the tetrahedron is not acute, then the sum of the measures of all the plane angles at this vertex is greater than $ \pi $.
From the above, it follows that all the plane angles at vertex $ A $ are acute.

problem:
XXXI - I - Problem 9

Prove that a natural number $ n > 1 $ divides the number $ a^{(n-1)! + 1} - a $ for every integer $ a $ if and only if $ n $ is a product of distinct prime numbers.
solution:
Integers that are not divisible by the square of any prime number are called square-free numbers. First, we will show that the condition for \( n \) to be a square-free number is necessary for \( n \) to divide \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \) for every integer \( a \). Suppose \( n \) is divisible by the square of a prime number \( p \) and let \( a = p \). In the difference \( p^{(n-1)!+1} - p \), the subtrahend is divisible by \( p^2 \), but the minuend is not divisible by \( p^2 \), so \( p^{(n-1)!+1} - p \) is not divisible by \( p^2 \), and therefore it is not divisible by the number \( n \), which is a multiple of \( p^2 \).

For the sufficiency of the condition, assume that \( n \) is a square-free number, \( n = p_1 p_2 \ldots p_k \), where \( p_i \) are prime numbers and \( p_i \ne p_j \) for \( i \ne j \). To show that \( n \) divides \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \), it suffices to state that \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \) is divisible by \( p_i \) for \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \). If \( p_i \) divides \( a \), then \( p_i \) obviously divides \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \). Let's consider the case when \( p_i \) does not divide \( a \). In this case, \( p_i \) does not divide any of the \( p_i \) numbers \( 1, a, a^2, \ldots, a^{p_i-1} \), so some two of these numbers give the same remainder when divided by \( p_i \); let these be \( a^k \) and \( a^l \) for \( 0 \leq k < l < p_i \): \( a^k = t \cdot p_i + r \), \( a^l = s \cdot p_i + r \). Therefore, the number \( a^l - a^k \) is divisible by \( p_i \), and thus \( a^{l-k} - 1 \) is divisible by \( p_i \). Since \( l - k < p_i \leq n \), \( l - k \) divides \( (n-1)! \). Therefore, \( (n-1)! = (l - k) \cdot w \), and thus \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a = (a^{l-k} - 1) (a^{(l-k)(w-1)} + a^{(l-k)(w-2)} + \ldots + a^{l-k} + 1) \). Therefore, \( a^{l-k} - 1 \) divides \( a^{(n-1)!} - 1 \), and thus it also divides \( a(a^{(n-1)!} - 1) = a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \). It follows that \( p_i \), being a divisor of \( a^{l-k} - 1 \), also divides \( a^{(n-1)!+1} - a \), which completes the proof.

Note. The proof of the sufficiency of the condition that \( n \) is a square-free number can be slightly shortened by using Fermat's Little Theorem.
For any integer \( a \) and prime number \( p_i \), the number \( a^{p_i} - a \) is divisible by \( p_i \).
In the case where \( p_i \) does not divide \( a \), it follows directly from this theorem that \( p_i \) divides \( a^{p_i-1} - 1 \).

XV OM - II - Task 3

Prove that if three prime numbers form an arithmetic progression with a difference not divisible by 6, then the smallest of these numbers is $3$.
solution:
Suppose that the prime numbers $ p_1 $, $ p_2 $, $ p_3 $ form an arithmetic progression with a difference $ r > 0 $ not divisible by $ 6 $, and the smallest of them is $ p_1 $. Then

Therefore, $ p_1 \geq 3 $, for if $ p_1 = 2 $, the number $ p_3 $ would be an even number greater than $ 2 $, and thus would not be a prime number. Hence, the numbers $ p_1 $ and $ p_2 $ are odd, and the number $ r $ equal to the difference $ p_2 - p_1 $ is even and one of the cases holds: $ r = 6k + 2 $ or $ r = 6k + 4 $, where $ k $ is an integer $ \geq 0 $.
We will prove that $ p_1 $ is divisible by $ 3 $. Indeed, if $ p_1 = 3m + 1 $ ($ m $ - an integer) and $ r = 6k + 2 $, it would follow that $ p_2 = 3m + 6k + 3 $ is divisible by $ 3 $, and since $ p_2 > 3 $, $ p_2 $ would not be a prime number. If, on the other hand, $ p_1 = 3m + 1 $ and $ r = 6k + 4 $, then $ p_3 = 3m + 12k + 9 $ would not be a prime number. Similarly, from the assumption that $ p_1 = 3m + 2 $ and $ r = 6k + 2 $, it would follow that $ p_3 = 3m + 12k + 6 $ is not a prime number, and from the assumption that $ p_1 = 3m + 2 $ and $ r = 6k + 4 $, we would get $ p_2 = 3m + 6k + 6 $, and thus $ p_2 $ would not be a prime number.
Therefore, $ p_1 $ is a prime number divisible by $ 3 $, i.e., $ p_1 = 3 $.

Given is a sequence $ (c_n) $ of natural numbers defined recursively: $ c_1 = 2 $, $ c_{n+1} = \left[ \frac{3}{2}c_n\right] $. Prove that there are infinitely many even numbers and infinitely many odd numbers among the terms of this sequence.
solution:
It is enough to prove the following two statements:
(a) For any even number $ p $ being a term of the sequence $ (c_n) $, there exists a larger odd number that is a term of this sequence.
(b) For any odd number $ q $ being a term of the sequence $ (c_n) $, there exists a larger even number that is a term of this sequence.
Proof of statement (a). Let $ p = 2^km $, $ k,m \geq1 $, $ m $ odd. If $ p = c_n $, then $ c_{n+1} = 2^{k-1}\cdot 3m $; when $ k -1 \geq 1 $, then $ c_{n+2} = 2^{k-2}\cdot 3^2m $; etc., generally, for $ j \in \{1,\ldots, k\} $ we have $ c_{n-j} = 2^{k-j} \cdot 3^j m $. In particular, for $ j = k $ we get $ c_{n+k} = 3^km $. This is a larger than $ p $ odd number.
Proof of statement (b). Now $ q - 1 $ is an even, positive number ($ q - 1 $ cannot be zero, because $ c_n \geq 2 $ for all $ n $; this follows immediately by induction from the definition of the sequence $ (c_n) $). Thus $ q = 2^km+1 $, $ k,m \geq 1 $, $ m $ odd. If $ q = c_n $, then $ c_{n+1} = 2^{k-1}\cdot 3m + 1 $ and generally, as before, for $ j\in \{1, \ldots, k\} $ we have $ c_{n+j} = 2^{k-j}\cdot 3^jm+1 $; in particular $ c_{n+k} = 3^km + 1 $. This is a larger than $ q $ even number.

problem:
I OM - B - Task 19

The centers of four identical spheres lie on the circumference of a circle, and the center of mass of these spheres is at the center of the circle. Show that the centers of the spheres are the vertices of a rectangle.
solution:
Let $A, B, C, D$ denote the consecutive vertices of a quadrilateral formed by the centers of the spheres, and $M$ and $N$ - the midpoints of two opposite sides $AB$ and $CD$ of this quadrilateral.
Replace the spheres with centers $A$ and $B$ with a sphere twice as heavy with center $M$, and the spheres with centers $C$ and $D$ - with a sphere twice as heavy with center $N$. The center of gravity of the system of these two new spheres is the same as the center of gravity of the system of the previous four spheres, since the gravitational forces acting at points $A$ and $B$ have been replaced by their resultant acting at point $M$, and similarly, the gravitational forces acting at points $C$ and $D$ have been replaced by their resultant acting at point $N$. Therefore, the center of gravity of the two spheres placed at points $M$ and $N$, i.e., the midpoint of segment $MN$, lies at the center of the considered circle.
Chords $AB$ and $CD$, whose midpoints $M$ and $N$ lie on the diameter of the circle, are perpendicular to this diameter; these chords are therefore parallel. Similarly, the other two sides $BC$ and $AD$ of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ are parallel. This quadrilateral is thus an inscribed parallelogram in a circle, which means it is a rectangle.

problem:
XXXIX OM - III - Problem 6

Calculate the maximum volume of a tetrahedron contained within a hemisphere of radius 1.
solution:
Let us denote the given hemisphere by $H$, the whole sphere by $K$, and the circle forming the flat part of the boundary of $H$ by $E$. Let $O$ be any tetrahedron contained in $H$. Its interior is the intersection of four open half-spaces determined by the planes of the faces. The center of the sphere $K$ does not belong to the interior of the tetrahedron; hence it does not belong to at least one of these half-spaces. Therefore, there is a face $S$ of the tetrahedron $Q$ such that the opposite vertex of the tetrahedron and the center of the sphere $K$ lie on opposite sides of the plane of this face (or, in the limiting case, the center of the sphere lies on this plane).

Thus, $Q$ is contained in the smaller of the two parts (or in one of the two equal parts) into which the plane of the face $S$ divides the sphere $K$. Therefore, the height of the tetrahedron $Q$ dropped onto the face $S$ has a length not greater than $1$, so the volume of $Q$ does not exceed one third of the area of this face. The area of the face $S$, being a triangle, is not greater than the area of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle which is the section of the sphere $K$ by the plane of this face (see Note); and even more so, it is not greater than the area of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the great circle $E$. The latter area equals $3\sqrt{3}/4$. Therefore, the volume of $Q$ is less than or equal to $\sqrt{3}/4$.

In all the estimates mentioned, we can achieve equality by taking $O$ to be a tetrahedron whose base is an equilateral triangle inscribed in $E$, and the fourth vertex is placed at the farthest point from $E$ on the hemisphere $H$ (at the "north pole").

The number $\sqrt{3}/4$ is the sought maximum.

Note: For completeness, we will provide an elementary proof of the fact that among all triangles inscribed in a fixed circle of radius $r$, the one with the largest area is the equilateral triangle.

Let $ABC$ be any such triangle. By placing point $C$ at the midpoint of the larger of the two arcs into which points $A$ and $B$ divide the circle circumscribed around triangle $ABC$, we obtain an isosceles triangle $ABC$, acute or right, with an area not less than that of triangle $ABC$. Therefore, in searching for a triangle with the maximum area (inscribed in a given circle), we can limit our attention to the class of isosceles triangles without obtuse angles (inscribed in this circle).

If now $ABC$ is a triangle from this class ($|AC| = |BC|$), then denoting by $x$ the distance from side $AB$ to the center of the circle, we get the relationships: $|AB| = 2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$, $h_C = r + x$ (the height dropped from vertex $C$), and thus

We have used here the inequality between the geometric mean and the arithmetic mean of four numbers: $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = r + x$, $a_4 = 3r - 3x$. This inequality becomes an equality if and only if these numbers are equal, i.e., for $x = r/2$. It remains to note that the last equality means that triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

If $ q > 0 $, then in view of the inequality $ N < (n + 1)! $, it must be that $ q < n! $. By the induction hypothesis, the number $ q $ is a sum of the form

problem:
XXIV OM - I - Problem 3

Let $ w(x) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Prove that if a natural number $ d $ is a divisor of each of the numbers $ a_n = 3^n + w(n) $, where $ n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots $, then $ d $ is a power of 2 with an integer exponent.
solution:
Let the prime number $ p $ be a divisor of each of the numbers $ a_n $, where $ n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots $. It suffices to prove that $ p = 2 $.
In particular, we have $ p \mid a_0 $ and $ p \mid a_p $. Hence . Let $ w(x) = c_0 + c_1x + \ldots + c_rx^r $, where the numbers $ c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_r $ are integers. The number $ w(p) - w(0) = c_1p + c_2p^2 + \ldots + c_rp^r $ is of course divisible by $ p $. Therefore, $ p \mid 3^p - 1 $. Hence $ p \ne 3 $. From Fermat's Little Theorem, it follows that $ p \mid 3^{p-1} - 1 $. Therefore, $ p \mid (3^p - 1) - (3^{p-1} - 1) = 2 \cdot 3^{p-1} $. Since $ p \ne 3 $, it follows that $ p = 2 $.

problem:
VI OM - III - Task 2

Prove that among seven natural numbers forming an arithmetic progression with a difference of $30$, one and only one is divisible by $7$.
solution:
Seven numbers forming an arithmetic progression with a difference of $30$ can be written in the form: $a, a + 30, a + 2 \cdot 30, \ldots, a + 6 \cdot 30$. The difference between any two of these numbers has the form

\[
(k - m) \cdot 30
\]

where $k$ and $m$ are integers, with $0 \leq k \leq 6$, $0 \leq m \leq 6$, $k \ne m$, so $-6 \leq k - m \leq 6$ and $k - m \ne 0$. The number $(k - m) \cdot 30$ is divisible by $7$, and the number $(k - m) \cdot 2$ is not divisible by $7$, because its absolute value is an even natural number not greater than $12$. Therefore, the sum of these numbers, i.e., the number $r$, is not divisible by $7$. Hence, each of the seven numbers gives a different remainder when divided by $7$, and thus one and only one of these seven remainders equals zero, c. n. d.

In a plane with a given coordinate system, there is a convex polygon whose all vertices have integer coordinates. Prove that twice the area of this polygon is an integer.
solution:
We choose any vertex of the polygon and draw all diagonals from it. In this way, we divide the given polygon into triangles, whose vertices have integer coordinates. It is therefore sufficient to prove the considered theorem for a triangle.
om34_2r_img_5.jpg
We draw lines through the vertices of the triangle parallel to the coordinate axes. These lines intersect at points with integer coordinates, thus forming a rectangle whose area is an integer and on whose sides the vertices of the considered triangle lie. The triangle is formed from this rectangle by cutting off one, two, or three right-angled triangles with legs parallel to the coordinate axes and vertices at points with integer coordinates. The lengths of the legs of these triangles are integers, so the area of each triangle (equal to half the product of the lengths of the legs) is an integer or half an integer. Therefore, the area $ S $ of the considered triangle is the difference between an integer (the area of the rectangle) and one, two, or three numbers, each of which is an integer or half an integer. Thus, $ 2S $ is an integer.

problem:
XLVIII OM - III - Problem 4

The sequence $ a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots $ is defined by the formulas

For every integer $ k \geq 0 $, determine the number of indices $ n $ satisfying the conditions

Note: $ [n/2] $ is the greatest integer not exceeding $ n/2 $.
solution:
For each integer $ n \geq 1 $, we assign a finite sequence of two types of symbols: dots and commas. We write the number $ n $ in binary. Between each pair of consecutive digits, we insert a dot if the digits are the same, and a comma if they are different. If $ n $ satisfies the inequality $ 2^k \leq n < 2^{k+1} $, meaning it is a $(k+1)$-digit number in binary, then the dots and commas inserted in this manner form a $k$-term sequence. We will call this the *code* of the number $ n $. Each such sequence of dots and commas is the code of exactly one number $ n $: it starts with a one, and the subsequent digits are determined by the successive symbols of the code. A $k$-term code determines a $(k+1)$-digit number.
Let $ b_n $ be the number of dots, and $ c_n $ be the number of commas in the code of the number $ n $, and let $ d_n = b_n - c_n $.
Let $ n $ be any $(k+1)$-digit number ($ k \geq 1 $). By erasing its last digit, we obtain the binary representation of the number $ [n/2] $. If the last two digits of the number $ n $ are the same, then $ b_n = b_{[n/2]} + 1 $, $ c_n = c_{[n/2]} $. If the last two digits of the number $ n $ are different, then $ b_n = b_{[n/2]} $, $ c_n = c_{[n/2]} + 1 $. The first of these situations occurs when $ n \equiv 0 $ or $ n \equiv 3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4) $, and the second when $ n \equiv 1 $ or $ n \equiv 2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4) $. The difference $ d_n - d_{[n/2]} $ is $ 1 $ in the first case, and $ -1 $ in the second case.
The difference $ a_n - a_{[n/2]} $ takes exactly the same values. For $ n = 1 $, we have $ a_1 = b_1 = c_1 = d_1 = 0 $. Hence, it follows that $ a_n = d_n $, i.e., $ a_n = b_n - c_n $, for $ n = 1,2,3,\ldots $ . Therefore, for a $(k+1)$-digit number $ n $, the equality $ a_n = 0 $ holds if and only if its $k$-term code contains an equal number of each type of symbol. The number of such $k$-term sequences is $ {k \choose {k/2}} $ when $ k $ is even, and $ 0 $ when $ k $ is odd. Thus, there are as many numbers $ n $ that satisfy the given conditions.

problem:
XXII OM - III - Problem 2

On a billiard table in the shape of a triangle, whose angles are proportional, a ball was struck from a certain internal point. The ball bounces off the walls according to the law "angle of incidence equals angle of reflection." Prove that the number of directions in which the ball can move is finite. (Assume that the ball does not hit the vertex of the triangle).
solution:
We will first prove the following
Lemma. After a ball is reflected twice in succession from the sides $\overline{CA}$ and $\overline{AB}$ of triangle $ABC$ (Fig. 14), the direction of the ball's movement changes by an angle of $2 \measuredangle BAC$.
Proof. Consider the image $AB'$ of triangle $ABC$ in the symmetry with respect to line $AC$ and the image $AB''$ of triangle $AB'$ in the symmetry with respect to line $AB$. Denote by $k$, $l$, $m$ the vectors representing the ball's movement, and by $l'$, $m'$ the images of vectors $l$, $m$ in the first symmetry, and by $m''$ the image of vector $m$ in the second symmetry (Fig. 14).
From the law "the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection," it follows that vectors $k$, $l'$, $m'$ have the same direction. Since the composition of the considered symmetries is a rotation around point $A$ by an angle of $2\measuredangle BAC$, triangle $AB''$ is the image of triangle $ABC$ under this rotation, and vector $m''$ is the image of vector $m$. It follows that the directions of vectors $k$ and $m''$ differ by an angle of $2 \measuredangle BAC$.
We will now proceed to solve the problem. Since the measures of the angles of triangle $ABC$ are proportional, there exists a number $\lambda$ and natural numbers $r$, $s$, $t$ such that $\measuredangle BAC = r\lambda$, $\measuredangle ABC = s\lambda$, $\measuredangle ACB = t\lambda$. Therefore, $\lambda (r + s + t) = \pi$. Denoting $n = r + s + t$, we get that $\lambda = \frac{\pi}{n}$.
Thus, by the lemma, after an even number of reflections, the direction of the ball's movement changes by an angle whose measure is an even multiple of the number $\lambda = \frac{\pi}{n}$, i.e., one of the numbers $2\lambda, 4\lambda, 6\lambda, \ldots, 2n\lambda = 2\pi$. Therefore, after an even number of reflections, the ball can move in one of $n$ directions. Similarly, after an odd number of reflections, the ball can move in one of $n$ directions. The total number of directions in which the ball can move is therefore no greater than $2n$.
Note. Similarly, it can be proven that if in the problem the triangle is replaced by any polygon whose angle measures are proportional, then the number of directions in which the ball can move in such a polygon is also finite.

problem:
XLV OM - II - Task 4

Each vertex of a cube is assigned the number $ 1 $ or $ -1 $, and each face is assigned the product of the numbers assigned to the vertices of that face. Determine the set of values that the sum of the $ 14 $ numbers assigned to the faces and vertices can take.
solution:
Let's consider an arbitrary assignment of the numbers $1$ and $-1$ to the vertices of a cube; denote the sum of these numbers by $S_1$. Assign numbers to the faces according to a given rule; denote the sum of these numbers by $S_2$. The sum of all $14$ considered numbers is $S_1 + S_2$.
If we change the number at one vertex (it doesn't matter which one), this will affect the numbers assigned to three faces. The value of the sum $S_1$ will increase or decrease by $2$. The value of the sum $S_2$ will increase or decrease by $2$ or $6$. The total sum $S = S_1 + S_2$ will increase or decrease by $4$ or $8$, or remain unchanged.
If all vertices are assigned the number $1$, then all faces are also assigned the number $1$, and in this case $S = 8 + 6 = 14$. (This is, of course, the maximum possible value of the sum $S$.) From this configuration, any other can be reached by changing the numbers at the vertices one by one. According to the previous observation, at each step of this procedure, the sum $S$ will change by $\pm 4$, $\pm 8$, or $0$. Therefore, the values taken by the sum $S$ will differ from the initial value $14$ by multiples of the number $4$. The set of possible values is thus a subset of the set $\{14, 10, 6, 2, -2, -6, -10, -14\}$.
The number $-14$ can be immediately eliminated: we would need to have $-1$ at all vertices and all faces, but this is contradictory to the conditions of the problem.
It is also not possible to achieve the value $S = 10$. This would require $12$ ones to appear with a positive sign and two with a negative sign. If all vertices were assigned a positive one, then all faces would also be assigned a positive one. If exactly one vertex were assigned a negative one, then three faces would receive a negative sign. If, finally, exactly two vertices were assigned a negative sign, then some faces would also receive a negative sign. Therefore, the configuration "10 positives, 2 negatives" is not achievable in any way.
The range of possible values for $S$ is thus limited to the set

Of these six values, each can be achieved in various ways. Here are examples of configurations that realize these values:
If all vertices of the cube are assigned the number $+1$, then $S_1 = 8$, $S_2 = 6$, and $S = 14$.
If all vertices of the cube are assigned the number $-1$, then $S_1 = -8$, $S_2 = 6$, and $S = -2$.
If one vertex is assigned the number $+1$ and the rest $-1$, then $S_1 = -6$, $S_2 = 0$, and $S = -6$.
If one vertex is assigned the number $-1$ and the rest $+1$, then $S_1 = 6$, $S_2 = 0$, and $S = 6$.
If two opposite vertices of the cube are assigned the number $+1$ and the rest $-1$, then $S_1 = -4$, $S_2 = -6$, and $S = -10$.
If two opposite vertices of one face are assigned the number $-1$ and the rest of the vertices of the cube are assigned the number $+1$, then $S_1 = 4$, $S_2 = -2$, and $S = 2$.

problem:
XLVI OM - I - Zadanie 1

Wyznaczyć wszystkie pary $ (x,y) $ liczb naturalnych, dla których liczby $ \frac{x+1}{y} $ oraz $ \frac{y+1}{x} $ są naturalne.
solution:
Niech $ (x,y) $ będzie jedną z szukanych par. Liczby naturalne $ y \geq 1 $ oraz $ x \geq 1 $ są odpowiednio dzielnikami liczb $ x + 1 $ oraz $ y + 1 $. Zatem iloczyn $ xy $ jest dzielnikiem iloczynu $ (x + 1)(y+ 1) $, równego sumie $ xy + x + y + 1 $. Jest więc też dzielnikiem sumy $ x + y + 1 $, a zatem zachodzi nierówność $ xy \leq x + y + 1 $, czyli $ (x-1)(y -1) \leq 2 $. Wartość iloczynu $ (x-1)(y-1) $ może być w takim razie równa tylko $ 2 $, $ 1 $ lub $ 0 $.
W pierwszym przypadku jeden z czynników $ (x - 1) $ i $ (y- 1) $ jest równy $ 2 $, a drugi $ 1 $, czyli para $ (x,y) $ jest jedną z par $ (3,2) $ i $ (2,3) $.
W drugim przypadku mamy $ x -1 = y -1 = 1 $, czyli $ x = y = 2 $. Jednak para $ (x,y) = (2,2) $ nie spełnia warunku zadania (iloraz $ 3/2 $ nie jest liczbą naturalną).
W trzecim przypadku co najmniej jeden z czynników $ (x - 1) $ i $ (y- 1) $ jest zerem. Jeśli na przykład $ y - 1 = 0 $, czyli $ y = 1 $, to liczba $ x $, jako dzielnik sumy $ y + 1 = 2 $, musi być równa $ 1 $ lub $ 2 $; tak więc $ x = y = 1 $ lub $ y = 1 $, $ x = 2 $ lub - przez symetrię - $ x = 1 $, $ y = 2 $.
Rekapitulując, widzimy, że tylko następujące pary $ (x,y) $ mogą spełniać postawione warunki: $ (3,2) $, $ (2,3) $, $ (1,1) $, $ (2,1) $, $ (1,2) $ - i istotnie je spełniają; sprawdzenie jest natychmiastowe.

problem:
XIV OM - III - Task 2

In space, there are four distinct points $ A $, $ B $, $ C $, $ D $. Prove that the three segments connecting the midpoints of segments $ AB $ and $ CD $, $ AC $ and $ BD $, $ AD $ and $ BC $ have a common midpoint.
solution:
It is enough to prove that any two of the three segments mentioned have a common midpoint. We will show that the midpoint $H$ of segment $MN$ coincides with the midpoint $K$ of segment $PQ$, where $M$, $N$, $P$, $Q$ denote the midpoints of segments $AB$, $CD$, $AC$, $BD$ respectively.
Consider the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ as material points, assigning them masses equal to $1$. We will determine the center of mass (center of gravity) of the system of points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. The center of mass of the pair $A$, $B$ is the point $M$, and the center of mass of the pair $(C, D)$ is the point $N$. Assign masses equal to the sum of the masses of $A$ and $B$ and the sum of the masses of $C$ and $D$ to the points $M$ and $N$, i.e., masses equal to $2$. The center of mass of the quadruplet of points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ is the center of mass of the pair of points $M$, $N$ with equal masses, i.e., the midpoint $H$ of segment $MN$. But the center of mass of the quadruplet $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ is also the midpoint $K$ of segment $PQ$. Therefore, the points $H$ and $K$ coincide, q.e.d.
Note 1. It might seem that the proof conducted in method 2 is not a mathematical proof, as it uses the physical concept of the center of mass. However, this is not the case, as the center of mass can be defined in a purely mathematical way; we will briefly explain this. Assign positive numbers $m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_n$ to points in space $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$, which we will call their masses. The following theorem holds: There exists one and only one point $S$ such that

\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{SA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{SA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{SA_n} = 0 \]

Proof 1. Choose an arbitrary point $O$ in space. The point $S$ defined by the formula

\[ \overrightarrow{OS} = \frac{m_1 \overrightarrow{OA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{OA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{OA_n}}{m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_n} \]

satisfies condition (1). Indeed, from (2) it follows that

\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{SA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{SA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{SA_n} = m_1 (\overrightarrow{OA_1} - \overrightarrow{OS}) + m_2 (\overrightarrow{OA_2} - \overrightarrow{OS}) + \ldots + m_n (\overrightarrow{OA_n} - \overrightarrow{OS}) \]

but $\overrightarrow{OA_i} - \overrightarrow{OS} = \overrightarrow{SA_i}$ ($i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$), so

\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{SA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{SA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{SA_n} = m_1 \overrightarrow{SA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{SA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{SA_n} = 0 \]

2. There is only one point that satisfies condition (1). If for point $S$ the equality (1) holds, and for point $T$ the equality

\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{TA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{TA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{TA_n} = 0 \]

then subtracting (1) from (3), we get

\[ m_1 (\overrightarrow{TA_1} - \overrightarrow{SA_1}) + m_2 (\overrightarrow{TA_2} - \overrightarrow{SA_2}) + \ldots + m_n (\overrightarrow{TA_n} - \overrightarrow{SA_n}) = 0 \]

which simplifies to

\[ (m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_n) \overrightarrow{TS} = 0 \]

Since $m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_n > 0$, it follows from the above equality that $\overrightarrow{TS} = 0$, i.e., points $T$ and $S$ are identical.
The point $S$ uniquely defined by equation (1) is called the center of mass of the system of material points $A_1(m_1), A_2(m_2), \ldots, A_n(m_n)$.
Examples. a) The center of mass of the pair of points $A(1)$, $B(1)$ is the midpoint $S$ of segment $AB$, because from the equality $\overrightarrow{AS} = \overrightarrow{SB}$ it follows that $\overrightarrow{SA} = \overrightarrow{SB}$, hence $\overrightarrow{SA} + \overrightarrow{SB} = 0$.
b) The center of mass of the triplet of points $A(1)$, $B(1)$, $C(1)$ is the point of intersection $S$ of the medians of triangle $ABC$, because, according to the notation given in Fig. 27, $\overrightarrow{AS} = 2\overrightarrow{SM}$, so

\[ \overrightarrow{SA} + \overrightarrow{SB} + \overrightarrow{SC} = 0 \]

Divide the system of points $A_1(m_1), A_2(m_2), \ldots, A_n(m_n)$ with center of mass $S$ into two parts $A_1(m_1), \ldots, A_k(m_k)$ and $A_{k+1}(m_{k+1}), \ldots, A_n(m_n)$, with centers of mass $T$ and $U$ respectively. Then

\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{SA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{SA_2} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{SA_n} = 0 \]
\[ m_1 \overrightarrow{TA_1} + m_2 \overrightarrow{TA_2} + \ldots + m_k \overrightarrow{TA_k} = 0 \]
\[ m_{k+1} \overrightarrow{UA_{k+1}} + m_{k+2} \overrightarrow{UA_{k+2}} + \ldots + m_n \overrightarrow{UA_n} = 0 \]

Subtracting the second and third equations from the first, we get

\[ (m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_k) \overrightarrow{ST} + (m_{k+1} + m_{k+2} + \ldots + m_n) \overrightarrow{SU} = 0 \]

which simplifies to

\[ (m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_k) \overrightarrow{ST} = -(m_{k+1} + m_{k+2} + \ldots + m_n) \overrightarrow{SU} \]

and

\[ \overrightarrow{ST} = -\frac{m_{k+1} + m_{k+2} + \ldots + m_n}{m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_k} \overrightarrow{SU} \]

The point $S$ is therefore the center of mass of the pair of points $T$, $U$ with masses $m_1 + \ldots + m_k$ and $m_{k+1} + \ldots + m_n$. The following theorem holds:
The center of mass of a system of points does not change if the system is divided into parts and each part is replaced by its center of mass, assigning it a mass equal to the sum of the masses of the points in that part.
Using this theorem, we can determine the center of mass $S$ of the triplet of points $A(1)$, $B(1)$, $C(1)$ more simply than in the previous example b). Namely, $S$ (Fig. 27) is the center of mass of the pair $A(1)$ and $M(2)$, so it lies on the median $AM$ of triangle $ABC$; similarly, it lies on each of the other medians. Hence, the three medians of the triangle intersect at one point. Moreover,

\[ \overrightarrow{SA} + \overrightarrow{SB} + \overrightarrow{SC} = 0 \]

so the point $S$ divides the median in the ratio $2:1$.
Note 2. The assumption that the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are distinct can be omitted; in none of the previous proofs did we use this assumption, i.e., we proved a stronger theorem.

problem:
LV OM - II - Task 4

Determine all positive integers $ n $ that have exactly $ \sqrt{n} $ positive divisors.
solution:
The number $ n = 1 $ satisfies the conditions of the problem. Let's assume, for the rest of the solution, that $ n > 1 $.
From the conditions of the problem, it follows that $ n = k^2 $ for some positive integer $ k $. The number of positive divisors of $ n $ that are less than $ k $ is equal to the number of its divisors that are greater than $ k $. Indeed: to each divisor $ d < k $ of $ n $, there corresponds a divisor $ n/d $ of $ n $, which is greater than $ k $. Additionally, the number $ k $ itself is a divisor of $ n $, which implies that $ n $ has an odd number of divisors. Therefore, $ k $, and thus $ n $, is an odd number.
The problem thus reduces to finding such odd numbers $ n = k^2 $ $ (n > 1) $, for which the number of divisors less than $ k $ is equal to $ \frac{1}{2} (k-1) $.
Since $ k^2 $ is an odd number, no even number is a divisor of $ k^2 $. Therefore, for the number of divisors less than $ k $ of $ k^2 $ to be equal to $ \frac{1}{2} (k-1) $, every odd number less than $ k $ must be a divisor of $ k^2 $. In particular, $ k^2 $ must be divisible by $ k-2 $. Since $ k^2 = (k-2)(k+2)+4 $, the number $ k-2 $ is an odd divisor of 4. This means that $ k - 2 = 1 $, or $ k = 3 $.
We directly verify that the number $ n = 3^2 = 9 $ satisfies the conditions of the problem. Therefore, the sought numbers are $ n = 1 $ and $ n = 9 $.

problem:
XXVII OM - I - Zadanie 4

Samolot leci bez zatrzymywania się po najkrótszej drodze z Oslo do miasta $ X $ leżącego na równiku w Ameryce Południowej. Z Oslo startuje dokładnie w kierunku zachodnim. Wiedząc, że współrzędne geograficzne Oslo są : $ 59^{\circ}55 szerokości północnej i $ 10^{\circ}43 długości wschodniej, obliczyć współrzędne geograficzne miasta $ X $. Jakie to miasto? Obliczyć długość drogi samolotu z dokładnością do 100 km. Zakładamy, że Ziemia jest idealną kulą o długości równika 40 000 km oraz, że samolot leci na wysokości nie większej niż 10 km.
solution:
Najkrótsza droga na powierzchni kuli łącząca dwa punkty tej kuli jest łukiem koła wielkiego, tzn. łukiem okręgu, którego środkiem jest środek kuli. Zatem samolot leci po łuku koła wielkiego przechodzącego przez Oslo. Przy tym Oslo jest najbardziej na północ wysuniętym punktem tego koła wielkiego, ponieważ samolot startuje w kierunku zachodnim. Wynika stąd, że łuk o końcach w Oslo i mieście $ X $ jest czwartą częścią koła wielkiego. Długość tego łuku jest więc równa $ 10 000 $ km, a długości geograficzne miasta $ X $ i Osio różnią się o $ 90^\circ $. Zatem miasto $ X $ leży na równiku w punkcie mającym $ 79^\circ 17 długości zachodniej. Przekonujemy się za pomocą mapy, że jedynym większym miastem posiadającym lotnisko, w pobliżu tego punktu jest stolica Ekwadoru Quito.
Jeżeli uwzględnimy, że droga samolotu znajduje się nie na powierzchni ziemi, lecz np. $ 10 $ km nad ziemią, to otrzymamy, że długość tej drogi jest równa $ \frac{1}{4} [2\pi (R + 10)] = \frac{1}{4} 2\pi R + 5\pi \approx 10 000 + 15 $ km, gdzie $ R $ jest długością promienia Ziemi.
Uwaga: Szerokość geograficzna Oslo nie ma wpływu na rozwiązanie. Gdyby więc samolot startował z dowolnego punktu Ziemi, o długości geograficznej wschodniej $ 10^\circ 43 i spełnione były pozostałe warunki zadania, to wylądowałby w Quito po przebyciu drogi długości około $ 10 000 $ km.

problem:
XVIII OM - I - Problem 12

Prove that if points $ A, B, C, D, E $ in space are positioned such that












then points $ A, B, C, D, E $ lie on the same plane.
solution:
Assume that points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ satisfy conditions (1) and (2). First, we will show that no two of these points can coincide. It suffices to prove that point $A$ cannot coincide with $B$ or with $C$, as any other case of coinciding points can be reduced to one of these two by changing the labels.
a) If point $A$ coincided with point $B$, then by equality (1) all five points would coincide, and condition (2) would not be satisfied, as the angles mentioned in it would not exist.
b) If point $A$ coincided with point $C$, $\measuredangle ABC$ would be equal to $0$, so by (2) points $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$ would lie on the same line $p$. From the equalities $\measuredangle BAD = 0$ and $\measuredangle EAB = 0$, it would then follow that points $B$, $D$, $E$ lie on $p$ on the same side of point $A$, and from the equality $\measuredangle DEA = 0$ it would follow that point $D$ lies between $A$ and $E$, and according to the equality $\measuredangle ADE = 0$ point $E$ must lie between $A$ and $D$. Given this contradiction, case b) cannot occur.
From the equality of all sides and all angles of the pentagon $ABCDE$, it follows that all its diagonals are equal. For example, $AC = BD$, since triangles $ABC$ and $BCD$ are congruent. Let $a$ denote the length of the sides, $b$ the length of the diagonals of the pentagon, and the symbol $O(r)$ the surface of a sphere with center $O$ and radius $r$.
Let us choose three non-adjacent vertices of the pentagon, for example, $A$, $B$, $D$, and consider the position of the remaining vertices $C$ and $E$ relative to $A$, $B$, and $D$. Point $C$ is the common point of spheres $A(b)$, $B(a)$, and $D(a)$, and point $E$ is the common point of spheres $B(b)$, $A(a)$, and $D(a)$, which arise from the three previous spheres when they are transformed by symmetry with respect to the plane bisector of segment $AB$. In this transformation, point $C$ corresponds to the common point $E$ of spheres $A(a)$, $B(b)$, and $D(a)$. Therefore, one of the following two cases occurs:
a) Point $E$ coincides with point $E$, i.e., $C$ and $E$ lie symmetrically with respect to the plane bisector of segment $AB$; diagonal $CE$ is then parallel to line $AB$ and points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie in the same plane;
b) Point $E$, common to spheres $A(a)$, $B(b)$, and $D(a)$, is different from their common point $E$; then $E$ is the point symmetric to $E$ with respect to the plane $ABD$ of the centers of these spheres, and thus $E$ is the point symmetric to $C$ with respect to the bisector $DM$ of segment $AB$. Diagonal $CE$ then intersects line $DM$ at some point $N$. Cases a) and b) can, of course, occur simultaneously.
Two similar possibilities exist for each diagonal of the pentagon $ABCDE$. If case a) holds for any two diagonals, then there are two different sets of four vertices of the pentagon, each lying in the same plane, so all vertices lie in the same plane.
If, however, case b) holds for at least three diagonals of the pentagon, then two of these diagonals emanate from the same vertex; let these be, for example, $CE$ and $CA$; then $CE$ intersects the bisector $DM$ of segment $AB$ at some point $N$, and $CA$ intersects the bisector $BK$ of segment $DE$ at some point $L$. In this case, points $D$, $E$, $C$, $K$, $M$, $N$ lie in the same plane; the same is true for points $A$, $B$, $C$, $K$, $L$, $M$. Therefore, all these points lie in the same plane.
Note. The above solution to the problem can be stated more simply if we use the properties of isometries, i.e., transformations that do not change the distances between points. Let us associate points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ with points $B$, $A$, $E$, $D$, respectively. Given the equality of the sides and the equality of the diagonals of the pentagon, this transformation of the first set of points to the second is an isometry. It can be extended to an isometric transformation of the entire space. It is known that an isometry of space in which points $A$, $B$, $D$ correspond to points $B$, $A$, $D$ is a symmetry with respect to the plane bisector of segment $AB$, or a symmetry with respect to the bisector $MD$ of this segment. Therefore, $E$ is the point symmetric to point $C$ with respect to this plane or with respect to the line $MD$. The rest of the proof remains unchanged.

The set $ A $ of remainders when dividing $ n-r_1, n-r_2, \ldots, n-r_k $ by $ m $ contains more than $ \displaystyle \frac{m}{2} $ elements. Similarly, the set $ B $ of remainders when dividing $ r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_k $ by $ m $ also contains more than $ \displaystyle \frac{m}{2} $ elements. Sets $ A $ and $ B $ are contained within the $ m $-element set of all remainders when dividing integers by $ m $.
Therefore, sets $ A $ and $ B $ are not disjoint, meaning that for some $ i $ and $ j $, the number $ r_i $ gives the same remainder when divided by $ m $ as the number $ n-r_j $. The difference between these numbers, equal to $ r_i + r_j - n $, is thus divisible by $ m $.

First, note that if the angles of the tetrahedron $SABC$ are acute, then a plane perpendicular to any edge of the tetrahedron at a point different from $S$ intersects the other edges at points different from $S$, so the section of the tetrahedron by this plane is a triangle. For example, a plane passing through point $M$ on edge $SA$, perpendicular to $SA$, intersects edge $SB$ at point $N$ determined by the equation $SN = \frac{SM}{\cos \measuredangle ASB}$.
Let the plane $\alpha$ intersect the edges $SA$, $SB$, $SC$ of the tetrahedron at points $M$, $N$, $P$ (different from $S$), respectively. We will prove that if this plane is perpendicular to one of the edges, then $\measuredangle NMP$ is a right angle. When $\alpha \bot SA$, this is obvious, as $\measuredangle NMP$ is then the linear angle of a right dihedral angle. When $\alpha \bot SB$, then $\alpha \bot \textrm{plane } SAB$, and since $\textrm{plane } SAC \bot \textrm{plane } SAB$, the line of intersection of planes $\alpha$ and $SAC$, i.e., the line $MP$ is perpendicular to plane $SAB$; thus, line $MP$ is perpendicular to line $MN$ lying in plane $SAB$, so $\measuredangle NMP = 90^\circ$. In the case where $\alpha \bot SC$, the proof is analogous (Fig. 13).

problem:
XXVI - II - Problem 6

Let $ f(x) $ and $ g(x) $ be polynomials with integer coefficients. Prove that if for every integer value $ n $ the number $ g(n) $ is divisible by the number $ f(n) $, then $ g(x) = f(x) \cdot h(x) $, where $ h(x) $ is a polynomial. Show by example that the coefficients of the polynomial $ h(x) $ do not have to be integers.
solution:
In the solution to the preparatory task D of Series III, we proved that if polynomials $f$ and $g$ have integer coefficients, $\mathrm{st} f \leq \mathrm{st} g$, and for every natural number $n$, the number $f(n)$ is a divisor of the number $g(n)$, then there exists an integer $c$ such that $g(x) = c \cdot f(x)$. Therefore, either $\mathrm{st} f = \mathrm{st} g$ (when $c \ne 0$), or $g$ is the zero polynomial (when $c = 0$). It is sufficient to consider the case where $\mathrm{st} g > \mathrm{st} f$.

Let $h$ and $r$ be the quotient and remainder, respectively, of the division of the polynomial $g$ by $f$. Then

Polynomials $h$ and $r$ have rational coefficients. Let $a$ be the least common denominator of the coefficients of polynomials $h$ and $r$. Then the polynomials $H = ah$ and $R = ar$ have integer coefficients, and multiplying equation (1) by $a$ on both sides, we obtain

Therefore, the polynomial $ag$ also has integer coefficients.
For every natural number $n$, the number $f(n)$ is, of course, a divisor of the number $ag(n)$. Therefore, by (2), the number $f(n)$ is a divisor of the number $R(n) = ag(n) - H(n) \cdot f(n)$ for $n=1,2, \ldots$. Since $\mathrm{st} R = \mathrm{st} r < \mathrm{st} f$, it follows from the initial remark in this solution that $R = ar$ is the zero polynomial. Therefore, $r$ is also the zero polynomial, and from (1) we obtain $g = hf$.

We will show by example that the coefficients of the polynomial $h$ may not be integers. Let $f(x) = 2$, $g(x) = x^2 + x$. For every integer $n$, the number $g(n) = n(n + 1)$ is even, because one of the numbers $n$ and $n+1$ is even. Therefore, the number $f(n) = 2$ is a divisor of the number $g(n)$ for $n = 1, 2, \ldots$. The coefficients of the polynomial $\displaystyle h(x) = \frac{g(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{1}{2} x^2 + \frac{1}{2} x$ are, of course, not integers.

problem:
XIV OM - III - Task 6

Through the vertex of a trihedral angle, in which no edge is perpendicular to the opposite face, a line perpendicular to the opposite edge is drawn in the plane of each face. Prove that the three obtained lines lie in one plane.
solution:
Let $SM$, $SN$, and $SP$ denote the lines perpendicular to the edges $SA$, $SB$, and $SC$ of the tetrahedron $SABC$ and lying in the planes of the faces $BSC$, $CSA$, and $ASB$, respectively. Given that no edge of the tetrahedron is perpendicular to the opposite face, the lines $SM$, $SN$, and $SP$ are uniquely determined.
Let $\lambda$, $\mu$, and $\nu$ denote the planes passing through the edges $SA$, $SB$, and $SC$ and perpendicular to the lines $SM$, $SN$, and $SP$, respectively. The planes $\lambda$, $\mu$, and $\nu$ are perpendicular to the planes $SBC$, $CSA$, and $ASB$, respectively, and therefore they have a common line $d$ (see problem 18). Since $SM$ is perpendicular to the plane $\lambda$ containing the line $d$, we have $SM \bot d$ and similarly $SN \bot d$, $SP \bot d$.
The lines $SM$, $SN$, and $SP$ thus lie in a single plane perpendicular to the line $d$ (Fig. 33).

problem:
XXXI - I - Problem 7

On a sphere of radius 1, 13 points are chosen. Prove that among these points, there are two whose distance is less than $ \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} $.
solution: Consider a regular dodecahedron inscribed in a sphere bounded by a given sphere. Among the radii of the sphere connecting certain points with the center, two of them intersect one face of the dodecahedron. The angle formed by these radii is no greater than the angle formed by the radii passing through two non-adjacent vertices of the face of the dodecahedron, and thus the distance between the mentioned two points does not exceed the length of the diagonal of the face of the dodecahedron. Let us choose one diagonal on each face of the dodecahedron as shown in Fig. 2. By the symmetry of the dodecahedron, these diagonals are the edges of a cube inscribed in the dodecahedron (and thus a cube inscribed in the sphere circumscribed around the dodecahedron). Since the diagonal of a cube with edge length $a$ has a length of $a\sqrt{3}$, and the diagonal of the cube is the diameter of the sphere circumscribed around it, the edge length $a$ of the cube inscribed in the considered dodecahedron satisfies $a\sqrt{3} = 2$, i.e., $a = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$. This number is also the length of the diagonal of the face of the dodecahedron, and thus, as we have stated, the distance between certain two of the thirteen points on the sphere does not exceed this value.

problem:
XX OM - III - Problem 5

For what values of $ n $ does there exist a polyhedron with $ n $ edges?
solution:
A polyhedron with $ n $ edges exists if and only if $ n \geq 6 $ and $ n \ne 7 $.
Proof. a) An example of a polyhedron with $ n = 2m $ ($ m \geq 3 $) edges is a pyramid whose base is a polygon with $ m $ sides.
b) An example of a polyhedron with $ n = 2m+1 $ ($ m \geq 4 $) edges can be obtained using a pyramid with $ 2(m-1) $ edges. For this purpose, we draw a plane through the midpoints $ M $, $ N $, $ P $ of three edges of the pyramid that emanate from the same vertex $ S $ of the base of the pyramid. The solid that results from discarding the tetrahedron $ SMNP $ from the pyramid is a polyhedron that has $ 3 $ more edges than the pyramid, i.e., it has $ 2m-2+3 = 2m+1 $ edges. In this construction, $ m $ can be any number satisfying the condition $ m-1 \geq 3 $, i.e., the condition $ m \geq 4 $.
c) There is no polyhedron with $ 7 $ edges. This can be proven as follows. If any face of the polyhedron is not a triangle, i.e., has $ 4 $ or more sides, then the polyhedron has at least $ 8 $ edges, because from each vertex of that face, besides the two sides of the face, at least one more edge emanates, and all these edges are different.
If, on the other hand, all faces of the polyhedron are triangles, and the number of faces is $ s $, then the number of edges $ k = \frac{3s}{2} $, so the number $ k $ is divisible by $ 3 $, hence $ k \ne 7 $.
d) There is no polyhedron with fewer than $ 6 $ edges, because every polyhedron has at least $ 4 $ vertices, and from each vertex at least $ 3 $ edges emanate, so the number of edges is greater than or equal to $ \frac{4 \cdot 3}{2} = 6 $.

problem:
XXX OM - I - Task 3

Numbers $ a, b, c, d, e $ are positive rational numbers. Prove that there exist rational numbers $ u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n $ and non-negative rational numbers $ w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n $, such that
solution:
Let $ A $ be the set of all non-zero polynomials with rational coefficients. A number $ \alpha $ is called algebraic if it is a root of some polynomial belonging to $ A $.
First, we will prove a few simple properties of algebraic numbers.
If $ \alpha $ is an algebraic number, then $ \alpha + 1 $ is also an algebraic number. If $ f \in A $ and $ f(\alpha) = 0 $, then the polynomial $ g $ defined by $ g(x) = f(x - 1) $ also belongs to $ A $ and $ g(\alpha + 1) = f(\alpha) = 0 $.
Next, we will show that if $ \alpha $ is an algebraic number, then $ \alpha^2 $ is an algebraic number.
Assume that there exists a polynomial $ f \in A $ such that $ f(\alpha) = 0 $. By moving all terms containing $ \alpha $ in even powers to one side and those in odd powers to the other side, and squaring both sides, we obtain an equation of the form $ f_1 (\alpha^2) = f_2(\alpha^2) $, where $ f_1 $ and $ f_2 $ are different polynomials with rational coefficients. Therefore, $ f_1 - f_2 \in A $ and $ (f_1 - f_2) (\alpha^2) = 0 $. Hence, $ \alpha^2 $ is algebraic.
Next, we will prove that if $ \alpha $ is an algebraic number and $ \omega $ is a positive rational number, then the number $ \alpha \cdot \sqrt[4]{\omega} $ is algebraic. As we have shown, the number $ \alpha^2 $, and thus the number $ \alpha^4 = (\alpha^2)^2 $, is algebraic, meaning there is an equation of the form

\[
c_k \alpha^{4k} + c_{k-1} \alpha^{4(k-1)} + \cdots + c_1 \alpha^4 + c_0 = 0
\]

where $ c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_k $ are rational numbers and $ c_k \ne 0 $.
By setting

\[
g(x) = c_k x^{4k} + c_{k-1} x^{4(k-1)} + \cdots + c_1 x^4 + c_0
\]

we easily see that $ g \in A $ and $ g(\alpha \sqrt[4]{\omega}) = 0 $. Therefore, the number $ \alpha \sqrt[4]{\omega} $ is algebraic.
Finally, we will show that if the number $ \alpha $ is algebraic and the number $ u $ is a positive rational number, then the number $ \alpha + \sqrt[4]{u} $ is algebraic.
This follows from the easily verifiable equation

\[
(\alpha + \sqrt[4]{u})^4 = \alpha^4 + 4\alpha^3 \sqrt[4]{u} + 6\alpha^2 \sqrt{u} + 4\alpha u^{3/4} + u
\]

and the previous part of the proof.
It follows that the number $ \beta = \sqrt[4]{a} + \sqrt[4]{b} + \sqrt[4]{c} + \sqrt[4]{d} + \sqrt[4]{e} $ given in the problem is algebraic. Therefore, there is an equation of the form

\[
b_m \beta^m + b_{m-1} \beta^{m-1} + \cdots + b_1 \beta + b_0 = 0
\]

where $ b_0, b_1, \ldots, b_m $ are rational numbers and $ b_m \ne 0 $. Since $ \beta \ne 0 $, we can assume that $ b_0 \ne 0 $, and by dividing both sides of the last equation by $ b_0 $, we can assume that $ b_0 = 1 $. Thus, from this equation, we obtain that

\[
\beta^m + b_{m-1} \beta^{m-1} + \cdots + b_1 \beta + 1 = 0
\]

From the definition of the number $ \beta $, it follows that the right-hand side of the last equation can be written as a sum of fourth roots of certain positive rational numbers, with rational coefficients.
Note. The following theorem is true: *The sum, difference, product, and quotient of algebraic numbers is an algebraic number*. From this theorem, it immediately follows that the left-hand side of the equation given in the problem is an algebraic number.

Prove that in any convex pentagon, all of whose sides have length \( a \), an equilateral triangle with sides of length \( a \) can be placed.
solution:
om33_1r_img_2.jpg
Let $ABCDE$ be any convex pentagon whose all sides have length $a$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $\overline{AC}$ is the diagonal of maximum length. We will show that an equilateral triangle with side length $a$ can be placed inside the quadrilateral $ACDE$. For this purpose, we will prove two lemmas.
Lemma 1. $|\measuredangle AEC| > 60^\circ, \ |\measuredangle ADC| > 60^\circ.$
Proof. $\overline{AC}$ is the base of an isosceles triangle, where the angle between the legs is greater than $60^\circ$ (this angle is at least $\frac{1}{5} 540^\circ = 108^\circ$, since $\measuredangle ABC$ is the largest angle in the pentagon).
Therefore, we obtain the inequality $AC > a$. This follows from the theorem stating that in a triangle, the side opposite the larger angle is longer. By assumption, we get the inequality $AC \geq CE$ and $AC \geq AD$. Therefore, $\overline{AC}$ is the side of maximum length in both triangle $ACE$ and triangle $ACD$. Since neither of these triangles is equilateral ($AC > a$, $AE = CD = a$), we have $|\measuredangle AEC| > 60^\circ$ and $|\measuredangle ADC| > 60^\circ$.
Lemma 2. $|\measuredangle EAC| \geq 60^\circ$ or $|\measuredangle ACD| \geq 60^\circ$.
Proof. Suppose that $|\measuredangle EAC| < 60^\circ$ and $|\measuredangle ACD| < 60^\circ$. Extending the sides $\overline{AE}$ and $\overline{CD}$, we obtain triangle $ACF$, in which $|\measuredangle APC| > 60^\circ$, so $AC > AP$, $AC > CP$. Since $AC$ is a diagonal of the pentagon $ABCDE$, we have $AC < 2a$. Therefore, the inequalities (*) $AP < 2a$, $CP < 2a$ hold.
om33_1r_img_3.jpg
Let $F$ and $G$ be the midpoints of sides $\overline{AP}$ and $\overline{CP}$, respectively. The segment $\overline{FG}$ connecting the midpoints of sides of triangle $ACP$ has length $\frac{1}{2} AC$. Therefore, $DG < a$.
From the condition $AE = CD = a$ and the inequalities (*), it follows that $E \in \overline{FP}$, $D \in \overline{GP}$. The segment $\overline{ED}$ is not longer than the longest side $\overline{FG}$ of triangle $FGP$. Therefore,

We have obtained a contradiction by assuming that each of the angles $EAC$, $ACD$ has a measure less than $60^\circ$. Therefore, at least one of the inequalities $|\measuredangle EAC| \geq 60^\circ$ or $|\measuredangle ACD| > 60^\circ$ holds.
We can now show that the quadrilateral $ACDE$ contains an equilateral triangle with side length $a$. Suppose that $|\measuredangle EAC| \geq 60^\circ$ (the reasoning is analogous in the case where $|\measuredangle ACD| \geq 60^\circ$). In triangle $AEC$, the base $AE$ has length $a$, and both angles at the base are greater than $60^\circ$. An equilateral triangle with base $\overline{AE}$ is contained in this triangle.

problem:
XXXVIII OM - I - Problem 11

Prove that a sphere can be illuminated by four point light sources placed outside it, but cannot be illuminated by three.
solution:
The reasoning is based on the observation that the smaller of the two hemispheres into which any plane dividing the interior of a sphere but not passing through its center can be illuminated by a single point light source placed outside the sphere; however, such a source cannot illuminate the entire hemisphere.
We inscribe a tetrahedron in the sphere so that the center of the sphere lies inside the tetrahedron. Let $ S_1 $, $ S_2 $, $ S_3 $, $ S_4 $ be the faces of this tetrahedron. The plane of the face $ S_i $ divides the sphere into two hemispheres; the smaller of these is denoted by $ C_i $ ($ i = 1, 2, 3, 4 $). The sets $ C_i $ cover the entire surface of the sphere; if $ P $ is any point on the surface of the sphere, then the segment connecting $ P $ to the center of the sphere intersects one of the faces $ S_i $, and thus $ P $ belongs to the corresponding hemisphere $ C_i $. As we noted, each hemisphere $ C_i $ can be illuminated by a point light source. Therefore, four sources are sufficient to illuminate the entire sphere.
To show that three such sources are not sufficient, note that any arc of a great circle contained in the area illuminated by a single light source is shorter than a semicircle. It follows that at least three point light sources outside the sphere are necessary to illuminate any great circle. Suppose now that the sphere is illuminated by three such sources $ A $, $ B $, $ C $. There exists a great circle lying outside the range of light from point $ A $. The entire circle is thus illuminated from points $ B $ and $ C $, contradicting the previous conclusion. This proves the second part of the thesis.

problem:
XXV - I - Problem 9

A set of documents has been divided into $ n $ parts, each given to one of $ n $ people, each of whom has a phone. Prove that for $ n \geq 4 $, it suffices to have $ 2n - 4 $ phone calls, after which each of the $ n $ people knows the content of all the documents.
solution:
For four people $ A $, $ B $, $ C $, $ D $, four conversations suffice. Specifically, first $ A $ and $ B $, as well as $ C $ and $ D $, inform each other about the documents they possess. Then $ A $ and $ C $, as well as $ B $ and $ D $, exchange the information they have.
If the number of people $ n $ exceeds $ 4 $, we select some $ 4 $ people $ A $, $ B $, $ C $, $ D $. First, each of the remaining $ n - 4 $ people informs $ A $ about the content of the documents they possess. Then the people $ A $, $ B $, $ C $, $ D $ have $ 4 $ conversations among themselves (as above) and exchange the information they have. Finally, each of the remaining $ n - 4 $ people calls $ A $ and learns from him about the content of all the documents.
A total of $ (n - 4) + 4 + (n - 4) = 2n - 4 $ conversations have been conducted, and each person knows the content of all the documents.

problem:
XXXV OM - III - Task 5

A regular hexagon with side length 1 is contained within the union of six circles, each having a diameter of 1. Prove that no vertex of the hexagon belongs to two of these circles.
solution:
Suppose a certain vertex of a hexagon belongs to two circles. If neither of these two circles contained any other vertex of the hexagon, then each of the remaining five vertices would belong to one of the remaining four circles. It follows that there is a circle $ k_1 $ containing two vertices of the hexagon. The diameter of this circle is a side of the hexagon (say $ \overline{AB} $). In any neighborhood of each of the points $ A $ and $ B $, there are points not belonging to the circle $ k_1 $ but belonging to the hexagon. Therefore, the point $ A $ is a point of some circle different from $ k_1 $, similarly, the point $ B $ is a point of another circle. Thus, the six vertices of the hexagon belong to five circles different from $ k_1 $. Therefore, there are two vertices belonging to a circle $ k_2 $, which is one of the five circles. Circles $ k_1 $ and $ k_2 $ cover two sides of the hexagon, with no more than one vertex having the property that some neighborhood of it is covered by the sum of circles $ k_1 $ and $ k_2 $. The remaining five vertices belong to the remaining four circles. Therefore, among these circles, there is a circle containing two vertices. We continue this reasoning by stating that each circle contains two vertices of the hexagon and, therefore, its diameter is a side of the hexagon. But then the center of the hexagon does not belong to any of these six circles, because its distance from the center of a side is $ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $ and is greater than the radius of each of the circles.
It follows that if the considered circles cover the hexagon, then no vertex belongs to two circles.

Let $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$ denote the circumcircles of triangles $ANP$, $BPM$, and $CMN$, respectively. Circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ have a common point $P$, so they have another common point $Q$, or they are tangent at point $P$. One of the following cases holds:
1. Circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ intersect at points $P$ and $Q$, and point $Q$ lies on the opposite side of line $AB$ from point $C$ (Fig. 15).
Line $PQ$ does not intersect any of the segments $AN$ and $BM$, as all its points, except for segment $PQ$, lie outside circles $k_1$ and $k_2$; therefore, it intersects segment $MN$ at some point $K$, so angle $NQM$ is the sum of angles $NQP$ and $PQM$.
On circle $k_1$, the points under consideration lie in the order $A$, $N$, $P$, $Q$, and the pair of points $A$, $Q$ does not separate the pair of points $N$, $P$, so the inscribed angles $NAP$ and $NQP$ are equal:

\[
\angle NAP = \angle NQP
\]

Similarly,

\[
\angle MBP = \angle MQP
\]

Therefore,

\[
\angle NQM = \angle NQP + \angle PQM = \angle NAP + \angle MBP
\]

Notice that points $Q$ and $P$ lie on the same side of line $MN$, while points $P$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of this line; hence, points $Q$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $NM$. 
Therefore, points $C$, $N$, $Q$, $M$ are vertices of a quadrilateral in which the sum of the angles at opposite vertices $Q$ and $C$ is $180^\circ$. This implies that points $C$, $N$, $Q$, $M$ lie on a circle, i.e., point $Q$ lies on circle $k_3$, and is thus a common point of circles $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$.
2. Circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ are tangent at point $P$. The previous proof applies to this case as well, with the common tangent $PK$ of circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ (Fig. 16) replacing the common secant.
3. Circles $k_1$ and $k_2$ intersect at points $P$ and $Q$, and point $Q$ lies on the same side of line $AB$ as point $C$.
a) If point $Q$ lies on ray $BC$ or $AC$, then it coincides with point $M$ or $N$, respectively, and is thus a common point of circles $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$.
b) If point $Q$ lies inside triangle $ABC$ (Fig. 17), then segments $QM$, $QN$, and $QP$ divide the triangle into three parts: quadrilateral $APQN$ inscribed in circle $k_1$, quadrilateral $PQMB$ inscribed in circle $k_2$, and quadrilateral $NQMC$; the following equalities hold:

\[
\angle NAP = \angle NQP
\]
\[
\angle MBP = \angle MQP
\]

Therefore, in quadrilateral $NQMC$, the sum of the angles at vertices $Q$ and $C$ is equal to the sum of $\angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ$. Points $N$, $Q$, $M$, $C$ lie on a circle, so point $Q$ is a common point of circles $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$.
c) If point $Q$ lies outside triangle $ABC$, it cannot lie inside the external angle at vertex $C$, as this angle contains no points of circles $k_1$ or $k_2$. Therefore, point $Q$ lies inside one of the angles $ABC$ and $CAB$, say inside angle $ABC$ (Fig. 18).
On circle $k_1$, the points under consideration lie in the order $A$, $P$, $N$, $Q$, and the pair of points $(P, N)$ does not separate the pair of points $(A, Q)$, so, as in case 1,

\[
\angle NAP = \angle NQP
\]

On circle $k_2$, the points lie in the order $Q$, $P$, $B$, $M$, and the pair of points $(Q, B)$ separates the pair of points $(P, M)$, so

\[
\angle MBP = \angle MQP
\]

Points $N$ and $M$ lie on the same side of line $PQ$, since points $A$ and $N$, as well as points $A$ and $B$, lie on opposite sides of line $PQ$, and points $B$ and $M$ lie on the same side of line $PQ$. Note that $\angle PQN < \angle PQM$, since $\angle A < 180^\circ - \angle B$; hence, ray $QN$ lies within angle $PQM$ and the following equality holds:

\[
\angle NQM = \angle NQP + \angle PQM = \angle NAP + \angle MBP
\]

Points $Q$ and $C$ lie on the same side of line $MN$. Indeed, ray $QN$ lies, as shown above, within angle $PQM$, so it intersects one of the segments $PB$ and $BM$ at some point $K$. Points $Q$ and $K$ lie on opposite sides of line $MN$, and points $K$ and $C$ also lie on opposite sides of this line, so points $Q$ and $C$ lie on the same side of line $MN$. Therefore, from the previous equality, we conclude that points $Q$, $N$, $M$, $C$ lie on a circle. Point $Q$ is thus a common point of circles $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$.

Prove that if triangle $ DEF $ is equilateral, then triangle $ ABC $ is also equilateral.
solution:
Let's denote the common value of the given ratios by $ \lambda $:




We assume that triangle $ DEF $ is equilateral. We will present a proof of the regularity of triangle $ ABC $, encouraging the Reader to find other methods of solving (e.g., through vector calculations; using complex numbers; by comparing different angles; etc.).
We will use the concept and properties of affine transformations (see, e.g., J. Bednarczuk, The Charm of Affine Transformations, Warsaw 1978).
There exists an affine transformation $ h $ that maps triangle $ ABC $ to a certain equilateral triangle $ A. An affine transformation preserves collinearity of points and the ratio of division of a segment. Therefore, points $ D, $ E, $ F $ lie on the sides $ B, $ C, $ A $ of triangle $ A $ and divide them in the same ratios as points $ D $, $ E $, $ F $ divide the sides of triangle $ ABC $ - that is, in equal ratios. Hence, we conclude that triangle $ D $ is equilateral.
There thus exists a similarity $ g $ such that $ g(D) = D, $ g(E)= E, $ g(F)=F. The images of points $ D $, $ E $, $ F $ are the same in both of these transformations ($ g $ and $ h $). But an affine transformation is uniquely determined by its values at any three non-collinear points. This means that the transformations $ g $ and $ h $ under consideration are the same transformation - that is, $ h $ is a similarity.
The image of triangle $ ABC $ under the transformation $ h $ is the equilateral triangle $ A. Since $ h $ is a similarity, triangle $ ABC $ is also equilateral.

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $P$ and $B$ are chosen on the opposite sides $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{GD}$, and points $Q$ and $S$ are chosen on the opposite sides $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BC}$ such that $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{DR}{RC} = a$, $\frac{AQ}{QD} = \frac{BS}{SC} = b$. Prove that if $O$ is the intersection point of segments $\overline{PR}$ and $\overline{QS}$, then $\frac{PO}{OR} = b$ and $\frac{QO}{OS} = a$.
solution:
We place masses of $1$, $a$, $ab$, and $b$ at points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ respectively, and calculate the center of mass $T$ of the system $U$ composed of these four points.
From the conditions of the problem, it follows that the centers of mass of the systems $\{A, B\}$ and $\{C, D\}$ are the points $P$ and $R$ respectively. The point $ A_2 $ symmetric to $ A_1 $ with respect to the line $ s $ also belongs to figure $ F $; we can, of course, choose the notation so that the point $ A_2 $ is on the opposite side of the line $ s $ from point $ O $. Consider two more points of figure $ F $, namely the point $ A_3 $ symmetric to $ A_2 $ with respect to point $ O $, and the point $ A_4 $ symmetric to $ A_3 $ with respect to the line $ s $. Let $ R $ denote the intersection of the line $ A_3A_4 $ with the axis $ s $, and $ U $ - the intersection of the line $ A_2S $ with the line $ A_3A_4 $.

It turns out that if there is a point on figure $ F $ at a distance $ a $ from the axis $ s $, then there is also a point on it at a distance $ a + 2d $ from this axis. By induction, we conclude from this that there is a point on figure $ F $ at a distance $ a + 2nd $ from the axis $ s $, where $ n $ is any natural number. In this case, figure $ F $ cannot have finite dimensions (i.e., it cannot be bounded), contrary to the assumption. The negation of the thesis of our theorem has led to a contradiction, so the theorem has been proven.

Since the expression $\frac{1}{2} (n^2 + n + 2)$ has for $n = 1$ the value $\frac{1}{2} (1^2 + 1 + 2) = 2$, the theorem is true in the case $n = 1$. Positive numbers $ a $, $ b $, $ c $, $ d $ satisfy the system of equations






Prove that $ a = b = c = d $.
solution:
Let $ \langle p,q\rangle $ be the smallest interval containing the numbers $ a $, $ b $, $ c $, $ d $. Then at least one of the numbers $ d $, $ a $, $ b $ coincides with an end (left or right) of the interval $ \langle p,q\rangle $.
If $ d=p $, then by the first equality we have $ 3d^3 = a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \geq 3d^3 $. This implies that each of the numbers $ a $, $ b $, $ c $ must be equal to $ d $, i.e., $ a = b = c = d $. If, however, $ d = q $, we get $ 3d^3 = a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \leq 3d^3 $, which similarly gives $ a = b = c = d $.
Similarly, using the second or third equation, we prove that $ a=b=c=d $ when one of the numbers $ a $, $ b $ is equal to $ p $ or $ q $. This completes the solution of the problem.
