Given is a convex polygon with an even number of sides. Each side of the polygon has a length of 2 or 3, and the number of sides of each of these lengths is even. Prove that there exist two vertices of the polygon that divide its perimeter into two parts of equal length.
solution:
Let the number of sides of the polygon be $2n$. Denote the vertices of the polygon in order as $A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots, A_{2n}$. For $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 2n$ let

\[
f(i) = \text{the difference in the lengths of the parts into which the perimeter of the polygon is divided by the points } A_i \text{ and } A_{i+n}
\]

where $A_{k+2n} = A_k$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots, 2n-1$. In other words, $f(i)$ is the difference in the lengths of the parts into which the perimeter of the polygon is divided by the points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$.
For $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 2n$, the number $f(i)$ is an even integer, and

\[
f(i) = -f(i + n).
\]

Therefore, the sequence of numbers

\[
f(1), f(2), \ldots, f(2n)
\]

consists of even numbers, and the difference between consecutive terms is no more than 2. Hence, there exists an $i$ such that $f(i) = 0$, which is what we needed to prove.

If we choose a point $ D_1 $ arbitrarily on the extension of diagonal $ BD $—such that the segment $ x = BD_1 $ is shorter than $ a + d $ and $ b + c $—then we can construct (as indicated in Fig. 26) a specified quadrilateral $ A_1BC_1D_1 $ with sides $ a $, $ b $, $ c $, $ d $. In this case, $ A_1 > A $ and $ C_1 > C $.
As point $ D_1 $ moves away from point $ D $, angles $ A_1 $ and $ C_1 $ increase, and we can find a position of point $ D_1 $ such that $ A_1 + C_1 > 180^\circ $. If, for example, $ a + d < b + c $, it suffices to construct a triangle $ A_1BD_1 $ in which $ A_1 = 180^\circ - C $; then $ A_1 + C_1 = 180^\circ - C + C_1 > 180^\circ $.
The sum $ A_1 + C_1 $ is a continuous function of the variable $ x = BD_1 $, which can be easily verified by calculating angles $ A_1 $ and $ C_1 $ from triangles $ A_1BD_1 $ and $ BC_1D_1 $ in terms of $ x $ and $ a $, $ b $, $ c $, $ d $. As point $ D_1 $ moves along the extension of segment $ BD $ starting from point $ D $, this function transitions from values less than $ 180^\circ $ to values greater than $ 180^\circ $, so it must pass through the value $ 180^\circ $, i.e., there exists a point $ D_1 $ such that quadrilateral $ A_1BC_1D_1 $ is cyclic, which was to be proved.
The above theorem b) is a special case of Cramer's theorem (Swiss mathematician, 1704 - 1752):
Among all polygons with given sides $ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n $ (where $ n \geq 3 $), the one with the largest area is the one that can be inscribed in a circle.

XLI OM - I - Problem 4

From a chessboard with dimensions $8 \times 80$ squares, colored in the usual way, two squares of different colors have been removed. Prove that the remaining $62$ squares can be covered by 31 rectangles of dimensions $2 \times 1$.
solution:
Let $ R $ be the smallest rectangle containing both removed fields $ A $ and $ B $. Since these fields are of different colors and lie in opposite corners of the rectangle $ R $, the lengths of the sides of $ R $ are natural numbers of different parity. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the rectangle $ R $ consists of $ k $ vertical rows and $ l $ horizontal rows, where $ k $ is an even number and $ l $ is an odd number (see Figure 2).
We will show that the rectangle $ R $ without fields $ A $ and $ B $ can be covered with tiles of dimensions $ 2 \times 1 $. When $ l = 1 $, we have to cover a strip of length $ k - 2 $ and width $ 1 $; the way to cover it is obvious. When $ l > 1 $, then each of the extreme vertical rows (without field $ A $, respectively $ B $) has dimensions $ (l-1) \times 1 $ and, due to the oddness of $ l $, can be covered with $ 2 \times 1 $ tiles, placed vertically. The remaining part of the rectangle $ R $ is a rectangle of dimensions $ (k-2) \times l $ (or an empty set if $ k = 2 $) and can be covered with tiles placed horizontally.
It remains to cover the rest of the chessboard. The lines containing the vertical sides of the rectangle $ R $ cut out two rectangular strips running the entire height of the chessboard; in special cases, one of them (or both) may be an empty set. Each of these strips is covered with vertical $ 2 \times 1 $ tiles; this is possible because $ 8 $ is an even number.
The part of the chessboard between the mentioned lines, after removing the rectangle $ R $, splits into two rectangles (upper and lower), each of width $ k $ (again: one of them - or both - may be an empty set). Since $ k $ is an even number, we can cover these areas with $ 2 \times 1 $ tiles, placed horizontally.
In this way, we have covered the entire chessboard without fields $ A $ and $ B $ with $ 2 \times 1 $ tiles. This is not the only possible way; there are many others. Note also that the method described here is effective for any chessboard with even dimensions.

From any set composed of $ m + n $ squares of a chessboard with dimensions $ m \times n $ ($ m,n \geq 2 $), one can select a non-empty subset having an even number of squares in each row and each column of the chessboard.

problem:
XXXV OM - I - Problem 5

Prove that there exists a multiple of the number $ 5^n $, whose decimal representation consists of $ n $ digits different from zero.
solution:
The number $5^n$ has in its decimal representation no more than $n$ digits: $5^n = c_0 + c_1 \cdot 10 + c_2 \cdot 10^2 + \ldots + c_{n-1} \cdot 10^{n-1}$, where some of the digits $c_i$ may be zeros. Suppose that $k$ is the smallest natural number for which $c_k = 0$. Consider the number $5^n + 10^k \cdot 5^{n-k}$. This number has in its decimal representation the form $c_0 + c_1 \cdot 10 + \ldots + c_{k-1} \cdot 10^{k-1} + 5 \cdot 10^k + \ldots$, where $c_i \ne 0$ for $i \leq k$. If any of the subsequent digits of this number is zero, e.g., $c_r = 0$ for some $r > k$, but $c_j \ne 0$ for $j < r$, then we consider the number $5^n + 10^k \cdot 5^{n-k} + 10^r \cdot 5^{n-r}$, which in its decimal representation has $r + 1$ consecutive digits different from zero.
As a result of such operations, we obtain a number in which the non-zero digits in its decimal representation correspond to the orders $1$, $10$, $10^2$, $10^{n-1}$. Moreover, this number does not exceed $5^n + 10 \cdot 5^{n-t} + 10^2 \cdot 5^{n-2} + \ldots + 10^{n-t} \cdot 5 = 5^n + 2 \cdot 5^n + 2^2 \cdot 5^n + \ldots + 2^{n-1} \cdot 5^n = 5^n(1 + 2 + 2^2 + \ldots + 2^{n-1}) = 5^n(2^n - 1) < 10^n$.
This is therefore a number that has in its decimal representation exactly $n$ digits different from zero. It is also a multiple of the number $5^n$, as it is formed by adding to $5^n$ terms of the form $10^k \cdot 5^{n-k} = 5^n \cdot 2^k$, which are multiples of the number $5^n$.

problem:
XXV - I - Problem 5

Prove that for every $ k $, the $ k $-th digit from the end in the decimal representation of the numbers $ 5, 5^2, 5^3, \ldots $ forms a periodic sequence from some point onwards.
solution: Let $ a_n $ be the number formed by the last $ k $ digits of the number $ 5^n $. It suffices to prove that the sequence $ \{a_n\} $ is periodic. The number $ a_n $ is the remainder of the division of the number $ 5^n $ by $ 10^k $, i.e., $ 5^n = 10^k \cdot b_n + a_n $, where $ b_n \geq 0 $ and $ 0 \leq a_n < 10^k $. Therefore, $ 5^{n+1} = 5 \cdot 10^k \cdot b_n + 5 \cdot a_n $ and $ 5^{n+1} = 10^k \cdot b_{n+1} + a_{n+1} $. Thus, the numbers $ 5^{n+1} $ and $ 5 \cdot a_n $ give the same remainder $ a_{n+1} $ when divided by $ 10^k $. Hence, $ a_{n+1} $ is the number formed by the last $ k $ digits of the number $ 5 \cdot a_n $. It follows that each term of the sequence $ \{a_n\} $ uniquely determines the next term. Since the sequence $ \{a_n\} $ can take only a finite number of values (no more than $ 10^k $), some term of the sequence must repeat: $ a_r = a_{r+t} $ for some natural numbers $ r $ and $ t $. Therefore, $ a_{r+1} = a_{r+t+1} $ and generally $ a_{r+s} = a_{r+t+s} $ for $ s = 1, 2, \ldots $. The sequence $ \{a_n\} $ is thus periodic from some point onward.

IX OM - I - Problem 3

From triangle $ ABC $, three corner triangles have been cut off by lines parallel to the sides of the triangle and tangent to the inscribed circle of this triangle. Prove that the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in the cut-off triangles is equal to the radius of the circle inscribed in triangle $ ABC $.
solution:
Let $ r $ denote the radius of the circle inscribed in triangle $ ABC $, $ S $ - its area, $ r_1 $, $ r_2 $, $ r_3 $ - the radii of the circles inscribed in the corner triangles, lying at vertices $ A $, $ B $, $ C $, respectively, and $ a $, $ b $, $ c $ - the sides of the triangle opposite these vertices, and $ h_a $, $ h_b $, $ h_c $ - the heights dropped to these sides.
The ratio of the radius of the circle inscribed in one of the corner triangles to the radius of the circle inscribed in $ \triangle ABC $ equals the ratio of the heights of both triangles, as they are similar triangles. Considering that the heights of the corner triangles are equal to $ h_a - 2r $, $ h_b - 2r $, and $ h_c - 2r $, respectively, we obtain the proportion

\[
\frac{r_1}{r} = 1 - \frac{ar}{S}
\]

and similarly $ \frac{r_2}{r} = 1 - \frac{br}{S} $, $ \frac{r_3}{r} = 1 - \frac{cr}{S} $.
Adding these equations, we get

\[
\frac{r_1 + r_2 + r_3}{r} = 3 - \frac{a + b + c}{S} \cdot r
\]

Since $ a + b + c = 2S/r $, we have

\[
\frac{r_1 + r_2 + r_3}{r} = 3 - 2 = 1
\]

thus $ r_1 + r_2 + r_3 = r $, Q.E.D.

problem:
XXII OM - III - Task 3

How many locks at least need to be placed on the treasury so that with a certain distribution of keys among the 11-member committee authorized to open the treasury, any 6 members can open it, but no 5 can? Determine the distribution of keys among the committee members with the minimum number of locks.
solution:
Suppose that for some natural number $ n $ there exists a key distribution to $ n $ locks among an 11-member committee such that the conditions of the problem are satisfied. Let $ A_i $ denote the set of locks that the $ i $-th member of the committee can open, where $ i = 1, 2, \ldots, 11 $, and let $ A $ denote the set of all locks. Then from the conditions of the problem, we have

for any five-element subset $ \{ i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $ of the set $ \{1, 2, \ldots, 11\} $ and

for any six-element subset $ \{j_1, \ldots, j_6\} $ of the set $ \{1,2,\ldots,  11\} $.
From (1), it follows that the set $ A - (A_{i_1} \cup \ldots \cup A_{i_5}) $ is non-empty. Let $ x_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_5} $ be one of its elements, i.e., a lock that the group of committee members numbered $ i_1, \ldots, i_5 $ cannot open. From (2), it follows that for every $ j \not \in \{i_1, \ldots, i_5 \} $ we have $ x_{i_1 , \ldots, i_5} \in A_j $.
Suppose that $ x_{i_1,\ldots,i_5} = x_{k_1, \ldots, k_5} $ for some subsets $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $ and $ \{k_1, \ldots, k_5\} $. If these subsets were different, then, for example, $ i_t \not \in \{ k_1, \ldots, k_5 \} $. Therefore, $ x_{k_1, \ldots, k_5} \in A_{i_t} $; but on the other hand, this leads to a contradiction. The obtained contradiction proves that $ \{i_1, \ldots,i_5\} = \{ k_1, \ldots, k_5 \} $.
In other words, different five-element subsets $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $ correspond to different locks. Therefore, the number of locks is not less than the number of five-element subsets of an 11-element set, i.e., $ n \geq  \binom{11}{5} = 462 $.
We will now prove that if we install $  \binom{11}{5} $ locks on the treasury, then we can distribute the keys to them among the members of the 11-member committee in such a way that the conditions of the problem are satisfied.
Let us associate each of the $  \binom{11}{5} $ locks with a five-element subset of the set $ \{1, 2, \ldots, 11\} $ in a one-to-one manner. If a lock corresponds to the subset $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $, then the keys to it are given to all members of the committee whose numbers are different from $ i_1, \ldots, i_5 $.
We will show that no five members of the committee can open a certain lock, and therefore the treasury. Indeed, the members of the committee numbered $ i_1, \ldots, i_5 $ do not have the key to the lock corresponding to the subset $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $.
We will show that any six members of the committee can open any lock, and therefore the treasury. If the members of the committee have numbers $ j_1, \ldots, j_6 $ and want to open a lock corresponding to the subset $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $, then one of the six numbers $ j_1, \ldots, j_6 $ does not belong to this five-element subset, say $ j_t \not \in \{i_1, \ldots, i_5 \} $. Therefore, the member of the committee numbered $ j_t $ has the key to the lock corresponding to the subset $ \{i_1, \ldots, i_5\} $.
Thus, the smallest number satisfying the conditions of the problem is $  \binom{11}{5} = 462 $.

problem:
XXXVII OM - III - Problem 5

In a chess tournament, $2n$ ($n > 1$) players participate, and any two of them play at most one game against each other. Prove that such a tournament, in which no three players play three games among themselves, is possible if and only if the total number of games played in the tournament does not exceed $n^2$.
solution:
We need to prove the equivalence of the following two statements $A$ and $B$ (for given natural numbers $m$ and $n$, $n > 1$):
A. It is possible to organize a tournament with $2n$ participants such that

 $A_1$) every player plays at most one game with each other player,

 $A_2$) no trio of players plays three games among themselves,

 $A_3$) the total number of games in the tournament is $m$.


B. The numbers $m$ and $n$ satisfy the inequality $m \leq n^2$.
Proof of the implication $B \Longrightarrow A$. We divide the participants into two groups of $n$ players each. The number of pairs where the partners belong to different groups is $n^2$. We select any $m$ of these pairs and conduct the games in the selected pairs. The satisfaction of conditions $A_1$, $A_2$, and $A_3$ is obvious.
Proof of the implication $A \Longrightarrow B$. We use induction on $n$. When $n = 2$, we have $4$ players and $6$ possible pairs. If the number of games played exceeds $4$, it means that all possible matches are played except for at most one; this would then form a "triangle of matches" (and even two such triangles).
Assume the statement is true for some $n \geq 2$ and suppose a tournament with $2(n + 1)$ participants has been organized such that conditions $A_1$, $A_2$, and $A_3$ are satisfied. We need to show that $m \leq (n + 1)^2$. Choose any two players who play a game against each other and name them $X$ and $Y$. The number of games played between the remaining $2n$ players does not exceed $n^2$, by the induction hypothesis. Let $x$ be the number of games played by player $X$ (excluding the match with $Y$), and $y$ be the number of games played by player $Y$ (excluding the match with $X$). Then $x + y \leq 2n$; otherwise, $X$ and $Y$ would have a common opponent and a "triangle of matches" would form, contradicting condition $A_2$. Considering the match between $X$ and $Y$ as well, we see that the total number of matches in the tournament does not exceed $n^2 + 2n + 1$, which is $(n + 1)^2$. This completes the inductive proof.

problem:
XXXI - I - Problem 8

Find all subsets $ S $ of the set of rational numbers that satisfy the following conditions.
1. If $ a \in S $, $ b \in S $, then $ a + b \in S $.
2. If $ a $ is a rational number different from 0, then exactly one of the numbers $ a $ and $ -a $ belongs to $ S $.
solution:
From condition 2, it follows that the set $ S $ contains the number $ 1 $ or the number $ -1 $. Let's consider these two cases in turn.
Assume that $ 1 \in S $. Every natural number $ n $ is the sum of $ n $ terms, each equal to $ 1 $, so by condition 1, the number $ n $ belongs to $ S $. We will show that every positive rational number belongs to $ S $. If for some natural numbers $ m $, $ n $, $ \frac{m}{n} \not \in S $, then by condition 2, the number $ -\frac{m}{n} $ would be an element of $ S $, and hence by condition 1, the number $ -m = \left( - \frac{m}{n} \right) + \left( - \frac{m}{n} \right) + \ldots + \left( - \frac{m}{n} \right) $ would belong to $ S $. This would imply that the natural number $ m $ does not belong to $ S $, contrary to what we established above. Therefore, all positive rational numbers belong to $ S $; condition 2 ensures that no negative rational number belongs to $ S $. In this case, we have two possibilities: $ S $ is the set of positive rational numbers or $ S $ is the set of non-negative rational numbers. Each of these sets, of course, satisfies the conditions of the problem.
If, on the other hand, $ - 1 \in S $, then similarly, we conclude that all negative rational numbers belong to $ S $, while positive numbers do not belong to $ S $. In this case, we also have two possibilities: $ S $ is the set of negative rational numbers or $ S $ is the set of non-positive rational numbers.
Ultimately, the set $ S $ can be the set of positive rational numbers, the set of non-negative rational numbers, the set of negative rational numbers, or the set of non-positive rational numbers.

problem:
LIX OM - II - Task 4

In each field of a square table of size $ n \times n $, an integer is written. We can perform the following operation multiple times: We select any field of the table and decrease the number written in it by the number of adjacent fields (having a common side with the selected field), while increasing each of the numbers written in the adjacent fields by 1.
For each integer $ n \geqslant 2 $, determine whether from any initial table, in which the sum of all $ n^2 $ numbers is zero, one can obtain a table consisting entirely of zeros.
solution:
Let $ P $ denote the diagonal of the table connecting its top-left corner with the bottom-right corner. We will prove that as a result of performing the described operation, the parity of the sum of the numbers located on the diagonal $ P $ (the fields lying on the diagonal $ P $ are shaded in Fig. 2) does not change.
om59_2r_img_3.jpg
For each field on the diagonal $ P $, the number of adjacent fields is 2 or 4, and none of them lie on the diagonal $ P $. Each field adjacent to the diagonal $ P $ (marked with crosses in Fig. 2) is adjacent to exactly two fields lying on the diagonal $ P $. The remaining fields of the table do not lie on the diagonal $ P $ and do not adjoin it. Therefore, if the sum of the numbers on the diagonal $ P $ before performing the operation was $ s $, then as a result of its execution, this sum will be equal to $ s-4 $, $ s-2 $, $ s $, or $ s+2 $, i.e., its parity will not change.
Thus, if at the beginning we enter the number 1 in the top-left corner, the number -1 in the field located in the top-right corner, and the number 0 in each of the remaining fields, then the sum of all the numbers in the table will be zero, but after performing any number of operations, the sum of the numbers lying on the diagonal $ P $ will be odd. Therefore, it is not possible for the diagonal $ P $, let alone the entire table, to consist of all zeros.
Answer: For every $ n \geqslant 2 $, there exists an initial table with a sum of numbers equal to zero, from which it is not possible to obtain a table composed entirely of zeros.

problem:
XXVI - II - Task 3

In a certain family, the husband and wife have made the following agreement: If the wife washes the dishes on a certain day, then the husband washes the dishes the next day. If, however, the husband washes the dishes on a certain day, then who washes the dishes the next day is decided by a coin toss. Let $ p_n $ denote the probability that the husband washes the dishes on the $ n $-th day of the agreement. Prove that the limit $ \lim_{n\to \infty} p_n $ exists and calculate it. We assume $ p_1 = \frac{1}{2} $.
solution:
If the husband washes the dishes on the $(n+1)$-th day, then either the husband washed the dishes on the $n$-th day (the probability of this event is $ \displaystyle p_n \cdot \frac{1}{2} $), or the wife washed the dishes on the $n$-th day (the probability of this event is $ 1- p_{n} $). Therefore, we have $ \displaystyle p_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2} p_{n}+ (1-p_n) $, which simplifies to $ \displaystyle p_{n+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{2} p_n $. In other words, $ \displaystyle p_{n} - \frac{2}{3} $ is a geometric sequence with a common ratio of $ \displaystyle \frac{1}{2} $. Every geometric sequence with a common ratio $ q $, where $ |q| < 1 $, converges to zero. Therefore, $ \displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( p_{n} - \frac{2}{3} \right) = 0 $, which means $ \displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} p_n = \frac{2}{3} $.
Note. The value of $ p_1 $ does not affect the solution.

problem:
XV OM - II - Task 2

A circle is divided into four non-overlapping arcs $ AB $, $ BC $, $ CD $, and $ DA $. Prove that the segment connecting the midpoints of arcs $ AB $ and $ CD $ is perpendicular to the segment connecting the midpoints of arcs $ BC $ and $ DA $.
solution:
Let $ M $, $ N $, $ P $, $ Q $ denote the midpoints of arcs $ AB $, $ BC $, $ CD $, $ DA $ (Fig. 12).
The theorem will be proven when we show that the sum of the inscribed angles $ MNQ $ and $ PMN $ is $ 90^\circ $. The angle $ MNQ $ is subtended by the arc $ MAQ $ equal to the sum of the arcs $ MA $ and $ AQ $, and the inscribed angle $ PMN $ is subtended by the arc $ PCN $ equal to the sum of the arcs $ PC $ and $ CN $. Since inscribed angles in the same circle and subtended by equal arcs are equal, the sum of the inscribed angles $ MNQ $ and $ PMN $ equals the inscribed angle in the given circle subtended by an arc equal to the sum of the arcs $ MA $, $ AQ $, $ PC $, $ CN $. Now, arc $ MA $ = arc $ MB $, arc $ AQ $ = arc $ QD $, arc $ PC $ = arc $ DP $, arc $ CN $ = arc $ NB $, so the sum of the arcs $ MA $, $ AQ $, $ PC $, $ CN $ equals the sum of the arcs $ MB $, $ QD $, $ DP $, $ NB $, and each of these sums equals a semicircle. The sum of the inscribed angles $ MNQ $ and $ PMN $ equals the inscribed angle subtended by a semicircle, i.e., a right angle.

problem: 2. Answer: $x= \pm \frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi n, n \in Z$
solution:
Solution.

Let's find $x$ for which each of the parentheses equals zero.

A.
$\sin ^{2} x-\cos x-1 / 4=0 \rightarrow \cos ^{2} x+\cos x-3 / 4=0 \rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{c}\cos x=1 / 2 \\ \cos x=-3 / 2 \varnothing\end{array} \rightarrow\right.$

$\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1}=\frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi k, k \in Z \\ x_{2}=-\frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi n, n \in Z\end{array}\right.$

B.

$\cos 2 x+\cos x=0 \rightarrow \cos 2 x=\cos (\pi-x) \rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{l}2 x=\pi-x+2 \pi m, \\ 2 x=-\pi+x+2 \pi l\end{array} \rightarrow\right.$

$\rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{3}=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{2 \pi m}{3} \\ x_{4}=-\pi+2 \pi l\end{array}\right.$

The intersection of the series $x_{1} \cap x_{3}$ is $x_{1}$, i.e., $x=\frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi k, k \in Z$ is a solution.

The intersections of the series $x_{1} \cap x_{4}$ and $x_{2} \cap x_{4}$ are empty.

Let's find the intersection of the series $x_{2} \cap x_{3}:-\frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi n=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{2 \pi m}{3} \rightarrow m=3 n-1$, i.e., the series $x_{2}$ is included in the series $x_{3}$ and therefore is a solution.

Solution.

The roots of the polynomial $P_{1}(x)=x^{2}-x-6$ are $x_{1}^{1}=3, x_{1}^{2}=-2$. The roots of the polynomial $P_{2}(x)=P_{1}(2 x)$ are $x_{2}^{1}=3 / 2, x_{2}^{2}=-2 / 2=-1$. We assume that the roots of the polynomial $P_{k}(x)$ are $x_{k}^{1}=3 / 2^{k-1}, x_{k}^{2}=-2 / 2^{k-1}=-1 / 2^{k-2}$. Then the polynomial $P_{k+1}(x)=P_{k}(2 x)$ will have roots $x_{k+1}^{1}=x_{k}^{1} / 2=3 / 2^{k}, x_{k+1}^{2}=x_{k}^{2} / 2=-1 / 2^{k-1}$, i.e., $x_{n}^{1}=3 / 2^{n-1}, x_{n}^{2}=-1 / 2^{n-2}$.

The polynomial $P_{k}(x)$ has the form $P_{k}(x)=4^{(k-1)} x^{2}-2^{k-1} x-6$, and the polynomial $Q_{n}(x)=\left(1+4+\ldots+4^{n-1}\right) x^{2}-\left(1+2+\ldots+2^{n-1}\right) x-6 n=\frac{4^{n}-1}{3} x^{2}-\left(2^{n}-1\right) x-6 n$.

The discriminant of the polynomial $Q_{n}(x)$ is $D / 4=\left(2^{n}-1\right)^{2}+8 n\left(4^{n}-1\right)>0$, so there are real roots. By Vieta's theorem, their sum is $\frac{3\left(2^{n}-1\right)}{4^{n}-1}$.

problem: 5. Answer: $a \in\left[\frac{2}{11} ; \frac{2}{9}\right) \cup\left[\frac{2}{7} ;+\infty\right)$
solution:
Solution.

In the region $A(x>a, y>2 a)$, the system will take the form: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x+y=5 a \\ x+2 y=2\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}x_{1}=10 a-2 \\ y_{1}=2-5 a\end{array}\right.\right.$. This solution belongs to the region $A$ if $\left\{\begin{array}{l}10 a-2>a \\ 2-5 a>2 a\end{array} \rightarrow a \in\left(\frac{2}{9} ; \frac{2}{7}\right)\right.$.

In the region $B(x>a, y \leq 2 a)$, the system will take the form: $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=5 a \\ x+2 y=2\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}x_{2}=5 a \\ y_{2}=(2-5 a) / 2\end{array}\right.\right.$. This solution belongs to the region $B$ if $\left\{\begin{array}{c}5 a>a \\ (2-5 a) / 2 \leq 2 a\end{array} \rightarrow a \in\left[\frac{2}{9} ;+\infty\right)\right.$.

In the region $C(x \leq a, y \leq 2 a)$, the system can have solutions only when $a=0$ and takes the form: $\left\{\begin{array}{c}0=5 a \\ x+2 y=2\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}x_{3}=2-2 t \\ y_{3}=t, t \in R\end{array}\right.\right.$. The conditions for the solution to belong to the region $C$ lead to the inequalities $\left\{\begin{array}{c}2-2 t \leq 0 \\ t \leq 0\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}t \geq 1 \\ t \leq 0\end{array}\right.\right.$. The last shows that the system is inconsistent in the region $C$ for any $a$. In the region $D(x \leq a, y>2 a)$, the system will take the form: $\left\{\begin{array}{c}y=5 a \\ x+2 y=2\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}x_{3}=2-10 a \\ y_{3}=5 a\end{array}\right.\right.$. This solution belongs to the region $D$ if $\left\{\begin{array}{l}2-10 a \leq a \\ 2-5 a>2 a\end{array} \rightarrow a \in\left[\frac{2}{11} ; \frac{2}{7}\right)\right.$.

problem: 2. Answer: 1) $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=\frac{\pi}{4}+2 \pi k \\ y=(-1)^{n} \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi n\end{array}, k, n \in Z\right.$ 2) $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=-\frac{3 \pi}{4}+2 \pi k \\ y=(-1)^{n+1} \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi n\end{array}, k, n \in Z\right.$
solution:
Solution.

The numbers $x$ and $y$ must satisfy the system $\left\{\begin{array}{c}\sin x \cdot \cos x=\sin ^{2} y \\ \sin x+\cos x=2 \sin y\end{array}\right.$. Squaring the left and right parts of the second equation and subtracting twice the first, we get $1=2 \sin ^{2} y$. Then the first equation will take the form $\sin 2 x=1$ and has solutions $x=\frac{\pi}{4}+\pi m, m \in Z$.

If $\sin y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, then $\sin x>0$ and $\cos x>0$, so $m=2 k$ is even, i.e. $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=\frac{\pi}{4}+2 \pi k \\ y=(-1)^{n} \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi n\end{array}, k, n \in Z\right.$ - the first series of solutions.

If $\sin y=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, then $\sin x<0$ and $\cos x<0$, so $x=-\frac{3 \pi}{4}+2 \pi k, k \in Z$ and $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=-\frac{3 \pi}{4}+2 \pi k \\ y=(-1)^{n+1} \frac{\pi}{4}+\pi n\end{array}, k, n \in Z\right.$ - the second series of solutions to the problem.

Solution.

The number of numbers at the first step is $3=2^{1}+1$, at the second step $5=2^{2}+1$. We make an inductive assumption that the number of numbers in the line at the $(m-1)$-th step is $k_{n-1}=2^{n-1}+1$.

Then at the $n$-th step, $2^{n-1}$ arithmetic means will be added to them, so $k_{n}=k_{n-1}+2^{n-1}=2 \cdot 2^{n-1}+1=2^{n}+1$. The difference between any adjacent numbers at any step is constant, so the numbers written by Petya in a line at the $n$-th step form an arithmetic progression. The common difference at the $n$-th step is $d_{n}=\frac{b-a}{2^{n}}$, and the sum of all numbers $S_{n}=\frac{a+b}{2}\left(2^{n}+1\right)$.

Finally, the number $a_{n, m}=a+d_{n} \cdot(m-1)=a+\frac{b-a}{2^{n}}(m-1)$.

For the given variant 1 Answer: 1) $k_{n}=2^{n}+1=2^{15}+1$ 2) $S_{n}=\frac{a+b}{2}\left(2^{n}+1\right)=11 \cdot\left(2^{15}+1\right)$
3) $a_{n, m}=a+\frac{b-a}{2^{n}}(m-1)=5+\frac{144}{2^{15}}$

problem: 4. Answer: $p=\frac{1}{70}$
solution:
Solution.

Event $H$ - four vertices painted yellow are on the same face. The total number of ways to paint the vertices $n=C_{8}^{4}=\frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4}=70$. The number of ways to paint the vertices that are favorable to event $H$ is equal to the number of faces of the cube, i.e., $m=6$. Then the probability of event $H$ is $P(H)=\frac{m}{n}=\frac{3}{35}$. Event $A-$ four yellow vertices on the table surface - is the product of event $H$ and event $B$ - the face with all vertices painted yellow landing on the table surface. The conditional probability $P(B / H)=1 / 6$.

By the theorem of the probability of the product of events $P(A)=P(B \cdot H)=P(H) \cdot P(B / H)=\frac{3}{35} \cdot \frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{70}$.

solution:
Solution.

$d$ - the distance from the center of the first button $K_{1}$ to the center $O$ of the bottom $K$ of the box, $0 \leq d \leq 8$, point $O_{1}$ - its center, the second button $K_{2}$ has a center at point $O_{2}$.

If $0 \leq d \leq 6$, then the circle $K_{3}$ with center at $O_{1}$ and radius 2 is within the circle $K_{4}$ with center at point $O$ and radius 8. (see fig.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-12.jpg?height=622&width=579&top_left_y=140&top_left_x=687)

Any circle $K_{2}$, whose center $O_{2}$ is in the highlighted area, is favorable for the first player's win. The probability of winning in this range of $d$ does not depend on $d$ and is equal to the ratio of the area of the highlighted region to the area of the circle $K_{4}$, i.e., $P(A)=\frac{\pi(64-4)}{64 \pi}=\frac{15}{16} \approx 0.94$.

For $6 < d \leq 8$, the circle $K_{3}$ extends beyond the circle $K_{4}$, and the area of the highlighted region, corresponding to a favorable position of the centers of the circles $K_{2}$ for the first player, increases. (see fig.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-12.jpg?height=637&width=602&top_left_y=1235&top_left_x=607)

The maximum value of this area is achieved when $d=8$ and corresponds to the position of point $O_{1}$ on the boundary of the circle $K_{4}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-12.jpg?height=643&width=560&top_left_y=1983&top_left_x=634)

Calculation of the area of the red region.

The area of the red region is equal to the sum of the areas of two segments of the circles $K_{3}$ and $K_{4}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-13.jpg?height=486&width=574&top_left_y=174&top_left_x=632)

Triangle $A_{1}$ is isosceles with sides 8 and 2. Then $\cos \beta=\frac{1}{8}, \alpha=\pi-2 \beta$.

$\sin \alpha=\sin (\pi-2 \beta)=\sin 2 \beta=2 \sin \beta \cdot \cos \beta=2 \cdot \frac{1}{8} \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{64}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{32}$,

$\cos \alpha=\frac{31}{32} \rightarrow \alpha=\arccos \frac{31}{32}, \beta=\arccos \frac{1}{8}$

The area of the segment of the circle $K_{4}$ with central angle $2 \alpha$ is:

$S_{1}=64 \alpha-0.5 \cdot 64 \cdot \sin 2 \alpha=64 \cdot(\alpha-\sin \alpha \cos \alpha)=64\left(\arccos \frac{31}{32}-\frac{93 \sqrt{7}}{32^{2}}\right)=$

$=64 \arccos \frac{31}{32}-\frac{93 \sqrt{7}}{16} \approx 0.66$

Similarly, the area of the segment of the circle $K_{3}$ with angle $2 \beta$ is:

$S_{2}=4 \cdot(\beta-\sin \beta \cos \beta)=4\left(\arccos \frac{1}{8}-\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{64}\right)=4 \arccos \frac{1}{8}-\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{16} \approx 5.28$.

The area of the "red" region $S=S_{1}+S_{2}=64 \arccos \frac{31}{32}+4 \arccos \frac{1}{8}-6 \sqrt{7} \approx 5.95$

Then the maximum value of the probability of the first player's win is

$P_{\text {max }}(A)=1-\frac{S}{64 \pi}=1-\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\arccos \frac{31}{32}+\frac{1}{16} \arccos \frac{1}{8}-\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{32}\right) \approx 0.97$

In the general case, if the radius of the box is $R$, the radius of the button is $r$, then

$\sin \alpha=\frac{2 r \sqrt{(R-r) R}}{(R-r)^{2}}, \cos \alpha=\frac{R^{2}-2 R r-r^{2}}{(R-r)^{2}}, \sin \beta=\frac{\sqrt{(R-2 r) R}}{(R-r)}, \cos \beta=\frac{r}{R-r}$,

$S=(R-r)^{2} \cdot \alpha+4 r^{2} \cdot \beta-(R-r)^{2} \cdot \sin \alpha$,

$P_{\text {max }}(A)=1-\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\alpha+4 \beta \cdot \cos ^{2} \beta-\sin \alpha\right), \quad P_{\text {min }}(A)=1-\frac{4 r^{2}}{(R-r)^{2}}=\frac{(R-3 r)(R+r)}{(R-r)^{2}}$,

$P_{\text {min }}(\bar{A})=1-P_{\text {max }}(A)=\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\alpha+4 \beta \cdot \cos ^{2} \beta-\sin \alpha\right), P_{\text {max }}(\bar{A})=\frac{4 r^{2}}{(R-r)^{2}}$

Problem 5 Answer: $a \in(-2.5 ;-1.5] \cup[-1 ;-0.5] \cup[0 ; 0.5] \cup[1 ; 1.5] \cup[2 ; 3)$

Solution. The first three inequalities limit a triangle on the plane with vertices $A(a-2 ; 1), B(a ; 3), C(a+1 ; 1)$ (one must solve systems of equations for the boundaries pairwise)

As the parameter $a$ changes, the triangle $A B C$ moves parallel to the $OX$ axis, so that its base lies on the line $y=1$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-14.jpg?height=280&width=440&top_left_y=154&top_left_x=634)

All integer solutions of the system are inside the circle, on the midline of the triangle $A B C$ with the equation $y=2$. There are a total of 5 such points in the circle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-14.jpg?height=311&width=314&top_left_y=547&top_left_x=654)

Their abscissas are $-2,-1,0,1,2$. Let's determine for which $a$ the unique solution of the system will be the point with abscissa

1) $x_{1}=-2 \quad\left\{\begin{array}{c}a-1<-2<a+0.5 \\ -1 \geq a+0.5\end{array} \rightarrow a \in(-2.5 ;-1.5]\right.$
2) $x_{2}=-1 \quad\left\{\begin{array}{c}a-1<-1<a+0.5 \\ -2 \leq a-1 \\ 0 \geq a+0.5\end{array} \rightarrow a \in[-1 ;-0.5]\right.$
3) $x_{3}=0 \quad\left\{\begin{array}{c}a-1<0<a+0.5 \\ -1 \leq a-1 \\ 1 \geq a+0.5\end{array} \rightarrow a \in[0 ; 0.5]\right.$
4) $x_{4}=1 \quad\left\{\begin{array}{c}a-1<1<a+0.5 \\ 0 \leq a-1 \\ 2 \geq a+0.5\end{array} \rightarrow a \in[1 ; 1.5]\right.$
5) $x_{2}=2 \quad\left\{\begin{array}{c}a-1<2<a+0.5 \\ 1 \leq a-1\end{array} \rightarrow a \in[2 ; 3)\right.$

The union of the obtained sets forms the answer.

problem: 6. Answer: $2 \pi r-4 \varphi R$, where $\varphi-$ is the acute angle, $\sin \varphi=\frac{r}{R-r}$
solution:
Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3f94d691aa01194470c9g-14.jpg?height=528&width=485&top_left_y=2123&top_left_x=754)

Position of wheel $A$ - encountering obstacle $B$, position $C$ - end of overcoming the obstacle, $\measuredangle A O C=4 \varphi$, where $\sin \varphi=\frac{r}{R-r}$. The path traveled by the center of the wheel during the overcoming of the obstacle is equal to the length of the arc of a circle with radius $2r$ and angle $\pi-2 \varphi$, i.e., $S_{1}=2(\pi-2 \varphi) r$. The path traveled by the wheel outside the obstacle is equal to the length of the arc with radius $R-r$ and angle $(2 \pi-4 \varphi)$, i.e., $S_{2}=(2 \pi-4 \varphi)(R-r)$. Then the path traveled by the center of the wheel with the obstacle $S_{3}=S_{1}+S_{2}=2(\pi-2 \varphi) r+(2 \pi-4 \varphi)(R-r)=(2 \pi-4 \varphi) R$, i.e., $S_{3}$ is equal to the length of the arc AEC of the rim. The length of the path of the center of the wheel in the absence of the obstacle is $S_{4}=2 \pi(R-r)$.

Then $S_{3}-S_{4}=(2 \pi-4 \varphi) R-2 \pi(R-r)=2 \pi r-4 \varphi R$.

If $R=3, r=1$, then $\sin \varphi=\frac{r}{R-r}=\frac{1}{2} \rightarrow \varphi=\frac{\pi}{6}$. Then $S_{3}-S_{4}=2 \pi r-4 \varphi R=2 \pi-\frac{12 \pi}{6}=0$, i.e., the length of the path will not change in the absence of the obstacle.

Problem 1 Answer: $x=2$
solution:
Solution.

Transform the equation $f\left(\log _{2}\left(x\left(x^{2}-1\right)\right)-0.5 \log _{2}(x-1)^{2}\right)=f\left(\log _{2} 6\right)$. From the monotonicity of the function $f$, it follows that the equality is possible if $\log _{2}\left(x\left(x^{2}-1\right)\right)-0.5 \log _{2}(x-1)^{2}=\log _{2} 6\left(^{*}\right)$. The domain of valid values is $x(x-1)(x+1)>0 \rightarrow x \in(-1 ; 0) \cup(1 ;+\infty)$.

Transforming the equation:

1) In the domain $x \in(-1 ; 0): \log _{2} \frac{x(x-1)(x+1)}{1-x}=\log _{2} 6 \rightarrow x^{2}+x+6=0$ - no solutions.
2) In the domain $x \in(1 ;+\infty): \log _{2} \frac{x(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=\log _{2} 6 \rightarrow x^{2}+x-6=0 \rightarrow x=2$.

problem: 2. Answer: $S_{\min }=\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{7}$
solution:
Solution.

The first equation in the system is equivalent to the union of lines $\left[\begin{array}{c}2 x=\frac{\pi}{2}-y+2 \pi k \\ 2 x=\frac{\pi}{2}+y+2 \pi m, m, k \in Z\end{array} \rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{c}2 x+y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi k\left(l_{1}\right) \\ 2 x-y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi m\left(l_{2}\right)\end{array}\right.\right.$, on which the sides of the parallelogram can lie.

Similarly, the second equation in the system is equivalent to the union of lines:

$\left[\begin{array}{c}2 y=\frac{\pi}{2}-x-y+2 \pi k \\ 2 y=x+y-\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi m, m, k \in Z\end{array} \rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{c}x+3 y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi k\left(l_{3}\right) \\ x-y=\frac{\pi}{2}-2 \pi m\left(l_{4}\right)\end{array}\right.\right.$, on which the sides of the parallelogram can lie.

Two sides of the permissible parallelograms lie on any pair of parallel lines from $\left(l_{1}\right)$ or $\left(l_{2}\right)$, and the other pair of parallel sides lie on any pair of lines from $\left(l_{3}\right)$ or $\left(l_{4}\right)$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_2e1f37bf873362cdcd50g-1.jpg?height=340&width=345&top_left_y=1823&top_left_x=153)

Fig 1

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_2e1f37bf873362cdcd50g-1.jpg?height=382&width=257&top_left_y=1785&top_left_x=543)

Fig 3

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_2e1f37bf873362cdcd50g-1.jpg?height=422&width=386&top_left_y=1765&top_left_x=1266)

Fig 4

The parallelogram with the smallest area should be sought among the parallelograms whose parallel sides lie on lines for which the parameters $m$ (or $k$) differ by 1.

For example, $\left[\begin{array}{l}2 x+y=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(l_{1}\right) \\ 2 x+y=\frac{5 \pi}{2}\left(l_{1}^{\prime}\right)\end{array},\left[\begin{array}{l}2 x-y=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(l_{2}\right) \\ 2 x-y=\frac{5 \pi}{2}\left(l_{2}^{\prime}\right)\end{array},\left[\begin{array}{l}x+3 y=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(l_{3}\right) \\ x+3 y=\frac{5 \pi}{2}\left(l_{3}^{\prime}\right)\end{array},\left[\begin{array}{l}x-y=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(l_{4}\right) \\ x-y=\frac{5 \pi}{2}\left(l_{4}^{\prime}\right)\end{array}\right.\right.\right.\right.$.

The distance between the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{1}^{\prime}$ is $h_{1}=\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{5}}$, the distance between $l_{2}$ and $l_{2}^{\prime}-h_{2}=\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{5}}$, the distance between $l_{3}$ and $l_{3}^{\prime}-h_{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{10}}$, the distance between $l_{4}$ and $l_{4}^{\prime}-h_{4}=\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{2}}$.

We will use the formula for the area of a parallelogram through heights and its angle: $S=\frac{h \cdot H}{\sin \alpha}$. There are four variants of parallelograms that can have the smallest area. Case 1. The sides of the parallelogram consist of pairs of parallel lines $l_{1}, l_{1}^{\prime}$ and $l_{3}, l_{3}^{\prime}$ (Fig 1). The angle $\alpha_{1,3}$ between the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{3}: \cos \alpha_{1,3}=\frac{\left(\overrightarrow{n_{1}}, \overrightarrow{n_{3}}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n_{1}}\right| \cdot\left|\overrightarrow{n_{3}}\right|}, \overrightarrow{n_{1}}=(2 ; 1), \overrightarrow{n_{3}}=(1 ; 3) \rightarrow \cos \alpha_{1,3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \rightarrow \sin \alpha_{1,3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (other methods of finding the angle between the lines can also be chosen). The area of the parallelogram $S_{1,3}=\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{5}$.

Case 2. The sides of the parallelogram consist of pairs of parallel lines $l_{1}, l_{1}^{\prime}$ and $l_{4}, l_{4}^{\prime}$ (Fig 2). The angle between the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{4}: \cos \alpha_{1,4}=\frac{\left(\overrightarrow{n_{1}}, \overrightarrow{n_{4}}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n_{1}}\right| \cdot\left|\overrightarrow{n_{4}}\right|}, \overrightarrow{n_{1}}=(2 ; 1), \overrightarrow{n_{4}}=(1 ;-1) \rightarrow \cos \alpha_{1,4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \rightarrow \sin \alpha_{1,4}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$

The area of the parallelogram $S_{1,4}=\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{3}$.

Case 3. The sides of the parallelogram consist of pairs of parallel lines $l_{2}, l_{2}^{\prime}$ and $l_{3}, l_{3}^{\prime}$ (Fig 3). The angle between the lines $l_{2}$ and $l_{3}:$

$\cos \alpha_{2,3}=\frac{\left(\overrightarrow{n_{2}}, \overrightarrow{n_{3}}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n_{2}}\right| \cdot\left|\overrightarrow{n_{3}}\right|}, \overrightarrow{n_{2}}=(2 ;-1), \overrightarrow{n_{3}}=(1 ; 3) \rightarrow \cos \alpha_{2,3}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{50}} \rightarrow \sin \alpha_{2,3}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{50}}$

The area of the parallelogram $S_{2,3}=\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{7}$.

Case 4. The sides of the parallelogram consist of pairs of parallel lines $l_{2}, l_{2}^{\prime}$ and $l_{4}, l_{4}^{\prime}$ (Fig 4). The angle between the lines $l_{2}$ and $l_{4}:$

$\cos \alpha_{2,4}=\frac{\left(\overrightarrow{n_{2}}, \overrightarrow{n_{4}}\right)}{\left|\overrightarrow{n_{2}}\right| \cdot\left|\overrightarrow{n_{4}}\right|}, \overrightarrow{n_{2}}=(2 ;-1), \overrightarrow{n_{4}}=(1 ;-1) \rightarrow \cos \alpha_{2,4}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \rightarrow \sin \alpha_{2,4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$

The area of the parallelogram $S_{2,4}=4 \pi^{2}$.

problem: 4. Answer: For $a=-2,-4,-5,-7$ the system has two solutions (the maximum possible number)
solution:
Solution. The general solution of the equation $2 x-3 y=a$ is given by $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=2 a+3 t \\ y=a+2 t\end{array}, t \in Z(*)\right.$. Substituting it into the inequalities, we get the system of inequalities for the admissible values $(t ; a):\left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \leq 2 a+3 t \leq 5 \\ 2 \leq a+2 t \leq 5\end{array}\right.$ (**) . On the plane of variables $(t ; a)$, this set is a parallelogram bounded by the lines: $l_{1}: a+2 t=2, l_{2}: a+2 t=5, l_{3}: 2 a+3 t=1, l_{4}: 2 a+3 t=5$.

Vertices of the parallelogram: $A=l_{1} \cap l_{3}:\left\{\begin{array}{c}a+2 t=2 \\ 2 a+3 t=1\end{array} \rightarrow A(3 ;-4), \quad B=l_{1} \cap l_{4}:\left\{\begin{array}{c}a+2 t=2 \\ 2 a+3 t=5\end{array}\right.\right.$

$$
C=l_{2} \cap l_{4}:\left\{\begin{array}{c}

solution:
Solution. Notation: $n$ - number of boys, $m$ - number of girls, $k$ - number of laps run by each boy, $r$ - number of candies received by each boy.

Problem statement:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
n k+m(k-1)=286 \\
n r+m(r+1)=243
\end{array}, k \geq 2, r \geq 1\right.
$$

Add the equations of the system:

$$
n(k+r)+m(k+r)=529=23^{2} \rightarrow(n+m)(k+r)=23^{2}
$$

Considering the integrality of the variables and the simplicity of the number 23, we have

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
n+m=23 \\
k+r=23
\end{array}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we have:

$$
(m+n) k=286+m \rightarrow m=23 k-286
$$

$1 \leq m \leq 22 \rightarrow 1 \leq 23 k-286 \leq 22 \rightarrow \frac{287}{23} \leq k \leq \frac{308}{23} \rightarrow 12.4 \leq k \leq 13.4 \rightarrow k=13$ $m=13 \rightarrow n=10 \rightarrow r=10$

problem:
4. Let $x_{1}, x_{2}$ be the integer solutions of the equation $x^{2} + p x + 3 q = 0$ with prime numbers $p$ and $q$. Then, by Vieta's theorem,

$$
x_{1} + x_{2} = -p
$$

From this, we conclude that both roots must be negative. Further, since the roots are integers and the numbers $q, 3$ are prime, there are only two possible cases:

$$
x_{1} = -1, x_{2} = -3 q \text{ or } x_{1} = -3, x_{2} = -q.
$$

Consider the first case. If $x_{1} = -1, x_{2} = -3 q$, then $1 + 3 q = p$. Thus, $p$ and $q$ have different parities. The only even prime number is 2. If $p = 2$, then the equation $1 + 3 q = 2$ has no solution in prime numbers, so this case is impossible. If $p$ is odd, then $q$ is even. The only possible value is $q = 2$. In this case, $p = 1 + 2 \cdot 3 = 7$ is a prime number. We have the solution $p = 7, q = 2$. In this case, $x_{1} = -1, x_{2} = -6$.

Consider the second case. If $x_{1} = -3, x_{2} = -q$, then $3 + q = p$. Again, $p$ and $q$ have different parities. If $p = 2$, then the equation $3 + q = 2$ has no solution in prime numbers, so this case is impossible. If $p$ is odd, then $q$ is even. For $q = 2$, $p = 3 + 2 = 5$ is a prime number. We have another solution $p = 5, q = 2$. In this case, $x_{1} = -3, x_{2} = -2$.

We have considered all possible cases. There are no other solutions.
solution: Answer: there are two pairs of solutions: $p=5, q=2 ; p=7, q=2$.

Problem 2 Answer: $a= \pm 5-2 \sqrt{6}$.

Solution. By Vieta's theorem, the roots of the equation are $m=(a+2 \sqrt{6})$ and $n=\left(\frac{1}{a}-2 \sqrt{6}\right)$.

Then we have:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l}
a=m-2 \sqrt{6} \\
\frac{1}{a}=n+2 \sqrt{6}
\end{array} \rightarrow 1=m n+2 \sqrt{6}(m-n)-24 \rightarrow 2 \sqrt{6}(m-n)=25-m n\right.
$$

If $m, n \in Z, m \neq n$, then $2 \sqrt{6}=\frac{25-m n}{m-n}$ is a rational number, which is incorrect. Therefore, $m=n$ and then $m^{2}=25 \rightarrow m= \pm 5 \rightarrow a= \pm 5-2 \sqrt{6}$.

Problem 3 Answer: 5400 numbers.

Then, among the numbers that are multiples of 49, there are $3375+2025-675=4725$ numbers that are divisible by either 3 or 5. Therefore, the numbers that are not divisible by either 3 or 5 will be $10125-4775=$ 5400 desired numbers.

Event $H$ - the obtained number is a three-digit number. According to the problem, it has been realized.

The probability $P(H)=\frac{9}{10}$. Event $A$ - the sum of the digits in the number is divisible by 4. We need to find the conditional probability $P(A / \mathrm{H})=\frac{P(A \cdot H)}{P(H)}$. Event $H$ contains $q=9 \cdot 10^{2}=900$ equally possible outcomes, while event $A$ is favored by outcomes that satisfy the condition $x+y+z=4 k, k \in Z$ with the restriction $x=1,2, \ldots, 9, y=0,1, \ldots, 9, z=0,1, \ldots, 9, k=1,2, \ldots, 6$.

Notation: $y=u, z=v, x=4 k-u-v$.

Considering the restrictions, $\quad 1 \leq 4 k-u-v \leq 9 \rightarrow 4 k-9 \leq u+v \leq 4 k-1$.

Let $n=n(m)$ denote the number of solutions to the equation $u+v=m$ for a fixed $m$ and restrictions on $u$ and $v$. Then

$$
n=\left\{\begin{array}{c}
m+1, \text { for } m \in[0 ; 9] \\
19-m, \text { for } m \in[10 ; 18] \\
0, \text { for } m \in(-\infty ; 0) \cup(18 ;+\infty)
\end{array}\right.
$$

For a fixed $k$, the number of favorable triples $x, y, z$ is equal to the sum of the number of solutions to the equations $u+v=m$ for all $m \in[4 k-9 ; 4 k-1]$

Case $k=1 . m \in[-5,3] \rightarrow m=0,1,2,3 \rightarrow n_{1}=1+2+3+4=10$

Case $k=2 . m \in[-1,7] \rightarrow m=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 \rightarrow n_{2}=1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8=36$

Case $k=3 . m \in[3,11] \rightarrow m=3, \ldots, 8,9$ and $m=10,11 \rightarrow n_{3}=(4+5+\ldots+9+10)+(8+9)=66$

Case $k=4 . m \in[7,15] \rightarrow m=7,8,9$ and $m=10,11, \ldots, 15 \rightarrow n_{4}=(8+9+10)+(4+5+\ldots+9)=66$

Case $k=5 . m \in[11,19] \rightarrow m=11, . ., 18$ and $m=19 \rightarrow n_{5}=(1+2+\ldots+8)=36$

Case $k=6 . m \in[15,23] \rightarrow m=15,16,17,18$ and $m>18 \rightarrow n_{6}=1+2+3+4=10$

To obtain the total number $p$ of favorable triples $x, y, z$ in event $A \cdot H$, it is sufficient to sum the numbers $n_{1}, n_{2}, \ldots, n_{6}: p=2(10+36+66)=224$

solution:

Take the cosine of the left and right sides of the first equation: $2 x=\sqrt{1-y^{2}} \rightarrow 4 x^{2}+y^{2}=1$.

Transformation of the second equation: $\left[\begin{array}{c}2 x=y+2 \pi k \\ 2 x=\pi-y+2 \pi k\end{array}\right.$. Considering the constraints, the second series does not realize for any $k$, while the first one is possible only for $k=0$, i.e., $y=2 x$.

problem: 4. Answer: $P(A)=\frac{23}{81}$
solution:
Solution. Event $A$ - the composed number is greater than 300 and divisible by 3.

Hypothesis $H_{1}$ - the number starts with the digit 7, hypothesis $H_{2}$ - the digit 7 is in the second position, $H_{3}$ - the digit 7 is the last. By the condition, $P\left(H_{1}\right)=P\left(H_{2}\right)=P\left(H_{3}\right)=1 / 3$.

In hypothesis $H_{1}$, event $A$ is realized if for the number $\overline{7 y z}$ one of the following conditions is met:

1) $y+z=2$
2) $y+z=5$
3) $y+z=8$
4) $y+z=11$
5) $y+z=14$ 6) $y+z=17$

(then the sum of the digits of the number is divisible by 3, the condition: "the number is greater than 300" is always satisfied).

The total number of outcomes $n=9 \times 9=81$. The number of outcomes favorable to event $A$ under hypothesis $H_{1}$ and condition 1) is 1, under condition 2) - 4, under condition 3) - 7, under condition 4) - 8, under condition 5) - 5, under condition 6) - 2, i.e., a total of 27 outcomes. Then $P\left(A / H_{1}\right)=\frac{27}{81}=\frac{1}{3}$

In hypothesis $H_{2}$, the number $\overline{x 7 z}$ is favorable to event $A$ if $x \geq 3$ and the digits $x$ and $z$ satisfy one of the following conditions:

1) $x+z=5$ 2) $x+z=8$
2) $x+z=11$
3) $x+z=14$
4) $x+z=17$

The number of favorable outcomes under condition 1) is -2, under condition 2) - 5, under condition 3) - 7, under condition 4) - 5, under condition 5) - 2. In total, 21 outcomes are favorable to event $A$ under hypothesis $H_{2}$, i.e., $P\left(A / H_{2}\right)=\frac{21}{81}=\frac{7}{27}$.

In hypothesis $H_{3}$, the number of favorable outcomes is also 21 and $P\left(A / H_{3}\right)=\frac{7}{27}$.

Then $P(A)=P\left(A / H_{1}\right) \cdot P\left(H_{1}\right)+P\left(A / H_{2}\right) \cdot P\left(H_{2}\right)+P\left(A / H_{3}\right) \cdot P\left(H_{3}\right)=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{14}{27}\right)=\frac{23}{81}$.

problem: 3. Answer: $\operatorname{GCD}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)=2, \operatorname{LCM}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)=210$
solution:
Solution.

Let's factorize the free term of the equation into prime factors: $4200=2^{3} \cdot 3 \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 7$.

If $p$ is a prime common divisor of the roots, $4200=x_{1} \cdot x_{2} \cdot x_{3}$ is divisible by $p^{3}$. The factorization of the number 4200 into factors shows that such a common divisor can only be $p=2$.

We will prove that each of the roots is divisible by 2. Suppose the opposite, for example, $x_{1}$ is not divisible by 2. By the condition, $x_{1}^{3}-86 x_{1}^{2}+1180 x_{1}-4200=0 \rightarrow x_{1}^{3}=86 x_{1}^{2}-1180 x_{1}+4200$. Such an equality cannot exist, since the left side is an odd number, while the right side is even, i.e., $N O D\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)=2$. We will show that none of the roots of the equation is divisible by $5^{2}$. Indeed,
if one of the roots, for example, $x_{1}$, is divisible by $5^{2}$, then from the equality $x_{1}^{3}-86 x_{1}^{2}+1180 x_{1}-4200=0$ it follows that $x_{1}^{3}-86 x_{1}^{2}+1180 x_{1}=4200$. In the left part of the equality, $x_{1}^{3}$ and $x_{1}^{2}$ are divisible by $5^{3}$. Since $1180=5 \cdot 2^{2} \cdot 59, 1180 x_{1}$ is also divisible by $5^{3}$, i.e., the left part of the equality is divisible by $5^{3}$, while the right part is not. Thus, in the LCM of the roots, the factor 5 enters in the first power. The same can be said about the factor 2. Obviously, the other divisors of the number 4200, which entered it in the first powers, also enter the LCM in the first powers. LCM $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)=2 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 7=210$.

problem: 4. Answer: $\Sigma=4^{n}+1$
solution:
Solution.

Among the integers $a=2^{n}, 2^{n}+1,2^{n}+2, \ldots, 2^{n+1}-1,2^{n+1}$, belonging to the interval $\left[2^{n} ; 2^{n+1}\right]$, there are odd numbers $a_{k}=2^{n}+2 k-1, k=1,2, \ldots, 2^{n-1}$, for which $P\left(a_{k}\right)=a_{k}$. Their sum $S_{1}$ is equal to the sum of $2^{n-1}$ terms of the arithmetic progression $a_{k}: S_{1}=\frac{\left(2^{n}+1\right)+\left(2^{n+1}-1\right)}{2} \cdot 2^{n-1}=3 \cdot 4^{n-1}$.

The remaining numbers on the interval $a=2^{n}, 2^{n}+2,2^{n}+4, \ldots, 2^{n+1}-2,2^{n+1}$ are even, and dividing them by 2 does not change $P(a)$ for them, i.e., the sum of the largest divisors for the specified $a$ coincides with the analogous sum for the numbers $a=2^{n-1}, 2^{n-1}+1,2^{n-1}+2, \ldots, 2^{n}-1,2^{n}$. The sum of $P(a)$ for the odd ones (see above) is equal to $3 \cdot 4^{n-2}$, and the remaining (even) ones are divided by 2, the sum of $P(a)$ for the odd ones among them is equal to $3 \cdot 4^{n-3}$, and so on. At the last stage, two numbers 2 and 4 will remain. The sum of the divisors $P(a)$ for them is equal to 2. Thus, the desired sum of divisors $\Sigma$ is equal to the sum of the terms of the geometric progression: $3 \cdot 4^{n-1}+3 \cdot 4^{n-2}+3 \cdot 4^{n-3}+\ldots+3 \cdot 4^{0}+2=3 \cdot \frac{4^{n}-1}{4-1}+2=4^{n}+1$.

Solution (Geometric)

The line with the equation $x \cos a + y \sin a - 2 = 0$ is tangent to a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin. The system has a unique solution if it is tangent (common tangent) to the circle with the equation $x^{2} + y^{2} + 6x - 8y + 24 = 0 \leftrightarrow (x + 3)^{2} + (y - 4)^{2} = 1$, radius 1, and center at point $P(-3; 4)$. There are four cases of common tangents for two non-intersecting circles. Case 1.

Case 2. The second common tangent $L_{2}$ (see Fig. 1) is perpendicular to the x-axis and corresponds to the values of the parameter from the second series $\alpha_{2} = \pi + 2\pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

problem:
1. According to the problem, Sasha makes one step in 1 second, while Dan makes one step in $\frac{6}{7}$ seconds. Therefore, after 6 seconds, both Sasha and Dan will have made an integer number of steps, specifically, Sasha will have made 6 steps, and Dan will have made 7 steps. Consequently, we need to consider moments of time that are multiples of 6 seconds, i.e., $t=6k, k=1,2, \ldots$. Since Sasha's step length is 0.4 meters and Dan's step length is 0.6 meters, in $t=6k$ seconds, Sasha will have walked $6 \cdot k \cdot 0.4 = 2.4k$ meters, and Dan will have walked $7 \cdot k \cdot 0.6 = 4.2k$ meters. The distance between Sasha and Dan on the road at such moments of time is:

$$
d(k)=|200-2.4k|+|300-4.2k|.
$$

Consider the function $d(x), x \in \mathbb{R}$. For $x \leq x_{1}=\frac{300}{4.2}=71.42 \ldots$

$$
d(x)=200-2.4x+300-4.2x=500-6.6x
$$

For $x_{1} \leq x \leq x_{2}=\frac{200}{2.4}=83$,(3)

$$
d(x)=200-2.4x-300+4.2x=1.8x-100
$$

For $x \geq x_{2}$

$$
d(x)=-200+2.4x-300+4.2x=6.6x-500
$$

We have obtained that for $x \leq x_{1}$ the function $d(x)$ is decreasing, and for $x \geq x_{1}$ it is increasing. This means that at the point $x=x_{1}$ the function $d(x)$ attains its minimum value. To find the minimum of the function $d(k)$, consider the nearest integer values of $k$ to $x=x_{1}$: $k_{1}=\left[x_{1}\right]=71$ and $k_{2}=\left[x_{1}\right]+1=72$. Calculate $d(71)=500-6.6 \cdot 71=31.4$ and $d(72)=1.8 \cdot 72-100=29.6$. Therefore, the smallest possible distance between Sasha and Dan is 29.6 meters. Since this distance is achieved at $k=72$, the number of steps Sasha has taken by this time is $6 \cdot 72=432$, and the number of steps Dan has taken is $7 \cdot 72=504$.
solution: Answer: 1) $d_{\min }=29.6$ m; 2) Sasha made 432 steps, Dania made 504 steps.

2. Rewrite the equation in the form

$$
\cos 3 a \cdot \sin x+(\sin 3 a-\sin 7 a) \cos x=0
$$

Case 1. $\cos 3 a \neq 0, \sin 3 a-\sin 7 a \neq 0$. We have a homogeneous trigonometric equation, which, as is known, can be reduced to the form

$$
\operatorname{tg} x=\frac{\sin 7 a-\sin 3 a}{\cos 3 a}
$$

Its solutions are given by the formula

$$
x_{n}=\operatorname{arctg}\left(\frac{\sin 7 a-\sin 3 a}{\cos 3 a}\right)+\pi n, n \in Z
$$

from which it follows that there are no solutions among them for which the difference is not equal to $\pi k, k \in Z$.

Case 2. $\cos 3 a \neq 0, \sin 3 a-\sin 7 a=0$. We have the equation

$$
\cos 3 a \cdot \sin x=0
$$

Its solutions are given by the formula

$$
x_{n}=\pi n, n \in Z
$$

from which it follows that there are no solutions among them for which the difference is not equal to $\pi k, k \in Z$.

Case 3. $\cos 3 a=0, \sin 3 a-\sin 7 a \neq 0$. We have the equation $(\sin 3 a-\sin 7 a) \cos x=0$.

Its solutions are given by the formula

$$
x_{n}=\frac{\pi}{2}+\pi n, n \in Z
$$

from which it follows that there are no solutions among them for which the difference is not equal to $\pi k, k \in Z$.

Case 4. $\cos 3 a=0, \sin 3 a-\sin 7 a=0$. We have the equation

$$
0=0
$$

In this case, any $x$ is a solution to this equation. This means that among the solutions there are solutions for which the difference is not equal to $\pi k, k \in Z$.

$$
\text { Find } a, \text { for which }\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\cos 3 a=0, \\
\sin 3 a-\sin 7 a=0 .
\end{array}\right. \text { The first equation of the }
$$

system has solutions

$$
a=\frac{\pi(2 m+1)}{6}, m \in Z
$$

The second equation of the system can be rewritten as

$$
-2 \sin 2 a \cdot \cos 5 a=0
$$

Write its solutions

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l}
a=\frac{\pi n}{2}, n \in Z \\
a=\frac{\pi(2 k+1)}{10}, k \in Z
\end{array}\right.
$$

As a result, we obtain a combination of two systems

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { c } 
{ a = \frac { \pi ( 2 m + 1 ) } { 6 } , m \in Z , } \\
{ a = \frac { \pi n } { 2 } , n \in Z ; }
\end{array} \quad ( * ) \quad \text { and } \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=\frac{\pi(2 m+1)}{6}, m \in Z \\
a=\frac{\pi(2 k+1)}{10}, k \in Z
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

System (*) leads to the linear equation in integers $3 n-2 m=1$. Solving it, we get

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
n=2 t+1, t \in Z \\
m=3 t+1, t \in Z
\end{array}\right.
$$

Substituting $n$ into the expression for $a$, we find $a=\frac{\pi(2 t+1)}{2}, t \in Z$.

System (**) leads to the linear equation in integers $5 m-3 k=-1$. Solving it, we get

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
m=3 t+1, t \in Z \\
k=5 t+2, t \in Z
\end{array}\right.
$$

Substitute $m$ into the expression for $a$:

$$
a=\frac{\pi(2 m+1)}{6}=\frac{\pi(2 t+1)}{2}, t \in Z
$$

We have obtained the same solutions as for system (*). Therefore, no additional solutions have been added, and $a=\frac{\pi(2 t+1)}{2}, t \in Z$.
solution: Answer: $a=\frac{\pi(2 t+1)}{2}, t \in Z$.

3. Rewrite the original equation in the form

$$
16 z^{2}+4 x y z+\left(y^{2}-3\right)=0
$$

This is a quadratic equation in terms of z. It has a solution if $D / 4=4 x^{2} y^{2}-16\left(y^{2}-3\right) \geq 0$. After transformations, we obtain the inequality

$$
y^{2}\left(x^{2}-4\right)+12 \geq 0

If $x^{2}-4 \geq 0$, then the first term on the left side of the inequality is non-negative, and consequently, the left side is greater than or equal to 12 for any $y$. If $x^{2}-4<0$, then the first term on the left side of the inequality is negative, and by choosing $y$, we can make the left side of the inequality negative. Therefore, the condition of the problem is satisfied by $x$ for which $x^{2}-4 \geq 0$. From this, we find $x \in(-\infty ;-2] \cup[2 ;+\infty)$.

4. Let's write the natural number $a$ in its canonical form:

$$
a=p_{1}^{s_{1}} \cdot p_{2}^{s_{2}} \cdot \ldots \cdot p_{n}^{s_{n}}
$$

where $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}$ are distinct prime numbers, and $s_{1}, s_{2}, \ldots, s_{n}$ are natural numbers.

It is known that the number of natural divisors of $a$, including 1 and $a$, is equal to $\left(s_{1}+1\right)\left(s_{2}+1\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(s_{n}+1\right)$. According to the problem, this number is 101. Since 101 is a prime number, all the brackets in the product are equal to 1, except for one which is equal to 101. Therefore, the number $a=p^{100}$, and its divisors are $d_{1}=1, d_{2}=p, d_{3}=p^{2}, \ldots$, $d_{101}=p^{100}$.

Let's calculate the sum of the divisors:

$$
\Sigma_{d}=1+p+p^{2}+\ldots+p^{100}=\frac{p^{101}-1}{p-1}=\frac{a \sqrt[100]{a}-1}{\sqrt[100]{a}-1}
$$

Let's calculate the product of the divisors:

$$
\Pi_{d}=p^{1+2+\ldots+100}=p^{50 \cdot 101}=\sqrt{a^{101}}
$$

problem: 4. Answer: $S=\left(2^{9}-1\right) \cdot \frac{\left(3^{4}-1\right)}{2} \cdot \frac{\left(5^{7}-1\right)}{4}$
solution:
Solution

The sum of divisors of the form $2^{0} \cdot 3^{0} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1, . .6$ is $1+5+5^{2}+\ldots+5^{6}=\frac{5^{7}-1}{4}=s_{1}$.

The sum of divisors of the form $2^{0} \cdot 3^{1} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6 \quad$ is $3 \cdot \frac{5^{7}-1}{4}=3 s_{1}, \quad$ the sum of divisors of the form $2^{0} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6$ is $3^{2} \cdot \frac{5^{7}-1}{4}=3^{2} s_{1} \quad$ and so on, the sum of divisors of the form $2^{0} \cdot 3^{q} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6 ; q=1,2,3$ is

$\left(3^{1}+3^{2}+3^{3}\right) \frac{5^{7}-1}{4}=\left(1+3^{1}+3^{2}+3^{3}\right) \frac{5^{7}-1}{4}-s_{1}=s_{2} \rightarrow s_{1}+s_{2}=\frac{3^{4}-1}{2} \cdot \frac{5^{7}-1}{4}$

Finally, the sum of divisors of the form $2^{1} \cdot 3^{q} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6 ; q=1,2,3$ is $2\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right)$, the sum of divisors of the form $2^{2} \cdot 3^{q} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6 ; q=1,2,3$ is $2^{2}\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right) \quad$ and so on, the sum of divisors of the form $2^{r} \cdot 3^{q} \cdot 5^{p}, p=1,2, \ldots, 6 ; q=1,2,3 ; r=1,2, \ldots, 8$ is

$\left(2+2^{2}+\ldots+2^{8}\right)\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right)=\left(1+2+2^{2}+\ldots+2^{8}\right)\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right)-\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right)=s_{3}$.

From which the sum of all divisors $s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{3}=\left(2^{9}-1\right)\left(s_{1}+s_{2}\right)=\left(2^{9}-1\right) \cdot \frac{\left(3^{4}-1\right)}{2} \cdot \frac{\left(5^{7}-1\right)}{4}$

Using the property $\operatorname{GCD}(x, y) \cdot \operatorname{LCM}(x, y)=x y$, we get

Substituting $\operatorname{LCM}(x, y)$ into the equation above, we have

Dividing the last equation by $y^{2}$, we get a quadratic equation in terms of $\frac{x}{y}$:

Let $A$ and $E$ be the centers of circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ with radii $r$ and $R$, respectively $(r<R)$, and by the problem's condition, $A \in \omega_{2}$, while $B$ and $C$ are the points of intersection of these circles. Note that their common chord $BC$ is perpendicular to the segment $AE$. We have $AB = AC = r, \quad EB = EC = EA = R$. Let $\square BAE = \square CAE = \alpha, \quad \square BEA = \square CEA = \gamma$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_db9ce7a1cbcec365545eg-06.jpg?height=402&width=545&top_left_y=183&top_left_x=479)

Write the formula for calculating the area of the union of circles $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$, bounded by circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$:

$$
S_{\Omega_{1} \cup \Omega_{2}} = S_{\Omega_{1}} + S_{\Omega_{2}} - S_{\Omega_{1} \cap \Omega_{2}},
$$

where $S_{\Omega_{1}} = \pi r^{2}, S_{\Omega_{2}} = \pi R^{2}$ are the areas of circles $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$, and $S_{\Omega_{1} \cap \Omega_{2}}$ is the area of their intersection.

Find $S_{\Omega_{1} \cap \Omega_{2}}$. The intersection $\Omega_{1} \cap \Omega_{2}$ consists of two segments $BDC \in \Omega_{1}$ and $BAC \in \Omega_{2}$. Denote the areas of these segments by $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, respectively.

The area $S_{1}$ of segment $BDC$ is the difference between the area of sector $BDCA$ and the area of $\square ABC$:

$$
S_{1} = \frac{(2\alpha) r^{2}}{2} - \frac{1}{2} r^{2} \sin 2\alpha
$$

Since $\square ABE$ is isosceles $(AE = BE)$, we have $\cos \alpha = \frac{r}{2R}$. Then

$$
\begin{gathered}
\alpha = \arccos \frac{r}{2R}, \sin \alpha = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{r}{2R}\right)^{2}} \\
\sin 2\alpha = 2 \sin \alpha \cos \alpha = \frac{r}{2R} \cdot \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{r}{2R}\right)^{2}}
\end{gathered}
$$

By the problem's condition, $r = 1, \quad R = 2$. Substituting these values into the above formulas: $\quad \cos \alpha = \frac{1}{4}, \quad \alpha = \arccos \frac{1}{4}$, $\sin \alpha = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}, \sin 2\alpha = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}$. Then

$$
S_{1} = \arccos \frac{1}{4} - \frac{\sqrt{15}}{16}
$$

The area $S_{2}$ of segment $BAC$ is the difference between the area of sector $BACE$ and the area of $\square CBE$:

$$
S_{2} = \frac{(2\gamma) R^{2}}{2} - \frac{1}{2} R^{2} \sin 2\gamma
$$

Since $\square ABE$ is isosceles $(AE = BE)$, we have $\gamma = \pi - 2\alpha$. Find

$$
\begin{gathered}
\cos \gamma = \cos (\pi - 2\alpha) = -\cos 2\alpha = \sin^{2} \alpha - \cos^{2} \alpha = \frac{15}{16} - \frac{1}{16} = \frac{7}{8} \\
\sin \gamma = \sqrt{1 - \frac{49}{64}} = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}, \sin 2\gamma = \frac{7\sqrt{15}}{32}
\end{gathered}
$$

Then

$$
S_{2} = 4\left(\pi - 2 \arccos \frac{1}{4}\right) - \frac{7\sqrt{15}}{16}
$$

Calculate the area of the intersection of circles $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$:

$$
S_{\Omega_{1} \cap \Omega_{2}} = S_{1} + S_{2} = 4\pi - 7 \arccos \frac{1}{4} - \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}
$$

Substituting the obtained result into the formula for calculating the area of the union of circles $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$, we find:

$$
S_{\Omega_{1} \cup \Omega_{2}} = \pi + 4\pi - \left(4\pi - 7 \arccos \frac{1}{4} - \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}\right) = \pi + 7 \arccos \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.
$$
solution: Answer: $S=\pi+7 \arccos \frac{1}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$.

problem: 2. When solving the problem, the following reasoning is possible. All the required numbers are divisible by 6, which means that the numbers 2 and 3 must be present in their prime factorization. Let then \(a_{1}=2^{m} \cdot 3^{n}\). If in the subsequent numbers \(a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{9}\) the exponents \(m\) monotonically increase, and the exponents \(n\) monotonically decrease, for example, \(a_{2}=2^{m+1} \cdot 3^{n-1}, a_{3}=2^{m+2} \cdot 3^{n-2}, \ldots, a_{9}=2^{m+8} \cdot 3^{n-8}\), then none of the numbers can be divisible by another, thus satisfying the second condition of the problem. Further, the smallest exponent of two in the cubes of these numbers is \(3 m\) and it must be no less than the largest exponent of two in the squares of the numbers, that is, \(2(m+8)\). From \(3 m \geq 2(m+8)\) we get that \(m \geq 16\). Similarly, for the exponents of three, we have the condition \(3(n-8) \geq 2 n\). From which \(n \geq 24\). Thus, for \(m \geq 16\) and \(n \geq 24\), the cube of each of the numbers \(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{9}\) will be divisible by the square of any other of them.

For example, $a_{1}=2^{16} \cdot 3^{24}, a_{2}=2^{17} \cdot 3^{23}, a_{3}=2^{18} \cdot 3^{22}, \ldots$, $a_{9}=2^{24} \cdot 3^{16}$.

The area of the trapezoid $S = \frac{a+b}{2} h = (a+b) r = 8r^2 = \frac{c^2}{2}$. The area of the inscribed circle $S_1 = \pi r^2$, so $\frac{S}{S_1} = \frac{8r^2}{\pi r^2} = \frac{8}{\pi}$.

Next, $M D = M Q + Q D = \frac{a}{2} + \frac{b}{2} = \frac{a+b}{2} = c$. From $\triangle B M D$ we get: $\operatorname{tg} \beta = \frac{2r}{c} = \sin \alpha$, hence $\frac{1}{\cos^2 \beta} = 1 + \sin^2 \alpha = \frac{5}{4}$, thus $\frac{1}{\cos \beta} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$. Therefore, $B D = \frac{c}{\cos \beta} = \frac{c \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

By the Law of Sines, $2R = \frac{B D}{\sin \alpha} = c \sqrt{5} \Rightarrow R = \frac{c \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

Thus, the area of the circumscribed circle $S_2 = \pi R^2 = \frac{5 \pi c^2}{4}$.

Then $\frac{S}{S_2} = \frac{c^2}{2} \frac{4}{5 \pi c^2} = \frac{2}{5 \pi}$.
solution: Answer: $\quad \frac{S}{S_{1}}=\frac{8}{\pi}, \quad \frac{S}{S_{2}}=\frac{2}{5 \pi}$.

problem: 1. The given polynomials $p_{1}(x)$ and $p_{2}(x)$ of degrees 2 and 3, respectively, are such that the polynomial $p(x)=p_{1}(x)+p_{2}(x)$ has three roots $x_{1}=-1, x_{2}=2, x_{3}=-3$. It is known that all roots of the polynomial $p_{1}(x)$ are also roots of the polynomial $p_{2}(x)$. Find the polynomial product $p_{1}(x) \cdot p_{2}(x)$.
solution:
1. Solution. Let $p_{1}(x)=x^{2}+a x+b$. Since the roots of the polynomial $p_{1}(x)$ are contained among the roots of the polynomial $p_{2}(x)$, the latter is divisible by $p_{1}(x)$ without a remainder, that is, $p_{2}(x)=(x+c)\left(x^{2}+a x+b\right)$. Then

$p_{1}(x)+p_{2}(x)=(x+c+1)\left(x^{2}+a x+b\right)$.

On the other hand, by the condition $p(x)=p_{1}(x)+p_{2}(x)=(x+1)(x-2)(x+3)$.

There are three possible cases.

Case 1

$\left\{\begin{array}{c}x+c+1=x+1 \\ x^{2}+a x+b=(x-2)(x+3)\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}c=0 \\ a=1 \\ b=-6\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}p_{1}(x)=x^{2}+x-6 \\ p_{2}(x)=x\left(x^{2}+x-6\right)\end{array} \rightarrow p_{1} \cdot p_{2}=x\left(x^{2}+x-6\right)^{2}\right.\right.\right.$.

Case 2

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { c } 
{ x + c + 1 = x - 2 } \\
{ x ^ { 2 } + a x + b = ( x + 1 ) ( x + 3 ) }
\end{array} \rightarrow \left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ c = - 3 } \\
{ a = 4 } \\
{ b = 3 }
\end{array} \rightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{c}
p_{1}(x)=x^{2}+4 x+3 \\
p_{2}(x)=(x-3)\left(x^{2}+4 x+3\right)
\end{array} \rightarrow p_{1} \cdot p_{2}=(x-3)\left(x^{2}+4 x+3\right)^{2}\right.\right.\right.
$$

## Case 3

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { c } 
{ x + c + 1 = x + 3 } \\
{ x ^ { 2 } + a x + b = ( x + 1 ) ( x - 2 ) }
\end{array} \rightarrow \left\{\begin{array} { c } 
{ c = 2 } \\
{ a = - 1 } \\
{ b = - 2 }
\end{array} \rightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{c}
p_{1}(x)=x^{2}-x-2 \\
p_{2}(x)=(x+2)\left(x^{2}-x-2\right)
\end{array} \rightarrow p_{1} \cdot p_{2}=(x+2)\left(x^{2}-x-2\right)^{2}\right.\right.\right.
$$

problem: 2. On the number line, there is a set of positive, three-digit integers $a$, for which the sum of the digits in their notation equals 16. Find the greatest and the smallest distance between two numbers from this set.

The smallest number satisfying these conditions is $a_{\min }=169$, and the largest number is $a_{\max }=970$. The greatest distance is their difference $d_{\max }=a_{\max }-a_{\min }=801$. The smallest distance between numbers from this set is the smallest distance between adjacent numbers. Let some number from this set be of the form $a=N+10 x+y(N \geq 100)$, then the next number from this set is $b=N+10(x+1)+(y-1)$. The difference between them is $b-a=9$, for example, one can choose $a=169$, and $b=178$. Thus, $d_{\max }=801$, and $d_{\min }=9$.

problem: 3. Calculate the value of the expression $\sin \frac{b \pi}{36}$, where $b$ is the sum of all distinct numbers obtained from the number $a=987654321$ by cyclic permutations of its digits (in a cyclic permutation, all digits of the number, except the last one, are shifted one place to the right, and the last one is moved to the first place).
solution:
3. Solution. When summing all different numbers obtained from the number $a=987654321$, including the number $a$ itself, in each digit place we will get the sum of all its digits $9+8+7+\ldots+3+2+1=45$. Therefore, $b=45\left(10^{8}+10^{7}+10^{6}+\ldots+10^{2}+10+1\right)=45 \cdot 111111111=4999999995$. Calculate $\frac{\pi b}{36}=\frac{\pi \cdot 45 \cdot 111111111}{36}=\frac{\pi \cdot 555555555}{4}=138888888 \pi+\frac{3}{4} \pi$. From this, it follows that
$\sin \frac{\pi b}{36}=\sin \left(138888888 \pi+\frac{3}{4} \pi\right)=\sin \frac{3 \pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

problem: 4. Let $r_{n}$ denote the remainder of the division of $n$ by 3. Find the sequence of numbers $X_{n}$, which are the roots of the equation $(n+1) x^{r_{n}}-n(n+2) x^{r_{n+1}}+n^{2} x^{r_{n+2}}=0$ for any natural number $n$, and its limit is equal to 1.
solution:
4. Solution. Note that, since $r_{n}$ is the remainder of the division of $n$ by 3, it can take three different values: 0, 1, and 2.

Case 1. $n=3 k, k \in \square$, then $r_{n}=0, r_{n+1}=1, r_{n+2}=2$. The equation is: $n^{2} x^{2}-n(n+2) x+n+1=0$.

Its roots are

$x_{1, n}=\frac{1}{n}, \quad x_{2, n}=\frac{n+1}{n}$.

The condition of the problem ($x_{n} \rightarrow 1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$) is satisfied only by $x_{2, n}$.

Case 2. $n=3 k+1, k \in \square \cup\{0\}$, then $r_{n}=1, r_{n+1}=2, r_{n+2}=0$. The equation is: $-n(n+2) x^{2}+(n+1) x+n^{2}=0$.

Its roots are

$x_{1, n}=\frac{n+1-\sqrt{4 n^{4}+8 n^{3}+n^{2}+2 n+1}}{2 n(n+2)}, \quad x_{2, n}=\frac{n+1+\sqrt{4 n^{4}+8 n^{3}+n^{2}+2 n+1}}{2 n(n+2)}$.

The condition of the problem ($x_{n} \rightarrow 1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$) is satisfied only by $x_{2, n}$.

Case 3. $n=3 k+2, k \in \square \cup\{0\}$, then $r_{n}=2, r_{n+1}=0, r_{n+2}=1$. The equation is: $(n+1) x^{2}+n^{2} x-n(n+2)=0$.

Its roots are

$x_{1, n}=\frac{-n^{2}-\sqrt{n^{4}+4 n^{3}+12 n^{2}+8 n}}{2(n+1)}$

$x_{2, n}=\frac{-n^{2}+\sqrt{n^{4}+4 n^{3}+12 n^{2}+8 n}}{2(n+1)}=\frac{4 n^{3}+12 n^{2}+8 n}{2(n+1)\left(\sqrt{n^{4}+4 n^{3}+12 n^{2}+8 n}+n^{2}\right)}$.

The condition of the problem ($x_{n} \rightarrow 1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$) is satisfied only by $x_{2, n}$.

Thus, the desired sequence is

$x_{n}=x_{2, n}=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}\frac{n+1}{n}, & n=3 k, k \in \square, \\ \frac{n+1+\sqrt{4 n^{4}+8 n^{3}+n^{2}+2 n+1}}{2 n(n+2)}, & n=3 k+1, k \in \square \cup\{0\}, \\ \frac{-n^{2}+\sqrt{n^{4}+4 n^{3}+12 n^{2}+8 n}}{2(n+1)}, & n=3 k+2, k \in \square \cup\{0\} .\end{array}\right.$

problem:
5. Let the distance between points $A$ and $B$ be $L$ mm, and the length of the flea's jump be $d$ mm. If $L$ were divisible by $d$ exactly, the flea's strategy of jumping in a straight line connecting points $A$ and $B$ would be optimal. It would take $\frac{L}{d}=n, n \in \mathbb{N}$ jumps to reach the goal. Given $L=20190, d=13$, we have $\frac{L}{d}=\frac{20190}{13}=1553.07 \ldots$, and moving in a straight line $AB$, the flea would not be able to reach point $B$ from point $A$ in an integer number of steps $n=1553$. We will show that there exists a strategy to reach the goal in $n+1$ steps.

Since the double inequality $n d < L < (n+1) d$ holds, there exists a triangle with sides $BC = d = 13$, $AC = n d = 20189$, and $AB = L = 20190$. Using the cosine rule, we have

$$
\alpha = \arccos \frac{L^2 + n^2 d^2 - d^2}{2 \cdot n d \cdot L} = \arccos \frac{20190^2 + 20189^2 - 13^2}{2 \cdot 20189 \cdot 20190} \approx 0.04^\circ
$$

Then, the flea, making 1553 jumps in a direction that forms an angle $\alpha$ with the direction of ray $AB$, reaches point $C$. From there, it makes the last, 1554th, jump to point $B$.

problem:
5. Each vertex of the large cube is a vertex of one of eight small cubes. On the three faces adjacent to this vertex, three digits are drawn, the sum of which can take eight values $6,7,9,10,11,12,14,15$.

"The smallest angle" is defined by the digits $1,2,3$. "The largest angle" is defined by $4,5,6$. Then, if the entire cube is composed of "smallest angles," we get:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_2e21e31e5ef16f9e7b82g-3.jpg?height=479&width=486&top_left_y=669&top_left_x=803)
$6 \cdot 8=48$, from "largest angles" $-15 \cdot 8=120$.

We will prove that the value $s$ - the sum of the digits on the faces - takes all values in the interval $(48 ; 120)$. We reason by induction. It is established that the value $s=48$ is achieved. The value $s=49$ is achieved if one vertex with the set $(6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6)$ is changed to a vertex with the set $(6,6,6,7,6,6,6,6)$. Suppose $a \in (48 ; 120)$ and all values $s=k, 48 \leq k \leq a$ are achieved. We will prove that the value $s=a+1$ is also achieved. The statement is obvious if the set $\left(p_{1} ; p_{2} ; p_{3}, p_{4}, p_{5} ; p_{6} ; p_{7}, p_{8}\right)$, realizing the value $s=a$, contains one of $p=6,9,10,11,14$. In this case, it is possible to change such a $p$ to $p+1$ in one of the vertices of the large cube, which means increasing $s$ by one. In the opposite case, only $p=7,12,15$ are present, and not all $p=15$. If the set $\left(p_{1} ; p_{2} ; p_{3}, p_{4}, p_{5} ; p_{6} ; p_{7}, p_{8}\right)$, realizing $s=a$ in this case, contains two vertices with $p=7$, then one can be used to increase $s$ by 2, and the second to decrease the result by 1, i.e., in the end, $s$ will increase by 1. Similarly with two vertices with $p=12$. If the set, giving $s=a$, contains $p=7$ and $p=12$ once each, then there must be a vertex with $p=15$, which can be used to decrease $a+2$ by 1.
solution: Answer: all integers in the interval $[48 ; 120]$.

1. Consider an arbitrary fractional-linear function $f(x)=\frac{e x+b}{c x+d}, e d-b c \neq 0, c \neq 0$. Let's determine the relationship between the coefficients $e, b, c, d$ for which it coincides with its inverse

$$
f(f(x))=\frac{e \cdot \frac{e x+b}{c x+d}+b}{c \cdot \frac{e x+b}{c x+d}+d}=\frac{\left(e^{2}+b c\right) x+(e b+b d)}{c(e+d) x+\left(d^{2}+b c\right)} \equiv x, x \neq-\frac{d}{c}
$$

If $(e+d) \neq 0$, then the identity (*) is impossible, since the equality of the right and left parts of (*) can be no more than for two values of $x$. If $e+d=0$, then

$$
f(f(x))=\frac{\left(e^{2}+b c\right) x}{\left(e^{2}+b c\right)} \equiv x, e^{2}+b c \neq 0
$$

Thus, equation 1) has an infinite number of solutions if

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=-(a-2) \\
a^{2}-5 \neq 0 \\
a(a-2)+5 \neq 0
\end{array}\right.
$$

From this, we find $a=1$. The corresponding function is $f(x)=\frac{x-5}{x-1}$.

Equation 2) has an infinite number of solutions, in addition to $a=1$, in the case when the fractional-linear $(e+d \neq 0)$ function $g(x)=f(f(x))$ coincides with its inverse. According to (*), this happens if

$$
e^{2}+b c=-\left(d^{2}+b c\right) \text { or } e^{2}+2 b c+d^{2}=0
$$

Under the conditions of variant 1, the relation $(* *)$ will take the form:

$$
a^{2}-10+(a-2)^{2}=0 \text { or } a^{2}-2 a-3=0 \text {. }
$$

From this, we find $a=-1$ or $a=3$. The second condition $\left(e^{2}+b c\right)^{2}+c(e b+b d)(e+d) \neq 0$ is satisfied for $a=-1$ and $a=3$. The corresponding functions for these values are

$$

$$

2. If the number 2 is the sum of $\sin x + \sin y$, then $\sin x = 1$, $\sin y = 1$, and $\sin x - \sin y = 0$, but such a number is not among the given options. 1. According to the properties of logarithms, after transformations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log _{2}\left(b_{2} b_{3} \ldots b_{n}\right)=\log _{2} b_{1}^{2} \\
& b_{2} b_{3} \ldots b_{n}=b_{1}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the general term of a geometric progression, we get

$$
b_{2}=b_{1} q, b_{3}=b_{1} q^{2}, \ldots, b_{n}=b_{1} q^{n-1}
$$

and using these relations and the formula for the sum of an arithmetic progression

$$
1+2+\ldots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
$$

we transform the obtained equation to

$$
b_{1}^{n-1} q^{1+2+\ldots+(n-1)}=b_{1}^{2} \Rightarrow b_{1}^{n-3} q^{n(n-1) / 2}=1
$$

Taking the logarithm with base $q$, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (n-3) \log _{q} b_{1}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=0 \\
& \frac{n-3}{2} \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=0 \\
& \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-\frac{n(n-1)}{n-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\frac{n(n-1)}{n-3}=\frac{n(n-3)+2(n-3)+6}{n-3}=n+2+\frac{6}{n-3}
$$

then

$$
\log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-n-2-\frac{6}{n-3} .
$$

According to the problem's condition, the quantity

$$
\frac{6}{n-3}
$$

must be an integer. This is possible only for

$$
n \in\{2 ; 4 ; 5 ; 6 ; 9\}
$$

Substituting the specified values into the formula obtained above, we find all possible values of the desired quantity

$$
\begin{aligned}
& n=2 \Rightarrow \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=2 \\
& n=4 \Rightarrow \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-12 \\
& n=5 \Rightarrow \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-10 \\
& n=6 \Rightarrow \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-10 \\
& n=9 \Rightarrow \log _{q} b_{1}^{2}=-12
\end{aligned}
$$

From this, it is clear that the smallest value of the desired quantity is -12 and it is achieved for two values: $n=4$ and $n=9$.
solution: Answer: -12 when $n=4$ and $n=9$.

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l }

{ y \leq \frac { 5 } { 1 2 } L } \\
{ L - ( x + y ) \leq \frac { 5 } { 1 2 } L }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \leq \frac{5}{12} L \\
