Solution

The expression $\cos x + \cos y + \cos z = \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) + \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - y\right) + \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - z\right) = \sin u + \sin v + \sin w = 2 \cdot S_{ANMB}$,

where $u = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) \geq 0, v = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - y\right) \geq 0, w = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - z\right) \geq 0, u + v + w = \frac{\pi}{2}$

We will show that the triplet $(x; y; z), x + y + z = \frac{\pi}{2}, x > 0, y > 0, z > 0$ cannot be the desired one for the minimum. Indeed, under these conditions $u > 0, v > 0, w > 0$ and the area of the quadrilateral $ANMB$ (see figure) can be reduced

Then the expression

$\cos x + \cos y + \cos z = 1 + \cos x + \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = 1 + \sin x + \cos x = 1 + \sqrt{2} \sin \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right), x \in \left[0 ; \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$

We need to find the coordinates of points $M$ and $N$ for which $\rho^{2}$ takes its minimum possible value.

For a fixed point $M$, $\rho^{2}(t)$ depends on $t$, and at the point of minimum, its derivative with respect to the variable $t$ is zero: $-2(x-t)+2\left(x^{2}-4x+7+t\right)=0$ (*). solution:
Solution

Let $a=p_{1}^{r_{1}} \cdot p_{2}^{r_{2}} \cdot \ldots \cdot p_{m}^{r_{m}}, b=p_{2}^{r_{2}} \cdot \ldots \cdot p_{m}^{r_{m}} \cdot$ Here $p_{k}$ are prime divisors, $r_{k}$ are their multiplicities.

Let $q_{i}$ be any divisor of the number $b$. Then $q_{i}, p_{1} q_{i}, p_{1}^{2} q_{i}, \ldots, p_{1}^{r_{1}} q_{i}$ are divisors of the number $a$. Their sum $\sigma_{i}=q_{i}\left(1+p_{1}+p_{1}^{2}+\ldots+p_{1}^{r_{1}}\right)$. Then the sum of all divisors of the number $a$ is $\Sigma_{a}=\sum_{i} \sigma_{i}=\left(1+p_{1}+p_{1}^{2}+\ldots+p_{1}^{r_{1}}\right) \sum_{i} q_{i}=\left(1+p_{1}+p_{1}^{2}+\ldots+p_{1}^{r_{1}}\right) \Sigma_{b}$

Repeating the same for $\Sigma_{b}$, we get the formula for the sum of all divisors of the number $a$:

$\Sigma_{a}=\left(1+p_{1}+p_{1}^{2}+\ldots+p_{1}^{r_{1}}\right) \cdot\left(1+p_{2}+p_{2}^{2}+\ldots+p_{2}^{r_{2}}\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(1+p_{m}+p_{m}^{2}+\ldots+p_{m}^{r_{m}}\right)$

For the variant $1 a=540=2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5$ and $\Sigma_{a}=\left(1+2+2^{2}\right) \cdot\left(1+3+3^{2}+3^{3}\right) \cdot(1+5)=7 \cdot 40 \cdot 6=1680$

Solution

Prime factorization: $a=2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{3} \cdot 7^{2}$. The divisors of the numbers $a_{1}=2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 7^{2}$ and $a_{2}=2^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \cdot 7^{2}$ are divisors of $a$ that are not divisible by 15. The number $a_{1}$ has $4 \times 3 \times 3=36$ distinct divisors, and the number $a_{2}$ has $4 \times 4 \times 3=48$ distinct divisors. The GCD $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right)=2^{3} \cdot 7^{2}$, so all divisors of the GCD $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right)$ are common divisors of $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$. Their number is $4 \times 3=12$. Therefore, the number of divisors we are looking for is $36+48-12=72$. The largest of them is $a_{2}=49000$.

Solution.

Case 1. $a>0$

The solution to the first inequality is $x \leq \frac{2}{a}$, the solution to the second inequality is $x \geq-\frac{a}{2}$. The solution to the system is the interval $\left[-\frac{a}{2} ; \frac{2}{a}\right]$, the length of which is $\frac{2}{a}+\frac{a}{2}=2 \rightarrow \frac{(a-2)^{2}}{2 a}=0 \rightarrow a=2$.

Case 2. $a=0$

The first inequality is satisfied for all $x$, the second inequality is satisfied for $x \geq 0$. The solution to the system is a half-line, not an interval.

The solution to the first inequality is $x \geq \frac{2}{a}$, the solution to the second inequality is $-x \geq-\frac{a}{2}$. The solution to the system is the half-line $x \geq-\frac{a}{2}$, not an interval.

problem: 5. Answer: into $(n-2)$ triangles.
solution:
Solution.

Let the best dissection contain $m$ triangles. We will show that this number can be reduced by at least 1 if there is a triangle among them, all vertices of which are inside the polygon (Fig. 1)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b6d3c8ec908d21127f56g-2.jpg?height=560&width=434&top_left_y=1262&top_left_x=731)

Fig. 1

The highlighted triangle can be "collapsed into a point," suggesting a new way of dissection with fewer triangles. Therefore, the best dissection does not contain such triangles. We will show that the number $m$ can be reduced if among the triangles there is one with two vertices inside the polygon (Fig. 2)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b6d3c8ec908d21127f56g-2.jpg?height=551&width=414&top_left_y=2100&top_left_x=775)

Fig. 2

By "collapsing" the two points $A$ and $B$ into one, a dissection method with fewer triangles can be obtained. Therefore, in the best dissection method, there cannot be more than one vertex of the triangles inside the polygon. We will show that if there is one vertex, then in the best dissection, the other vertices of the triangles must coincide with the vertices of the polygon (Fig. 3)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b6d3c8ec908d21127f56g-3.jpg?height=560&width=420&top_left_y=394&top_left_x=824)

Fig. 3

By moving points $B$ and $C$ to the vertices of the polygon, the number of triangles in the dissection can be reduced. Therefore, if there is one vertex of the triangles inside the polygon, the best dissection contains $n$ triangles (Fig. 4)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b6d3c8ec908d21127f56g-3.jpg?height=543&width=414&top_left_y=1156&top_left_x=912)

Fig. 4

Finally, the case where none of the vertices of the triangles are inside the polygon, and all others must be at the vertices of the polygon, leads to a dissection along rays emanating from one vertex (it doesn't matter which one!) (Fig. 5)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b6d3c8ec908d21127f56g-3.jpg?height=565&width=397&top_left_y=1899&top_left_x=998)

Such a dissection contains $(n-2)$ triangles. In variant 1, $n=90$, so the minimum number of triangles is 88.

problem: 2. Answer: $a=\frac{3}{2}, a=-12$
solution:
Solution. $P\left(x^{2}\right)=a x^{4}-3 x^{2}+5 \rightarrow P\left(x^{2}\right)-P(x)=a x^{2}\left(x^{2}-1\right)-3 x(x-1)=0$.
$x=0, x=1$ are solutions for any $a$. The remaining roots satisfy the equation: $a x^{2}+a x-3=0$. The original equation has three roots if $x=0$ or $x=1$ are solutions of the equation $a x^{2}+a x-3=0$. For $x=0$ this is impossible, $x=1$ is a solution when $a=3 / 2$. In this case, $x=-2$ is the third root. The second option is when the discriminant of the equation $a x^{2}+a x-3=0$ is zero, i.e. $a^{2}+12 a=0 \rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{c}a=0 \\ a=-12\end{array}\right.$. . For $a=0$ there are no roots, and for $a=-12$ there is a root $x=-1 / 2$.

Solution.

Multiply both sides of the second equation by the GCD $(x, y)$ and use the equality GCD $(x, y) \cdot \operatorname{LCM}(x, y)=x \cdot y$. Then $x \cdot(\text { GCD }(x, y))^{2}=x y \rightarrow y=(\text { GCD }(x, y))^{2}$, i.e., $y$ is a square of an integer. Out of all possible $y \in[1 ; 11]$, there are only three such numbers: $y_{1}=1, y_{2}=4, y_{3}=9$. Let's check each of them:

Case 1. $y_{1}=1, x_{1}=11 \rightarrow$ GCD $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)=1, \operatorname{LCM}\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)=11 \rightarrow$ the equation is satisfied.

Case 2. $y_{2}=4, x_{2}=8 \rightarrow$ GCD $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)=4, \operatorname{LCM}\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)=8 \rightarrow$ the equation is not satisfied.

Case 3. $y_{3}=9, x_{3}=3 \rightarrow$ GCD $\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right)=3$, LCM $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)=9 \rightarrow$ the equation is satisfied.

problem: 3. In the decimal representation of a six-digit number $a$, there are no zeros and the sum of its digits is 18. Find the sum of all different numbers obtained from the number $a$ by cyclic permutations of its digits. In a cyclic permutation, all digits of the number, except the last one, are shifted one place to the right, and the last one is moved to the first place.
solution:
3. Solution. Case 1. The number $a=333333$. This number does not change under cyclic permutations, so it is the only one and the sum of the numbers is the number itself, that is, 333333.

Case 2. The number $a$ consists of three identical cycles of two digits each, for example, $a=242424$. Such numbers have two different cyclic permutations: 242424 and 424242, the sum of which is $666666=2 \cdot 333333$. For any other such number, we will get the same sum of its cyclic permutations: $151515+515151=666666$ and so on.

Case 3. The number $a$ consists of two identical cycles of three digits each, for example, $a=423423$. Such numbers have three different cyclic permutations: 423423, 342342, and 234234, the sum of which is $999999=3 \cdot 333333$. For any other such number, we will get the same sum of its cyclic permutations: $513513+351351+135135=999999$ and so on.

Case 4. All six cyclic permutations are different. Let $a=a_{5} \cdot 10^{5}+a_{4} \cdot 10^{4}+a_{3} \cdot 10^{3}+a_{2} \cdot 10^{2}+a_{1} \cdot 10+a_{0}$.

If we write out all its cyclic permutations in the same form, add the results, and regroup the terms, we get

$a_{5}\left(10^{5}+10^{4}+\ldots+1\right)+a_{4}\left(10^{5}+10^{4}+\ldots+1\right)+\ldots+a_{0}\left(10^{5}+10^{4}+\ldots+1\right)=$ $=\left(a_{5}+a_{4}+a_{3}+a_{2}+a_{1}+a_{0}\right)\left(10^{5}+10^{4}+\ldots+1\right)=18 \cdot 111111=1999998$

problem: 4. Let $r_{n}$ denote the remainder of the division of a natural number $n$ by 6. For which $n$ is the equality $r_{2 n+3}=r_{5 n+6}$ true?
solution: 4. Solution. The numbers $2 n+3$ and $5 n+6$ have the same remainder if their difference $5 n+6-(2 n+3)=3 n+3$ is divisible by 6, i.e., $3 n+3=6 k$. From this, we get $n=2 k-1, k \in \square$.

problem: 5. On a sheet of paper, 14 parallel lines $L$ and 15 lines $P$ perpendicular to them are drawn. The distances between adjacent lines from $L$ from the first to the last are given: 2;4;6;2;4;6;2;4;6;2;4;6;2. The distances between adjacent lines from $P$ are also known: 3;1;2;6;3;1;2;6;3;1;2;6;3;1. Find the greatest length of the side of a square whose boundaries lie on the lines $L$ and $P$.
solution: 5. Solution. We will prove that the maximum length of the side of the square is 40. Calculate the distance from the first to the last line in $P: 3+1+2+6+3+1+2+6+3+1+2+6+3+1=40$. Therefore, the side length of the square cannot be more than 40. On the other hand, in $L$ the distance from the second line to the third line from the end is $4+6+2+4+6+2+4+6+2+4=40$. This means that a square with a side length of 40 exists.

solution:
Solution. Let there be $2 n$ chairs around the table (i.e., there are $2 n$ people sitting around the table). On the circle, points mark the chairs. The number $K$ denotes the number of chairs separating Petya and the person sitting on that chair. Then the number of chairs counted by Petya, including Vasya, is

$$
2(1+2+3+\ldots+(n-2))+(n-1)=(n-1)(n-2)+(n-1)=(n-1)^{2}
$$

Let $K_{B}$ be the number of chairs calculated for Vasya. Then

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_546d084242501446d87cg-01.jpg?height=468&width=460&top_left_y=1933&top_left_x=1412)

\[
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(n-1)^{2}-K_{B}=60, \\
0 \leq K_{B} \leq(n-1)
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
0 \leq(n-1)^{2}-60 \leq n-1, \\
K_{B}=(n-1)^{2}-60
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
1+\sqrt{60} \leq n \leq \frac{3+\sqrt{241}}{2} \\
K_{B}=(n-1)^{2}-60
\end{array}\right.\right.\right.
\]

Considering that $n \in \mathbb{N}, 82$ (domain of definition). Note that on the domain of definition, $\log _{2} x \pm \sqrt{\log _{2}^{2} x+1} \neq 0, \quad \log _{2}(x-2) \pm \sqrt{\log _{2}^{2}(x-2)+1} \neq 0$.

Multiplying both sides of the original equation by $\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2} x+1}-\log _{2} x$ and considering that $\left(\log _{2} x+\sqrt{\log _{2}{ }^{2} x+1}\right)\left(\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2} x+1}-\log _{2} x\right)=1$, we get the equivalent equation

$$
\log _{2}(x-2)+\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2}(x-2)+1}=\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2} x+1}-\log _{2} x
$$

Further, multiplying both sides of the original equation by $\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2}(x-2)+1}-\log _{2}(x-2)$, we get another equivalent equation (below we have swapped the left and right sides)

$$
\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2}(x-2)+1}-\log _{2}(x-2)=\log _{2} x+\sqrt{\log _{2}^{2} x+1}
$$

Subtracting equation (2) from equation (1), we get $\log _{2} x+\log _{2}(x-2)=-\left(\log _{2} x+\log _{2}(x-2)\right)$, hence $\log _{2} x+\log _{2}(x-2)=0$, which is equivalent to the system $\left\{\begin{array}{c}\log _{2}(x(x-2))=0 \\ x>2\end{array}\right.$.

Thus, $\left\{\begin{array}{c}x^{2}-2 x=1 \\ x>2\end{array} \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}x=1 \pm \sqrt{2} \\ x>2\end{array} \Leftrightarrow x=1+\sqrt{2}\right.\right.$.

Problem 5 Answer: $P(A)=\frac{687}{7564} \approx 0.09$.

Solution. The sample space of the experiment is the selection of any four cells from the available 64. Then the total number of equally possible outcomes is $n=C_{64}^{4}$ (placement of four identical figures on 64 cells). A favorable outcome is when three identical figures are on the same line and one is not on that line, or four identical figures are on the same line. Then the number of favorable outcomes for one line (horizontal, vertical, or main diagonal) is $C_{8}^{3} \cdot C_{56}^{1}+C_{8}^{4}=3206=2 \cdot 7 \cdot 229$. There are 18 different lines (horizontals, verticals, and main diagonals). Therefore, the total number of favorable outcomes is $m=18 \cdot 2 \cdot 7 \cdot 229$. The desired probability is the ratio of the number of favorable outcomes to the total number of outcomes:

$$
P(A)=\frac{m}{n}=\frac{4 \cdot 9 \cdot 7 \cdot 229 \cdot 4!}{64 \cdot 63 \cdot 62 \cdot 61}=\frac{3 \cdot 229}{2 \cdot 62 \cdot 61}=\frac{687}{7564} \approx 0.09
$$

Problem 6 Answer: $V_{1}: V_{2}=7: 11$

Solution. Construct the section. Since the cutting plane is parallel to the edge $C D$, it will intersect the plane $A C D$ along the line $M P$, parallel to $C D$, and the plane $B C D$ along the line $N D$, also parallel to $C D$. Connecting points $P$ and $Q$, which lie in the same plane, and points $M$ and $N$, which lie in the same plane, we get $M P Q N-$ as the desired section. Let $V$ be the volume of the pyramid, $V_{1}$ be the sum of the volumes of the pyramids $P A B N M$ and $P Q B N$, and $V_{2}=V-V_{1}$.

From the similarity of the pairs of triangles $A C D$ and $A M P$ and from

the condition of the problem, we get that

$$
A M=x, M C=2 x, A P=y, P D=2 y
$$

From this, it follows that $H_{p}=\frac{y}{3 y} \cdot H_{D}=\frac{1}{3} H_{D}$, where $H_{p}$ is the height dropped from the vertex $P$ of the pyramid $P A B N M$, $H_{D}$ is the height dropped from the vertex $D$ of the pyramid $A B C D$, and the area of the base of the pyramid $P A B N M$ is $S_{A B N M}=S_{A B C}-S_{M N C}=S_{A B C}-\frac{2 x}{3 x} \cdot \frac{u}{2 u} \cdot S_{A B C}=\frac{2}{3} S_{A B C}$. Thus,

$$
V_{P A B N M}=\frac{1}{3} H_{p} \cdot S_{A B N M}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{3} H_{D} \cdot \frac{2}{3} S_{A B C}=\frac{2}{9} V
$$

Similarly, from the similarity of the pairs of triangles $B C D$ and $B N Q$ and from the condition of the problem, we get that

$$
C N=N B=u, B Q=Q D=z
$$

From this, it follows that $\tilde{H}_{p}=\frac{2 y}{3 y} \cdot H_{A}=\frac{2}{3} H_{A}$, where $\tilde{H}_{p}$ is the height dropped from the vertex $P$ of the pyramid $P Q B N$, $H_{A}$ is the height dropped from the vertex $A$ of the pyramid $A B C D$, and the area of the base of the pyramid $P Q B N$ is $S_{B N Q}=\frac{u}{2 u} \cdot \frac{z}{2 z} \cdot S_{B C D}=\frac{1}{4} S_{B C D}$. Thus, we find

$$
V_{P Q B N}=\frac{1}{3} \tilde{H}_{P} \cdot S_{Q B N}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{2}{3} H_{A} \cdot \frac{1}{4} S_{D B C}=\frac{1}{6} V
$$

Now we can write that

$$
V_{1}=V_{P A B N M}+V_{P Q B N}=\frac{2}{9} V+\frac{1}{6} V=\frac{7}{18} V, \quad V_{2}=V-V_{1}=\frac{11}{18} V, V_{1}: V_{2}=7: 11
$$

Solution.

The expression $|x|+|y|+|z| \leq \pi$, for all triples $(x ; y ; z)$, satisfying the second equation of the system (on the sphere), since any of the planes $\pm x \pm y \pm z=a$ for $a>\pi$ is at a distance greater than $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$ from the origin and has no common points with the sphere. problem: 4. Answer: $P(A)=\frac{3}{7}$
solution:
Solution

The area of the section by a plane containing at least three vertices of a cube can take three possible values. The first $s_{1}=\frac{a^{2} \sqrt{3}}{2}$, if no two vertices belong to the same edge of the cube (an equilateral triangle with side $a \sqrt{2}$). In the first variant, $a=2$, so $s_{1}=2 \sqrt{7} \approx 3.46$. The second area value $s_{2}=a^{2}$ is realized when the three vertices lie in the same face. In the first variant, $s_{2}=4$. The third value $s_{3}=a^{2} \sqrt{2}$ is realized when two vertices belong to the same edge, and the third vertex does not lie in the face to which this edge belongs. In the first variant, $S_{3}=4 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.65$. Thus, in the condition of variant 1, it is about the probability that $s_{3}$ will be realized.

The total number of different triplets of vertices through which a section plane can pass is $n=C_{8}^{3}=\frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{2 \cdot 3}=56$. If one of the eight vertices of the cube is fixed, then there is a unique triplet of vertices (including the chosen vertex) to which the area $s_{1}$ corresponds. Thus, the number of favorable triplets for this event is $m_{1}=8$. If one of the 6 faces is fixed, then the number of different triplets of vertices realizing $s_{2}$ is $C_{4}^{3}=4$. Thus, the number of different triplets favorable to $s_{2}$ is $m_{2}=4 \cdot 6=24$. If a pair of parallel edges not lying in the same face (there are 6 such pairs) is fixed, then the number of different triplets of vertices favorable to $s_{3}$ is $C_{4}^{3}=4$, so the total number of triplets favorable to this event is $m_{3}=6 \cdot 4=24$. The probability of the desired event is $P(A)=\frac{m_{3}}{n}=\frac{24}{56}=\frac{3}{7}$.

problem: 4. Answer: $s=10$ and $s=11$
solution:
Solution

Let $x, y, z$ be the numbers rolled on the first, second, and third dice. The random variable $s=x+y+z$ takes values from 3 to 18. The total number of outcomes of the experiment is $n=6^{3}$. Let $m(s)$ denote the number of trials (the number of different triples $(x; y; z)$) that favor the event $s=x+y+z$. We decompose this event into the sum of six mutually exclusive events based on the number $z=1,2, \ldots, 6$, rolled on the third die. Let $m_{z}(s)$ denote the number of different triples for a fixed $z$. Each $m_{z}(s)$ has its own domain of definition for $s$. For example, for $z=1 \rightarrow x+y=s-1 \rightarrow 2 \leq s-1 \leq 12 \rightarrow s \in[3 ; 13]$. We set $m_{1}(s)=0$ for $s \in[14 ; 18]$. problem: 2. The number $A$ in decimal form is represented as $A=\overline{7 a 631 b}$, where $a, b$ are non-zero digits. The number $B$ is obtained by summing all distinct six-digit numbers, including $A$, that are formed by cyclic permutations of the digits of $A$ (the first digit moves to the second position, the second to the third, and so on, with the last digit moving to the first position). How many numbers $A$ exist such that $B$ is divisible by 121? Find the largest such $A$.
solution:
2. Solution. The sum of the digits of number $A$ and the numbers obtained from $A$ by cyclic permutations of its digits is $a+b+17$. After summing these numbers (there are 6 of them), in each digit place of number $B$ we get

$a+b+17$, so $B=(a+b+17)\left(10^{5}+10^{4}+10^{3}+10^{2}+10+1\right)=(a+b+17) \cdot 111111$. Since

$111111=3 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 37$, $B$ is divisible by 121 if and only if $a+b+17$ is divisible by 11. Since $a$ and $b$ are digits, there are only two possible cases: $a+b=5$ and $a+b=16$. From this, we find the possible pairs of $a$ and $b$: $a=1, b=4 ; a=2, b=3 ; a=3, b=2 ; a=4, b=1 ; a=7, b=9 ; a=8, b=8 ; a=9, b=7$. Thus, 7 numbers satisfy the condition of the problem. The largest number is obtained when $a=9, b=7$. It is 796317.

problem: 3. For the polynomial $p(x)=2x+1$, find a polynomial $q(x)$ of the first degree such that $p^{2}(q(x))=q\left(p^{2}(x)\right)$ for any $x$.
solution:
3. Solution. Let $q(x)=a x+b$. Then

$$
p^{2}(q(x))=(2 q(x)+1)^{2}=4(a x+b)^{2}+4(a x+b)+1=4 q^{2}(x)+4 q(x)+1=4 a^{2} x^{2}+(8 a b+4 a) x+4 b^{2}+4 b+1
$$

and

$q\left(p^{2}(x)\right)=a\left(4 x^{2}+4 x+1\right)+b=4 a x^{2}+4 a x+a+b$.

By the condition of the problem $p^{2}(q(x))=q\left(p^{2}(x)\right)$. Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, we get the system:
$\left\{\begin{array}{c}4 a^{2}=4 a \\ 4 a b+4 a=4 a \\ 4 b^{2}+4 b+1=a+b\end{array}\right.$ or $\left\{\begin{array}{c}a^{2}=a \\ a b=0 \\ 4 b^{2}+3 b+1=a\end{array}\right.$.

From the first equation we have $a=1$ or $a=0$. For $a=0$ we get $4 b^{2}+3 b+1=0$. The last equation has no solutions. For $a=1$ we find $b=0$. Therefore, $q(x)=x$.

problem: 4. For which natural numbers $n$ does the equality $\operatorname{GCD}(6, n)+\operatorname{GCD}(8,2 n)=10$ hold?
solution:
4. Solution. Note that the possible values of $GCD(6, n)$ are $1,2,3,6$, and the possible values of $GCD(8, n)$ are $1,2,4,8$. Their sum, equal to 10, is possible in two cases.

Case 1. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}G C D(8,2 n)=8 \\ G C D(6, n)=2\end{array}\right.$. From the first equation, we get $n=4 k$, and from the second $n=2(3 m+1)$ or $n=2(3 m+2)$. Both conditions are satisfied by numbers of the form $n=12 t+4, \quad n=12 t+8, \quad t \in Z$.

Case 2. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}G C D(8,2 n)=4 \\ G C D(6, n)=6\end{array}\right.$. From the first equation, we get $n=2(2 k+1)$, and from the second $-n=6 m$. Both conditions are satisfied by numbers of the form $n=12 t+6, \quad t \in Z$.

Thus, the equality $GCD(6, n)+GCD(8,2 n)=10$ holds for $n=12 t+4, n=12 t+6, n=12 t+8, t \geq 0, t \in Z$.

problem: 5. In a rectangle, a segment $A B$ of length $l=4$, shorter than the lengths of its sides, is positioned such that its ends lie on the sides of the rectangle. As point $A$ makes a complete revolution around the rectangle, it travels a path equal to its perimeter. During this, point $C$ - the midpoint of segment $A B$, also travels a certain path. How much shorter is this path compared to the perimeter of the rectangle?
solution:
5. Solution. From the conditions of the problem (the length of segment $AB$ is less than the lengths of the sides of the rectangle), it follows that points $A$ and $B$ are either on the same side of the rectangle or on adjacent sides of the rectangle. If points $A$ and $B$ move along the same side of the rectangle, point $C$ moves along a straight line segment. If points $A$ and $B$ are on adjacent sides of the rectangle, then point $C$ moves along an arc of a circle with a central angle of $90^{\circ}$ and a radius of $l / 2$, since $DC$ (see figure) is the median of a right triangle drawn to the hypotenuse (it is equal to half the hypotenuse).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_a08dea28507761506bd0g-2.jpg?height=522&width=694&top_left_y=2012&top_left_x=612)

During one complete revolution, point $C$ travels four quarters of a circle with a radius of $l / 2$ and twice the straight-line segments of lengths $a-l$ and $b-l$, respectively. Therefore, in one complete revolution, point $C$ travels the path $s=2 \pi \cdot l / 2+2(a-l)+2(b-l)=2(a+b)-l(4-\pi)$. Since the perimeter of the rectangle is $2(a+b)$, then $\Delta s=L(4-\pi)$.

$$
=3 x^{3}-3 x^{2}\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\right)+3 x\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)-3 x_{1} x_{2} x_{3},
$$

from which $x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}=p / 3, \quad x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}=28 / 3$. Taking this into account, the target expression is transformed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left(x_{1}-2\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-2\right)^{2}+\left(x_{3}-2\right)^{2}=x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}-4\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\right)+12= \\
&=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\right)^{2}-2\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{1}\right)-4\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\right)+12= \\
&= \frac{p^{2}}{9}-\frac{56}{3}-\frac{4 p}{3}+12=\frac{p^{2}-12 p-60}{9} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now let's plot the graph of the equation $3 x^{3}-p x^{2}+28 x-p=0$ on the plane $(x, p)$. Since the parameter enters this equation linearly, it is more convenient to solve it for $p$:

$$
p\left(x^{2}+1\right)=3 x^{3}+28 x=3 x\left(x^{2}+1\right)+25 x \Rightarrow p(x)=3 x+\frac{25 x}{x^{2}+1}
$$

We will find the set of values of the parameter $p$ for which the equation has three real roots. For this, we will investigate $p(x)$:

$$

The odd function $p(x)$ has minima at points $\bar{x}_{2}=-\frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}, \bar{x}_{4}=2$ and maxima at points $\bar{x}_{1}=-2, \bar{x}_{3}=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}$,

For all $c \in\left(p_{2} ; p_{1}\right) \cup\left(p_{4} ; p_{3}\right)$, the line $p=c$ intersects the graph at three points, and the equation $3 x^{3}-p x^{2}+28 x-p=0$ has three distinct roots. problem:
4. Consider some intermediate step in Kuzia's movement. If she is at point $A$ at this step, the probability of being in $A$ on the next step is zero. If, however, she is at any of the remaining points, $B, C$ or $D$, the probability of being in $A$ on the next step is $1 / 3$, since from each such point there are three equally likely paths, only one of which leads to $A$. Let $p_{k}$ be the probability that the flea is at point $A$ on the $k$-th step. Accordingly, the probability that she is not at point $A$ is $\left(1-p_{k}\right)$. Then on the next step, she will be in $A$ with the probability

$$
p_{k+1}=\left(1-p_{k}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{3}+p_{k} \cdot 0=\left(1-p_{k}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{3}
$$

Thus, $p_{0}=1, \quad p_{1}=0, \quad p_{2}=\frac{1}{3}$, and further we get

$$
p_{3}=\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{9}, \ldots, p_{n}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27} \cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n}}{3^{n-1}}
$$

The formula for $p_{n}$ when $n \geq 2$ can be proven by mathematical induction.

Base case: $p_{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2}}{3^{2-1}}=\frac{1}{3}$ - true.

Inductive step: Suppose the formula is true for $n=k$, that is, $p_{k}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27} \cdots+\frac{(-1)^{k}}{3^{k-1}}$. Then

$$
p_{k+1}=\left(1-p_{k}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{3}=\left(1-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{27}+\cdots-\frac{(-1)^{k}}{3^{k-1}}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{3}=
$$

$$
=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3 \cdot 3}+\frac{1}{9 \cdot 3}-\frac{1}{27 \cdot 3}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{3^{k-1} \cdot 3}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27} \cdots+\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{3^{k}}
$$

Thus, the formula is also true for $n=k+1$. Therefore, it is true for any $n \geq 2$. We see that $p_{n}$ represents the sum of the terms of a geometric progression with a common ratio of $-1 / 3$. Consequently, $P(A)=p_{2020}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1-(-1 / 3)^{2019}}{1-(-1 / 3)}=\frac{1+(1 / 3)^{2019}}{4}=\frac{3^{2019}+1}{4 \cdot 3^{2019}} \simeq \frac{1}{4}$.

$$

Adding, we get

solution:
Answer: $|L|_{\min }=\frac{a}{2} \sqrt{4 \lambda^{2}+6 \lambda+3}$.

Solution. Let the curve $L$ be the desired one. It cannot fail to intersect the line $A B$ at some point $E$. Then the part of the curve from point $M$ to point $E$ is a straight line segment. Point $F$ is the midpoint of edge $A C$. The geometric locus of points equidistant from $N$ and $F$ is the median plane $P$, perpendicular to $N F$ and passing through the midpoint of segment $N F$. Plane $P$ coincides with plane $B C G$, where $G$ is the midpoint of edge $A D$.

Equality is achieved if point $E$ coincides with point $H$ - the intersection of lines $M F$ and $B C, \min |L| = M F$. The desired curve is the broken line $M H N$.

$$

problem: 1. Find the number of divisors of the number $a=2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{2}$, which are divisible by 3. Find the sum of such divisors.
solution: 1. Solution. Among the divisors of the number $a=2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{2}$, which are divisible by 3, the number 2 can be chosen with exponents $0,1,2,3$ (4 options), the number 3 - with exponents 1,2 (2 options), and the number 5 - with exponents $0,1,2$ (3 options). Therefore, the total number of divisors is $4 \cdot 2 \cdot 3=24$. The sum of the divisors of the number $b=2^{3} \cdot 5^{2}$ is $(1+2+4+8)(1+5+25)=465$. Then the sum of the divisors of the number $a$, which are divisible by 3, is $\left(3+3^{2}\right) \cdot 465=12 \cdot 465=5580$.

problem: 2. How many integers $b$ exist such that the equation $x^{2}+b x-9600=0$ has an integer solution that is a multiple of both 10 and 12? Specify the largest possible $b$.
solution:
2. Solution. Since the desired integer solution $x$ is divisible by 10 and 12, it is divisible by 60, hence it can be written in the form $x=60 t, t \in Z$. Substitute $x=60 t$ into the original equation:

$3600 t^{2}+60 b t-9600=0$. Express $b: b=\frac{160}{t}-60 t$. For $b$ to be an integer, $t$ must be a divisor of the number 160. $160=2^{5} \cdot 5$. The number $160=2^{5} \cdot 5$ has 12 positive divisors: $1,2,2^{2}, 2^{3}, 2^{4}, 2^{5}, 5,2 \cdot 5,2^{2} \cdot 5,2^{3} \cdot 5,2^{4} \cdot 5,2^{5} \cdot 5$. Taking the sign into account, we get 24 divisors. Each of them corresponds to a solution $x=60 t$ and an integer $b=\frac{160}{t}-60 t$. Therefore, the number of integers $b$ that satisfy the condition of the problem is 24. Since $b$ decreases as $t$ increases, the maximum $b$ corresponds to the smallest $t=-160$, so $b_{\max }=-1+60 \cdot 160=9599$.

problem: 3. How many three-digit positive numbers $x$ exist that are divisible by 3 and satisfy the equation $GCD(15, GCD(x, 20))=5$? Find the largest one.
solution: 3. Solution. Since 20 is not divisible by 3, $NOD(x, 20)$ is also not divisible by 3. Therefore, the equation $NOD(15, NOD(x, 20))=5$ is equivalent to the condition that $NOD(x, 20)$ is divisible by 5, which is possible if and only if $x$ is divisible by 5. Thus, the condition of the problem is equivalent to $x$ being divisible by 5 and by 3, that is, $x$ is divisible by 15. Therefore, $x$ can be written as $x=15m, m=1,2 \ldots$. The smallest three-digit $x=105$ is obtained when $m=7$, and the largest three-digit $x=990$ is obtained when $m=66$, making a total of 60 numbers.

problem: 4. The quadratic trinomial $p(x)=a x^{2}+b x+c, a>0$ when divided by ( $x-1$ ) gives a remainder of 4, and when divided by ( $x-2$ ) - a remainder of 15. Find the maximum possible value of the ordinate of the vertex of the parabola $y=p(x)$ under these conditions. For what value of $x$ is it achieved?
solution:
4. Solution. By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder of the division of a polynomial $p(x)$ by $x-a$ is $p(a)$.

Therefore, the conditions of the problem are equivalent to the system:

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}4 a+2 b+c=15 \\ a+b+c=4\end{array} \Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}b=11-3 a \\ c=2 a-7\end{array}\right.\right.$.

Thus, $p(x)=a x^{2}+(11-3 a) x+2 a-7$. The minimum value of the quadratic trinomial $p(x)$ (the ordinate of the vertex of the parabola) is achieved at its vertex $x_{s}=\frac{3 a-11}{2 a}$. It is equal to $p_{\text {min }}(x)=p\left(x_{k}\right)=p\left(\frac{3 a-11}{2 a}\right)=-\frac{a^{2}-38 a+121}{4 a}=\frac{19}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\left(a+\frac{121}{a}\right)=4-\left(\sqrt{a}-\frac{11}{\sqrt{a}}\right)^{2}$.

This value is maximal if and only if $\sqrt{a}-\frac{11}{\sqrt{a}}=0$, that is, $a=11$. When $a=11$, $x_{s}=1$,
and $p\left(x_{s}\right)=4$.

problem: 5. In a right triangle $ABC$, a height $CH$ is drawn from the vertex of the right angle. From point $N$ on the leg $BC$, a perpendicular $NM$ is dropped to the hypotenuse, such that line $NA$ is perpendicular to $CM$ and $MH: CH=1: \sqrt{3}$. Find the acute angles of triangle $ABC$.

Consider triangle $M C H$. It is a right triangle, so by the Pythagorean theorem we have:

$M C^{2}=M H^{2}+C H^{2}=M H^{2}+3 M H^{2}=4 M H^{2}$.

From this, we find $M H: M C=1: 2$, which implies that $\square M C H=30^{\circ}$. Since $M N \| C H$, then $\square N M C=\square M C H=30^{\circ}$. solution:
Solution. Let $a$ and $b$ (with $a > b$) be the lengths of the bases of the trapezoid (integers), and $p$ be a common divisor of $a$ and $b$.

Then $a = p \cdot a_1$, $b = p \cdot b_1$. The trapezoid can be divided into equal triangles only as shown in the figure.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_82168e1f2d6289cf87dag-2.jpg?height=588&width=643&top_left_y=1542&top_left_x=798)

Extend the trapezoid to form triangle $AED$ by extending its lateral sides until they intersect at point $E$. Divide the base $AD$ of trapezoid $ABCD$ into $a_1$ segments of length $p$ and draw lines through their endpoints parallel to sides $AE$ and $DE$ respectively. Connect the points of intersection of these lines with sides $AE$ and $DE$ by lines parallel to base $AD$. Since $BC$ is parallel to $AD$, the constructed lines will divide $BC$ into $b_1$ segments of length $p$. The total number of equal triangles into which triangle $AED$ is divided is $a_1^2$, and among them, $b_1^2$ triangles belong to triangle $BEC$. Then the number $n$ of triangles into which trapezoid $ABCD$ will be divided is $n = a_1^2 - b_1^2 = \frac{a^2 - b^2}{p^2}$. The smallest value of $n$ corresponds to $p = \text{GCD}(a, b)$. In the case of $a = 108 = 2^2 \cdot 3^3$, $b = 72 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2$, $\text{GCD}(a, b) = 2^2 \cdot 3^2 = 36$. Then $n_{\text{min}} = \frac{108^2 - 72^2}{36^2} = \frac{36^2 \cdot 9 - 36^2 \cdot 4}{36^2} = 5$.

problem: 4. Pete is trying to lay out a square on a table using identical cardboard rectangles measuring $14 \times 10$. Will he be able to do this? Propose your version of constructing such a square. What is the minimum number of rectangles he will need?
solution:
Solution. Let $n$ be the number of rectangles that form the square. Then the area of the square is $S=14 \cdot 10 \cdot n$. If the side of the square is formed by $m$ sides of length 14 and $k$ sides of length 10, then the length of the side of the square is $14 m + 10 k$, and its area is $S=(14 m + 10 k)^{2}$. Equating the expressions for the areas, we get

$$
14 \cdot 10 \cdot n = (14 m + 10 k)^{2} \rightarrow 7 \cdot 5 \cdot n = (7 m + 5 k)^{2}
$$

We can assume that the numbers $m$ and $k$ are coprime. Otherwise, the side of the square can be reduced by a factor of $p > 1$, where $p$ is a common divisor of $m$ and $k$.

The left-hand side of the equation (*) is divisible by 7, so the number $7 m + 5 k$ is divisible by 7, and $(7 m + 5 k)^{2}$ is divisible by 49. Therefore, the left-hand side of (*) is divisible by 49, which is possible only if $n$ is divisible by 7. Similarly, it can be shown that $n$ is divisible by 5. Thus, $n = 35 \cdot s, s \in \mathbb{Z}$, and the smallest possible number of rectangles is $n = 35$. The figure below shows a square assembled from 35 rectangles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_5ced405473fd649332a3g-2.jpg?height=603&width=662&top_left_y=298&top_left_x=731)

Answer: 35 rectangles.

problem: 3. For which numbers $n$ are the numbers $a_{n}=7 n-3$ divisible by 5 but not divisible by 3?
solution:
Solution. $a_{n}=7 n-3: 5 \rightarrow 7 n-3=5 k, k \in Z$. We obtain the linear Diophantine equation $7 n-5 k=3, k \in Z$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& k=\frac{7 n-3}{5}=n+\frac{2 n-3}{5} \rightarrow \frac{2 n-3}{5}=l \in Z \rightarrow n=\frac{5 l+3}{2}=2 l+1+\frac{l+1}{2} \rightarrow \\
& \rightarrow \frac{l+1}{2}=t \in Z \rightarrow l=2 t-1 \rightarrow n=2(2 t-1)+t=5 t-1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained $n=5 t-1, t \in N$. Then, $a_{n}=35 t-10, t \in N$. Rewrite $a_{n}$ as $a_{n}=36 t-9-t-1, t \in N$. Therefore, $a_{n} \vdots 3 \leftrightarrow t+1: 3 \leftrightarrow t=3 m-1, m \in N$. The problem's condition is satisfied by the numbers $n=5 t-1, t \neq 3 m-1, t, m \in N$.

Answer: $n=5 t-1, t \neq 3 m-1, t, m \in N$.

2. For all x, the equality must hold

$$
\begin{gathered}
f(x+5 \pi)=f(x) \text {, i.e., } \\
\sin (n x+5 \pi n) \cos \frac{6(x+5 \pi)}{n+1}=\sin n x \cos \frac{6 x}{n+1} .
\end{gathered}
$$

For \( n=0 \), this equality is satisfied, and therefore we can ignore this value in further analysis.

Case 1: \( n \) is even. The equality takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sin n x \cos \frac{6(x+5 \pi)}{n+1}-\sin n x \cos \frac{6 x}{n+1} \Leftrightarrow \\
& \sin n x\left(\cos \frac{6 x}{n+1}-\cos \frac{6 x+30 \pi}{n+1}\right)=0 \Leftrightarrow \\
& 2 \sin n x \cdot \sin \frac{6 x+15 \pi}{n+1} \cdot \sin \frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the zeros of the first two functions in the obtained product:

$$
\sin n x=0 \Leftrightarrow n x=\pi k(k \in \mathbb{Z}) \Rightarrow \frac{x}{\pi}=\frac{k}{n}
$$

$$
\sin \frac{6 x+15 \pi}{n+1}=0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{6 x+15 \pi}{n+1}=\pi m(m \in \mathbb{Z}) \Rightarrow \frac{x}{\pi}=\frac{m(n+1)-15}{6}
$$

For these, the ratio \( \frac{x}{\pi} \) is rational. Therefore, there exists a value of \( x \) for which the considered functions do not turn to zero (it is sufficient to take \( x=\pi y \), where \( y \) is an irrational number). Consequently, the condition of the problem is equivalent to the equality

$$
\sin \frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=0
$$

From this, we find \( \frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=\pi m, m \in \mathbb{Z} \) or \( \frac{15}{n+1}=m, m \in \mathbb{Z} \), and therefore \( n+1 \) must be an odd divisor of the number 15, i.e., \( n+1 \in\{1,-1,3,-3,5,-5,15,-15\} \) or \( n \in\{0,-2,2,-4,4,-6,14,-16\} \).

Case 2: \( n \) is odd. The equality takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
& -\sin n x \cos \frac{6(x+5 \pi)}{n+1}-\sin n x \cos \frac{6 x}{n+1} \Leftrightarrow \\
& \sin n x\left(\cos \frac{6 x}{n+1}+\cos \frac{6 x+30 \pi}{n+1}\right)=0 \Leftrightarrow \\
& 2 \sin n x \cdot \cos \frac{6 x+15 \pi}{n+1} \cdot \cos \frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly to the previous point, it is not difficult to see that if the ratio \( \frac{x}{\pi} \) is irrational, the first two functions in the product on the left side of the last equality do not turn to zero. Thus, this equality is equivalent to the relation

$$
\cos \frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=0
$$

From this, we find

$$
\frac{15 \pi}{n+1}=\frac{\pi(2 m+1)}{2}, m \in \mathbb{Z}, \text { or } \frac{30}{n+1}=2 m+1, m \in \mathbb{Z}
$$

Therefore, \( n+1 \in\{2,-2,6,-6,10,-10,30,-30\} \), and \( n \in\{1,-3,5,-7,9,-11,29,-31\} \).

Combining the found values, we get the answer.

From the equation $2 \cos ^{2} a_{n}=\cos a_{n+1}$, it follows that for all $n$, the value of $\cos a_{n+1} \geq 0$ and $\left|\cos a_{n}\right|=\sqrt{\frac{\cos a_{n+1}}{2}} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, i.e., on the unit circle, all values of $a_{n}$ fall within the interval $[\pi / 4 ; \pi / 2]$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_9164e34713684ec260eeg-06.jpg?height=636&width=684&top_left_y=203&top_left_x=381)

From the fact that the numbers $a_{n}$ form an arithmetic progression, it follows that the common difference $d$ of this progression must be a multiple of the circumference of the circle $2 \pi$. Indeed, if the value of $d$ is greater than the nearest multiple of $2 \pi$ to the number $a_{n}$, then one of the subsequent terms of the sequence, located on the unit circle counterclockwise from $a_{n}$ and moving from it by a constant value along the arc, will exit the arc segment $[\pi / 4 ; \pi / 2]$. Similarly, if the value of $d$ is less than the nearest multiple of $2 \pi$ to the number $a_{n}$, then one of the subsequent terms of the sequence, located on the unit circle clockwise from $a_{n}$ and moving from it by a constant value along the arc, will also exit the arc segment $[\pi / 4 ; \pi / 2]$. Thus,

$$
d=2 \pi k, k \in Z
$$

Here, $k \neq 0$ because by the problem's condition, $d \neq 0$.

From the proven statement, it follows that for all $n$,

$$
\cos a_{n}=\cos \left(a_{1}+(n-1) d\right)=\cos \left(a_{1}+(n-1) \cdot 2 \pi k\right)=\cos a_{1}
$$

This fact gives an equation for determining the first term of the progression

$$
2 \cos ^{2} a_{1}=\cos a_{1}
$$

Solving the equation, we find

$$
\left[\begin{array} { l } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } a _ { 1 } = 0 } \\
{ \operatorname { c o s } a _ { 1 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
a_{1}=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi m, m \in Z \\
a_{1}= \pm \frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi m, m \in Z
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

The first series gives

$$
a_{n}=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi m+(n-1) 2 \pi k \Rightarrow b_{n}=a_{n}
$$

and the two remaining series give

$$
a_{n}= \pm \frac{\pi}{3}+2 \pi m+(n-1) 2 \pi k \Rightarrow b_{n}= \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} a_{n}
$$

All series satisfy the conditions of the problem.

$$
\text { 1) } a_{1}=\frac{\pi}{2}+\pi m, m \in Z ; d=2 \pi k, k \in Z, k \neq 0
$$

problem: 2. Petya wrote down five consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression and encrypted them according to the principle: each digit was replaced with a letter, different digits with different letters, and vice versa. Here's what he got: A, BS, DE, AV, CB. What numbers did Petya write?
solution:
Answer: $3,15,27,39,51$.

Solution. From the condition, it follows that the terms of the arithmetic sequence are natural numbers and the difference of the progression, denoted as $d$, is positive. We will consider the letters A, B, C, D, E as digits or numbers, and the corresponding two-digit numbers will be denoted as $\overline{\mathrm{A}}$ and so on.

Let's calculate the difference $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}-\overline{\mathrm{BC}}$ in two ways. First, using the fact that the numbers form an arithmetic sequence, we get $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}-\overline{\mathrm{BC}}=(\overline{\mathrm{BC}}+3 d)-\overline{\mathrm{BC}}=3 d$, then $\overline{\mathrm{CB}}-\overline{\overline{\mathrm{CC}}}=$ $(10 C+5)-(10 B+C)=9(C-B)$. Therefore, the difference of the progression is a multiple of three.

Now, for the difference $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}-\mathrm{A}$, we have $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}-\mathrm{A}=(10 \mathrm{~A}+\mathrm{B})-\mathrm{A}=9 \mathrm{~A}+\mathrm{B}=3 d$, and since $d$ is a multiple of three, then $\mathrm{B}$ is a multiple of 9. Since this is a digit, $\mathrm{B}$ is either $0$ or $9$.

Suppose $\mathrm{B}=0$. Then $3 d=9 \mathrm{~A}+\mathrm{B}=9 \mathrm{~A}$, i.e., $d=3 \mathrm{~A}$, and the terms of the progression are respectively $\mathrm{A}, \overline{\mathrm{BC}}=4 \mathrm{~A}, \overline{\mathrm{DE}}=7 \mathrm{~A}, \overline{\mathrm{AB}}=10 \mathrm{~A}, \overline{\mathrm{CE}}=13 \mathrm{~A}$. Therefore, $\overline{\mathrm{BC}}+\overline{\mathrm{CE}}=4 \mathrm{~A}+13 \mathrm{~A}=17 \mathrm{~A}$, and on the other hand $\overline{\mathrm{BC}}+\overline{\mathrm{CB}}=(10 \mathrm{E}+\mathrm{C})+(10 \mathrm{C}+\overline{\mathrm{E}})=11(\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{C})$. Since the numbers 11 and 17 are prime, it follows from the equality $11(\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{C})=17 \mathrm{~A}$ that the digit $\mathrm{A}$ is a multiple of 11, which is impossible.

It remains to consider the case when $\mathrm{B}=9$. In this case, $3 d=9 \mathrm{~A}+\mathrm{B}=9 \mathrm{~A}+9$, i.e., $d=3 \mathrm{~A}+3$, and the terms of the progression are respectively $\mathrm{A}, \overline{\mathrm{BC}}=4 \mathrm{~A}+3, \overline{\mathrm{DE}}=7 \mathrm{~A}+6, \overline{\mathrm{AB}}=10 \mathrm{~A}+9$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CB}}=13 \mathrm{~A}+12$. Therefore, $\overline{\mathrm{BC}}+\overline{\mathrm{CB}}=(10 \mathrm{~B}+\mathrm{C})+(10 \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{E})=11(\mathrm{~B}+\mathrm{C})=(4 \mathrm{~A}+3)+(13 \mathrm{~A}+12)=17 \mathrm{~A}+15=11(\mathrm{~A}+1)+2(3 \mathrm{~A}+2)$. Since 11 is a prime number, it follows from the equality $11(\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{C})=11(\mathrm{~A}+1)+2(3 \mathrm{~A}+2)$ that $3 \mathrm{~A}+2$ is a multiple of 11. Therefore, since $\mathrm{A}$ is a digit, $\mathrm{A}=3, \overline{\mathrm{BC}}=4 \mathrm{~A}+3=15$, $\overline{\mathrm{DE}}=7 \mathrm{~A}+6=27, \overline{\mathrm{AB}}=10 \mathrm{~A}+9=39$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CE}}=13 \mathrm{~A}+12=51$. These numbers satisfy the condition of the problem.

problem:
2. Since $a^{2}-2 a+3=(a-1)^{2}+2$, then for $a \neq 1$ the value $a^{2}-2 a+3>2$ and the equation has no solutions, therefore the desired radius $R=\infty$. For $a=1$ the equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\sin (x+y-z)=1 \\
\cos (x+y-2 z)=1
\end{array}\right.
$$

Solving the system, we get

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x+y-z=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi n, n \in \mathbb{Z} \\
x+y+2 z=2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}
\end{array}\right.
$$

The first equation defines a family of planes with a normal vector $\{1 ; 1 ;-1\}$ and the distance between the planes is $d_{1}=2 \pi / \sqrt{3}$. The second equation defines a family of planes with a normal vector $\{1 ; 1 ; 2\}$ and the distance between the planes is $d_{2}=2 \pi / \sqrt{6}$. Since the dot product of the vectors $\{1 ; 1 ;-1\}$ and $\{1 ; 1 ; 2\}$ is zero, the planes from different families are mutually perpendicular. Thus, the solution to the considered system is represented by the intersections of these planes. These intersections form a family of lines parallel to the considered planes. When these lines intersect a plane perpendicular to them, we obtain a grid of points lying at the vertices of rectangles with sides $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_aa6a3a905462a0a225feg-03.jpg?height=337&width=842&top_left_y=607&top_left_x=193)

The circle circumscribed around the rectangle (in the figure, this is $A B C D$) has a radius equal to the maximum radius of the sphere that does not contain any of the lines from our family. They touch the surface of the sphere:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_aa6a3a905462a0a225feg-03.jpg?height=210&width=359&top_left_y=1192&top_left_x=501)

Using the Pythagorean theorem for triangle $B C D$, we get that the desired radius

$$
R=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{d_{1}^{2}+d_{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{3}+\frac{4 \pi^{2}}{6}}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
solution: Answer: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}R=\infty, \quad a \neq 1 \\ R=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad a=1\end{array}\right.$.

Consider the first case. Parallelism of lines is checked by the equality of their slopes. The condition for parallelism to the line $2 x-3 y+1=0$ is

$$

The value of the parameter is determined by passing through the points of intersection:

$$

For the point $(1 ; 1)$, we get $b=4$, for the point $(4 ; 3)$, the value of $b$ is 11, and for the point $(5 ;-1)$, the value of $b$ is 4. This completes the consideration of the first case.

$p_{n}(-2)=-8 a_{n}-4\left(a_{n}+1\right)+2\left(6 a_{n}-1\right)+6=0$, i.e., $x=-2$ is a root of the polynomial for all $n$.

$p_{n}(3)=27 a_{n}-9\left(a_{n}+1\right)+3\left(1-6 a_{n}\right)+6=0$, i.e., $x=3$ is a root of the polynomial for all $n$.

Then $p_{n}(x)=\left(a_{n} x-1\right)(x+2)(x-3)$.

The polynomials $p_{5}(x), p_{6}(x)$ and $p_{7}(x), \quad$ in addition to the roots $\quad x=-2, \quad x=3, \quad$ have the roots $\quad x=\frac{1}{a_{5}}=\frac{1}{11}, x=\frac{1}{a_{6}}=\frac{1}{13}, x=\frac{1}{a_{7}}=\frac{1}{15}$ respectively. Then the desired sum of the roots is $1+\frac{1}{11}+\frac{1}{13}+\frac{1}{15}=\frac{2648}{2145}$

problem:
6. Let's introduce the following notations: $a$ - the side of the base, $b$ - the lateral edge, $N$ - the midpoint of side $AB$, $M$ - the midpoint of side $AD$, $K$ - the midpoint of edge $SC$ of the regular quadrilateral pyramid $SABCD$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_f36d8ea35c99389d52e3g-05.jpg?height=1057&width=680&top_left_y=1156&top_left_x=745)

We construct the section of the pyramid $SABCD$ by a plane passing through points $N$ and $M$ and parallel to the median $DK$ of the lateral face $SDC$: through points $N$ and $M$ we draw the line $NM$ until it intersects with lines $BC$ and $CD$ at points $N_1$ and $M_1$ respectively; through point $M_1$ we draw a line parallel to the median $DK$, the points of intersection of this line with edges $SD$ and $SC$ are denoted as $P$ and $R$ respectively; we connect points $R$ and $N_1$; the point of intersection of $RN_1$ and $SB$ is denoted as $Q$; we connect $Q$ and $N$, $P$ and $M$. The section $NMPRQ$ is constructed. Let's find its area.

By the condition, $AM = MD = AN = NB = \frac{a}{2}$. Therefore, triangle $AMN$ is a right isosceles triangle and $MN = \frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$. Note that triangles $MDM_1$ and $NBN_1$ are right triangles. They are equal to triangle $AMN$ by the leg and angle. Therefore, $M_1D = N_1B = \frac{a}{2}$. Consider the plane of the lateral face $SDC$. Since $M_1R \parallel DK$, then $\frac{RK}{CK} = \frac{M_1D}{CD} = \frac{1}{2}$. Then $RK = \frac{CK}{2} = \frac{b}{4}$, $SR = SK - RK = \frac{b}{4}$. Moreover, $PR \parallel DK$, $\frac{SP}{PD} = \frac{SR}{RK} = 1$. Therefore, $SP = PD = \frac{b}{2}$. Since $P$ is the midpoint of edge $SD$ and $M$ is the midpoint of base $AD$, then $PM$ is the midline of triangle $ADS$ and $PM = \frac{AS}{2} = \frac{b}{2}$, $PM \parallel AS$. Similarly, we can obtain that $QN = \frac{AS}{2} = \frac{b}{2}$, $QN \parallel AS$. Therefore, quadrilateral $PMQN$ is a parallelogram. We will prove that it is a rectangle. Indeed, the projection of $AC$ of edge $AS$ is the diagonal of the square $ABCD$. Therefore, $AC$ is perpendicular to the diagonal $BD$, and since $BD \parallel MN$, then $AC$ is perpendicular to $MN$. Hence, $AS$ is perpendicular to $MN$. Since $PM \parallel AS$, it follows that $PM$ is perpendicular to $MN$. Thus, the section $NMPRQ$ consists of a rectangle $PMQN$ with sides $MN = \frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $PM = \frac{b}{2}$ and an isosceles triangle $PQR$ with base $PQ = \frac{b}{2}$ and height $RF$. Let's find the area of the rectangle: $MN \cdot PM = \frac{ab}{2\sqrt{2}}$. Since $\frac{CR}{RS} = \frac{CO}{OA} = 3$, then $\frac{OR}{AS} = \frac{CO}{OA} = \frac{3}{4}$. From this, we get $OR = \frac{3b}{4}$, and $FR = \frac{3b}{4} - \frac{b}{2} = \frac{b}{4}$. Then the area of triangle $PQR$ is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{a}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{b}{4} = \frac{ab}{8\sqrt{2}}$. The area of the section $NMPRQ$ is: $\frac{ab}{2\sqrt{2}} + \frac{ab}{8\sqrt{2}} = \frac{5ab}{8\sqrt{2}} = \frac{5ab\sqrt{2}}{16}$. Substituting $a = 1$, $b = 2$, we find $S = \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{8}$.
solution:
Answer: $S=\frac{5 \sqrt{2}}{8}$.

problem:
5. Let point $M$ divide edge $A B$ in the ratio $A M: M B=\lambda$, point $N$ divide edge $D C$ in the ratio $D N: N C=\mu$, and point $P$ divide edge $D B$ in the ratio $D P: P B=\theta$. We need to find the ratio $A Q: Q C$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_f36d8ea35c99389d52e3g-13.jpg?height=765&width=725&top_left_y=200&top_left_x=654)

Let $T$ be the intersection point of line $P N$ with line $B C$, then point $Q$ is the intersection point of line $M T$ with line $A C$. Let $B M=a$, $C N=b$, and $B P=c$. Then $M A=\lambda a$, $N D=\mu b$, and $P D=\theta c$.

Applying Menelaus' theorem to triangle $C B D$ and the transversal $P T$:

$$
\frac{C T}{T B} \cdot \frac{B P}{P D} \cdot \frac{D N}{N C}=1 \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{C T}{T B} \cdot \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot \mu=1.
$$

From this, we find $\frac{C T}{T B}=\frac{\theta}{\mu}$.

Now, applying Menelaus' theorem to triangle $A C B$ and the transversal $M T$:

$$
\frac{A Q}{Q C} \cdot \frac{C T}{T B} \cdot \frac{B M}{M A}=1 \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{A Q}{Q C} \cdot \frac{\theta}{\mu} \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda}=1.
$$

From this, we get

$$
\frac{A Q}{Q C}=\frac{\lambda \mu}{\theta}
$$

According to the problem, $\lambda=2$, $\mu=3$, and $\theta=\frac{1}{2}$, then $\frac{A Q}{Q C}=12$.
solution:
Answer: $A Q: Q C=12$.

If \( \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}} \in [0; a] \), then \( x = \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}} \) is the minimum point of the function \( T(x) \). In this case,

5. In triangle $ABC$ with area $s$, medians $AM, BN, CQ$ are drawn. A point $P$ is taken on line $AC$ such that $AP: PC = \lambda$.

Case 1. Point $P$ is located on side $AC$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{AP}{PC} = \lambda \rightarrow AP = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1} AC \rightarrow PN = \frac{|\lambda-1|}{2(\lambda+1)} AC \\
& S_{QPN}: S_{AQN} = \frac{PN}{AN} = \frac{|\lambda-1|}{\lambda+1} \rightarrow S_{QPN} = \frac{|\lambda-1| s}{4(\lambda+1)}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_f36d8ea35c99389d52e3g-19.jpg?height=343&width=554&top_left_y=211&top_left_x=1322)

For $0 < \lambda < 1$:

$$
S_{PNQM} = S_{PQN} + S_{PQM} = S_{PQN} + S_{NQM} = \frac{1-\lambda}{4(\lambda+1)} s + \frac{s}{4} = \frac{1}{2(\lambda+1)} s(*)
$$

For $\lambda > 1$:

$$
S_{PNQM} = S_{PQN} + S_{PQM} = S_{PQN} + S_{NQM} = \frac{\lambda-1}{4(\lambda+1)} s + \frac{s}{4} = \frac{\lambda}{2(\lambda+1)} s(* *)
$$

Case 2. Point $P$ does not lie on side $AC$ of the triangle.

For the case $0 < \lambda < 1$:

$$
PC: AC = \frac{1}{1-\lambda} \rightarrow \frac{S_{PMC}}{S_{AMC}} = \frac{PC}{AC} = \frac{1}{1-\lambda} \rightarrow S_{PMC} = \frac{s}{2(1-\lambda)}
$$

Then

$$
S_{PMQN} = S_{PMC} + \frac{s}{2} = \frac{s}{2(1-\lambda)} + \frac{s}{2} = \frac{1}{2(1-\lambda)} s(* * * *)
$$

For the case $\lambda > 1$:

$$
PC: AC = \frac{1}{\lambda-1} \rightarrow \frac{S_{PMC}}{S_{AMC}} = \frac{PC}{AC} = \frac{1}{\lambda-1} \rightarrow S_{PMC} = \frac{s}{2(\lambda-1)}
$$

Then

$$
S_{PMQN} = S_{PMC} + \frac{s}{2} = \frac{s}{2(\lambda-1)} + \frac{s}{2} = \frac{\lambda}{2(\lambda-1)} s(* * * *)
$$

Combining, we get the answer:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_f36d8ea35c99389d52e3g-19.jpg?height=306&width=591&top_left_y=1383&top_left_x=1372)
for $0 < \lambda < 1$ two possibilities

$$
S_{1} = \frac{1}{2(1-\lambda)} s \quad S_{2} = \frac{1}{2(\lambda+1)} s
$$

for $\lambda > 1$ two possibilities

$$
S_{1} = \frac{\lambda}{2(\lambda+1)} s \quad S_{2} = \frac{\lambda}{2(\lambda-1)} s
$$

solution:

$$

Considering the condition $k \in[0 ; 11]$, we get $0 \leq 11 n-259 \leq 11 \rightarrow \frac{259}{11} \leq n \leq \frac{270}{11}$. In this interval, there is only one integer $n=24$ and $k=5$. Therefore, the crossed-out number is $n+k=29$.

problem: 5. You have a cardboard circle with a radius of 4, a ruler, and a compass. On a sheet of paper, construct a rectangle equal in area to the circle.
solution:
Solution. Construction.

Let's draw on a plane using a compass and a ruler two mutually perpendicular lines

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_db180c9c727edb12c8a2g-2.jpg?height=340&width=694&top_left_y=1897&top_left_x=658)

and a circle of radius \( R \), tangent to the horizontal line, with its center at point \( P \) on the vertical line. Place the given circle on the constructed one so that their boundaries coincide, and the marked point \( A \) on the cardboard circle coincides with point \( O \) at the intersection of the lines. Aligning one edge of the ruler with the horizontal line, roll the cardboard circle along the ruler for one complete revolution without slipping. At this moment, point \( A \) will coincide with point \( B \) on the horizontal axis, and the center of the circle will be at point \( Q \) (see fig). The cardboard circle is then removed. Using a compass and a ruler, construct a perpendicular to the horizontal line at point \( B \), and mark segment \( B Q \) on it, equal in length to \( R \). Connecting points \( P \) and \( Q \), construct the rectangle \( A B Q P \).

By dividing segments \( B Q \) and \( A P \) in half, we obtain points \( C \) and \( D \). The rectangle \( A B C D \) is the desired one.

Analysis. The length of side \( A B \) is equal to the circumference of the circle, i.e., \( 2 \pi R \), and the length of side \( B C \) is \( R / 2 \) by construction. Therefore, the area of rectangle \( A B C D \) is \( \pi R^{2} \), i.e., the rectangle is equal in area to the circle.

solution:
Answer: 1) $O M: O C=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}+\frac{\mu}{\lambda} ; \quad$ 2) $B O: O N=\frac{(\lambda+\mu)(\alpha+\beta)}{\lambda \beta}$.

Finding the length of segment $A P$:

$$
\frac{A P}{C D}=\frac{A M}{M D} \rightarrow \frac{A P}{(\lambda+\mu) y}=\frac{\alpha x}{\beta x} \rightarrow A P=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}(\lambda+\mu) y \text { (similarity of triangles) }
$$

Finding the length of segment $D Q$:

$$
\frac{D Q}{B C}=\frac{D N}{N C}=\frac{\mu}{\lambda} \rightarrow D Q=\frac{\mu}{\lambda}(\alpha+\beta) \times \text { (similarity of triangles) }
$$

Calculating the ratio $B O: O N$:

$$
\frac{B O}{O N}=\frac{B P}{C N}=\frac{(\lambda+\mu) y+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}(\lambda+\mu) y}{\lambda y}=\frac{(\lambda+\mu)(\alpha+\beta)}{\lambda \beta}
$$

$(*) \quad$ (Similarity of triangles)

Calculating the ratio $O M: C O$:

$$
\frac{O M}{O C}=\frac{M Q}{B C}=\frac{\beta x+\frac{\mu}{\lambda}(\alpha+\beta) x}{(\alpha+\beta) x}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}+\frac{\mu}{\lambda}
$$

$(* *)$ (Similarity of triangles)

In variant 1, $\alpha=1, \beta=2, \lambda=2, \mu=3$. Using formula (**) we get $O M: O C=13: 6$.

Problem 2 Answer: $\cos 2 x=-\frac{1}{3}$

Solution

Let $a=\operatorname{arctg} \sqrt[6]{2}$.

Solving the equation $\sin (x+3 a)=3 \sin (a-x)$:

The function $\cos 2 x=\frac{1-\operatorname{tg}^{2} x}{1+\operatorname{tg}^{2} x}=\frac{1-2}{1+2}=-\frac{1}{3}$

2) $a=599 \ldots 9 \underset{7}{899} 89 . \ldots 9$

Solution

If the decimal representation of the number $a$ does not end in 9, then such a number cannot satisfy the condition of the problem. Indeed, then the sums of the digits of the numbers $a$ and $a+1$ differ by 1 and therefore cannot be divisible by 77 simultaneously.

Suppose that $a$ has the form: $a=a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{k} 99 \ldots 9$, 9 , where $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k}, a_{k} \neq 9$ - digits, $k-$ the number of higher-order digits, $n$ - the total number of digits, $n-k$ - the number of nines in the lower-order digits. Let $\sum a$ denote the sum of the digits of the number $a$. Then, by condition, there exist integers $m, l$, for which $\sum a=a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k}+9(n-k)=77 m, m \in Z \quad$ and $\sum(a+1)=a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k}+1=77 l, l \in Z$.

Subtracting one from the other, we get $9(n-k)-77(m-l)=1$. This Diophantine equation has solutions $\left\{\begin{array}{c}n-k=77 t-17 \\ m-l=9 t-2\end{array}, \forall t \in Z\right.$. Taking into account the positivity of $n-k$ and $m-l$, we have $t \geq 1$.

The minimum value of the sum of the digits of the lower-order digits $9 \cdot(n-k)$ corresponds to $t=1$, i.e., the number of nines cannot be less than 60. The sum of the digits of the higher-order digits $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k}=77 l-1$ is minimal for $l=1$ and equals 76. Since $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k} \leq 9(k-1)+8$, then $76 \leq 9(k-1)+8 \rightarrow k \geq 9$. Thus, the answer to the first question of the problem is: $a=a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{k} 99 \ldots 9$, 9 , where $k \geq 9$, $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k}-$ digits, $a_{1} \geq 1, a_{k} \leq 8$, the sum of which $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k}$ is 76.

For the answer to the second question of the problem, note that the minimum number of lower-order digits $n-k$ is 60. The minimum $a$ corresponds to the minimum $k=9$ and the minimum number $b=a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{9}$, the sum of the digits of which is 76. Such a number $b$ is $b=599999998$.

Then $a=599 \ldots 9899 \ldots 9$

problem: 1. The arithmetic progression $a_{n}$ is such that its difference is not equal to zero, and $a_{10}, a_{13}$, and $a_{19}$ are consecutive terms of some geometric progression. Find the ratio $a_{12}: a_{18}$.
solution:
Solution. Let $a_{n}=a_{1}+d(n-1)$, where $a_{1}$ is the first term of the progression, and $d$ is its common difference.

Then $a_{10}=a_{1}+9 d, a_{13}=a_{1}+12 d, a_{19}=a_{1}+18 d$. By the property of a geometric progression, we have $a_{10} \cdot a_{19}=a_{13}^{2}:\left(a_{1}+9 d\right)\left(a_{1}+18 d\right)=\left(a_{1}+12 d\right)^{2} \rightarrow 18 d^{2}+3 a_{1} d=0 \rightarrow a_{1}=-6 d$. Then

$$
a_{12}: a_{18}=\frac{a_{1}+11 d}{a_{1}+17 d}=\frac{-6 d+11 d}{-6 d+17 d}=\frac{5}{11} .
$$

Answer: $a_{12}: a_{18}=5: 11$.

problem: 2. How many solutions does the equation $\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]+2\{\cos 2 \pi x\}=0$ have? Indicate the smallest and the largest of them. Here $[a]$ is the integer part of the number $a$ - the greatest integer not exceeding $a$, $\{a\}=a-[a]$ is the fractional part of the number $a$.
solution:
Solution. Rewrite the equation as $\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=-2\{\cos 2 \pi x\}$. Since

$$
\{\cos 2 \pi x\} \in[0 ; 1) \rightarrow\left[2 x-x^{2}\right] \in(-2 ; 0] \rightarrow\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=-1,\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=0
$$

There are two possible cases:

Case 1. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}{\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=-1} \\ \{\cos 2 \pi x\}=\frac{1}{2}\end{array} ; \quad\right.$ Case 2. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}{\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=0} \\ \{\cos 2 \pi x\}=0\end{array}\right.$.

Case 1. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}{\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=-1} \\ \{\cos 2 \pi x\}=\frac{1}{2}\end{array} \leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}-1 \leq 2 x-x^{2}0\end{array}\right. \\ \cos 2 \pi x=\frac{1}{2}+n, n \in Z\end{array} \leftrightarrow\right.\right.\right.$

$$
\leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}
x \in[1-\sqrt{2} ; 0) \cup(2 ; 1+\sqrt{2}] \\
\cos 2 \pi x= \pm \frac{1}{2} \leftrightarrow x= \pm \frac{1}{6}+\frac{k}{2}, k \in Z
\end{array}\right.
$$

The first series $x=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{k}{2}$ falls into the interval $[1-\sqrt{2} ; 0)$ when $k=-1 \rightarrow x_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}$ and into the interval $(2 ; 1+\sqrt{2}]$ when $k=4 \rightarrow x_{2}=\frac{13}{6}$. The second series $x=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{k}{2}$ falls into the interval $[1-\sqrt{2} ; 0)$ when $k=0 \rightarrow x_{3}=-\frac{1}{6}$ and into the interval $(2 ; 1+\sqrt{2}]$ when $k=5 \rightarrow x_{4}=\frac{7}{3}$.

Case 2. $\left\{\begin{array}{l}{\left[2 x-x^{2}\right]=0} \\ \{\cos 2 \pi x\}=0\end{array} \leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}0 \leq 2 x-x^{2}0 \\ x(x-2) \leq 0\end{array}\right. \\ \cos 2 \pi x=n, n \in Z\end{array} \leftrightarrow\right.\right.\right.$

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{c}
x \in[0 ; 2], x \neq 1 \\
{\left[\begin{array} { c } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } 2 \pi x = \pm 1 } \\
{ \operatorname { c o s } 2 \pi x = 0 }
\end{array} \leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
x=\frac{k}{2}, k \in Z \\
x=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{k}{2}
\end{array}\right.\right.}
\end{array}\right.
$$

The first series belongs to $x \in[0 ; 2], x \neq 1$ when $k=0,1,3,4$ and the corresponding solutions are $x_{5}=0, x_{6}=\frac{1}{2}, x_{7}=\frac{3}{2}, x_{8}=2$. The second series belongs to $x \in[0 ; 2], x \neq 1$ when $k=0,1,2,3$ and the corresponding solutions are $x_{9}=\frac{1}{4}, x_{10}=\frac{3}{4}, x_{11}=\frac{5}{4}, x_{12}=\frac{7}{4}$.

Answer: There are a total of 12 solutions, $x_{\min }=-\frac{1}{3}, x_{\max }=\frac{7}{3}$.

problem:
4. For what least integer $n$ are all solutions of the equation

$$
x^{3}-(5 n-9) x^{2}+\left(6 n^{2}-31 n-106\right) x-6(n-8)(n+2)=0 \text { greater than }-1 \text { ? }
$$
solution:
Solution. Rewrite the equation as

$$
x^{3}-(5 n-9) x^{2}+\left(6 n^{2}-31 n-106\right) x-6 n^{2}+36 n+96=0 .
$$

Notice that $x_{1}=1>-1$ is a solution for all $n$ (the sum of the coefficients of the polynomial on the left side of the equation is zero for all $n$). Divide the equation by $x-1$:

$$
x^{2}-5(n-2) x+6\left(n^{2}-6 n-16\right)=0
$$

The roots of this equation are: $x_{2}=3(n+2), x_{3}=2(n-8)$. We seek when these solutions are greater than -1:

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 3 ( n + 2 ) > - 1 } \\
{ 2 ( n - 8 ) > - 1 }
\end{array} \rightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
n>-\frac{7}{3}, n \in Z \\
n>\frac{15}{2}, n \in Z
\end{array} \rightarrow n \geq 8\right.\right.
$$

Since $n$ is an integer, then $n \geq 8, n \in Z$.

Answer: $n_{\min }=8$.

Task 1. Answer: $k=16$ collisions.

A wire in the shape of a circle with radius $R$ has $m$ beads strung on it, equally spaced from each other. At a certain moment, $(m-1)$ beads are made to move with the same speed $v(1/$ sec) in the counterclockwise direction, while the remaining bead is made to move in the opposite direction at the same speed. It is assumed that after the collision of two beads, their speed remains unchanged, and the direction instantly reverses. How many collisions will occur between the beads in $T$ seconds.

4. There is a stick 15 cm long and a rope, the length of which is more than 1 m. You need to measure the length of the rope with an accuracy of 5 cm using the stick. You are allowed to: 1) lay the stick along the rope an integer number of times; 2) lay pieces of the rope, shorter than 15 cm, along the stick. You are not allowed to: 1) make additional marks on the stick; 2) make cuts or knots in the rope. The solution should describe the procedure for calculating the length of the rope with the specified accuracy. The rope and the stick are mathematical, i.e., they have no thickness, and the repositioning does not result in a loss of accuracy.
solution:
# Solution

## First Algorithm

Connect the beginning and the end of the rope to form a closed loop.

Step 1. Lay the stick along the rope from point A, for example, counterclockwise until the remaining piece of the rope is less than 15 cm (point $A_{1}$).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_fe74dcff8f31bf84a619g-2.jpg?height=420&width=1373&top_left_y=1372&top_left_x=433)

The number of stick placements up to this point is denoted by $n_{1}=\left[\frac{L}{15}\right]$

(the integer part of the ratio of the unknown length of the rope to the length of the stick, a measurable quantity). Then the length of the rope is $L \approx L_{1}^{\text {def }}=15 n_{1}$ in the case where the length of the remainder $l_{1}=L-15 n_{1}$ is less than half the length of the stick (underestimation) and is $L \approx L_{1}^{\text {excess }}=15\left(n_{1}+1\right)$ in the opposite case (overestimation) with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{2} \mathrm{~cm}.$

Step 2. In the case of "underestimation," perform a series of $n_{1}$ stick placements in the same direction (counterclockwise). The end of the stick at the last placement in the series will be at point $A_{2}$, which is a distance $l_{1}$ from $A_{1}$ in the clockwise direction. After performing $n_{2}-1$ series of $n_{1}$ placements, we obtain point $A_{n_{2}}$, which is a distance $l_{2}=L-n_{2} \cdot l_{1}<l_{1}$ from $A$, where $n_{2}=\left[\frac{L}{l_{1}}\right]$ (a measurable quantity is determined by the criterion: the next, $n_{2}$-th series will end with a transition across point A). Then the length of the rope in the case $l_{2}<\frac{l_{1}}{2}$ (underestimation) is $L \approx L_{2}^{\text {def }}=n_{2} \cdot l_{1}=n_{2} \cdot\left(L-15 n_{1}\right) \rightarrow L_{2}^{\text {def }}=\frac{15 n_{1} n_{2}}{n_{2}-1}=L_{1}^{\text {def }}+\frac{15 n_{1}}{n_{2}-1}$ with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{4}$ cm. In the case $\frac{l_{1}}{2}<l_{2}$ (with excess), the approximate length of the rope is calculated by the formula: $L \approx L_{2}^{\text {excess }}=\left(n_{2}+1\right) l_{1}=\left(n_{2}+1\right)\left(L-15 n_{1}\right) \rightarrow L_{2}^{\text {excess }}=\frac{15 n_{1}\left(n_{2}+1\right)}{n_{2}}=L_{1}^{\text {def }}+\frac{15 n_{1}}{n_{2}}$ with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{4}<5$ cm.

The conditions $l_{1} \leq l / 2=15 / 2$ (or $l_{2} \leq l_{1} / 2$) are established by laying the remainder along the stick or by folding the rope in half.

When calculating the length of the arc with "excess" on the first step, the end of the stick at the $n_{1}+1$ placement will stop at point $B_{1}$, which is a distance $l_{1}=15\left(n_{1}+1\right)-L \leq \frac{15}{2}$ from $A$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_fe74dcff8f31bf84a619g-3.jpg?height=237&width=1048&top_left_y=1052&top_left_x=344)

After performing a series of $n_{1}+1$ stick placements in the same direction (counterclockwise), its end will be at point $B_{2}$. After performing $n_{2}-1$ such series, we will reach point $B_{n_{2}}$, which is a distance $l_{2}=L-n_{2} \cdot l_{1}<l_{1}$ from $A$. If $l_{2}<\frac{l_{1}}{2}$ (with underestimation), the length of the rope is calculated by the formula:

$$
L \approx L_{2}^{\text {excess}}=n_{2} \cdot l_{1}=n_{2}\left(15\left(n_{1}+1\right)-L\right) \rightarrow L_{2}^{\text {excess}}=\frac{15 n_{2}\left(n_{1}+1\right)}{n_{2}+1}=L_{1}^{\text {excess}}-\frac{15\left(n_{1}+1\right)}{n_{2}+1}
$$

with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{4}<5$ cm.

If $\frac{l_{1}}{2}<l_{2}$ (with excess), to continue the calculation process, it is necessary to perform one more series of $n_{1}$ stick placements to cross point A and reach point $B_{n_{2}+1}$, which is no more than $\frac{15}{4}$ cm from A. Then the approximate length of the rope is calculated by the formula:

$L \approx L_{2}^{\text {excess}}=\left(n_{2}+1\right) l_{1}=\left(n_{2}+1\right)\left(\left(n_{1}+1\right) 15-L\right) \rightarrow L_{2}^{\text {excess}}=\frac{15\left(n_{1}+1\right)\left(n_{2}+1\right)}{n_{2}+2}=L_{1}^{\text {excess}}-\frac{15\left(n_{1}+1\right)}{n_{2}+2}$ with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{4}<5$ cm.

The described procedure allows the length of the rope to be calculated with an error no greater than $\frac{15}{2} \text{ cm}$ on the first step, no greater than $\frac{15}{4} \text{ cm}$ on the second step, no greater than $\frac{15}{8} \text{ cm}$ on the third step, and so on. Thus, using a stick, the length of the rope can be calculated with arbitrary precision. We will conclude the description of the procedure with an example of the approximate calculation of the length of a rope 14.53 meters long using a 15 cm stick.

solution:
Answer: $B D=\frac{p}{p+2 q} \cdot \sqrt{4 b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c}$

## Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_5b90898f214fc60b7b26g-3.jpg?height=325&width=671&top_left_y=2199&top_left_x=772)

Triangle $A B C$ and the transversal $M P$ are arbitrary: $\frac{A M}{M B} \cdot \frac{B N}{N C} \cdot \frac{C P}{P A}=1$

Calculations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\sqrt{4 b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c}-B D}{B D} \cdot \frac{p x}{q x} \cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \rightarrow \sqrt{4 b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c}-B D=\frac{2 q}{p} \cdot B D \rightarrow \\
& \rightarrow B D=\frac{p}{p+2 q} \cdot \sqrt{4 b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
b=4, c=3, p=3, q=2 \rightarrow \sqrt{4 b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c}=\sqrt{64+9-24}=7 \rightarrow B D=\frac{3}{3+4} \cdot 7=3

6. A wolf is surrounded by dogs located at points $M, N, P$ and $Q$ on the sides of a square $A B C D$, $M \in[A ; B], N \in[B ; C], P \in[C ; D], Q \in[D ; A]$ such that $A M: M B=B N: N C=C P: P D=D Q: Q A=1: 3$. The wolf, located inside the square at the intersection of lines $M P$ and $N Q$, can run in a straight line in any direction with a speed of $v_{w}$. The dogs run only along the sides of the square with a speed not exceeding $v_{c}$. The wolf can escape if it meets no more than one dog on the boundary of the square. For what values of the ratio $v_{c} / v_{w}$ does the wolf have a chance to escape?

## Answers and Solutions

Problem 1 Answer: $(x-2 y)_{\max }=\frac{25}{6}$
solution:
Solution

If $\varphi \in[0 ; 2 \pi]$, then the numbers $x=\frac{5}{2} \cos \varphi$ and $y=\frac{5}{3} \sin \varphi$ satisfy the equation. Then $x-2 y=\frac{5}{2} \cos \varphi-\frac{10}{3} \sin \varphi=\frac{5}{6}(3 \cos \varphi-4 \sin \varphi)=\frac{25}{6}\left(\frac{3}{5} \cos \varphi-\frac{4}{5} \sin \varphi\right)=$ $=\frac{25}{6}(\cos \theta \cos \varphi-\sin \theta \sin \varphi)=\frac{25}{6} \cos (\varphi+\theta)$
where $\theta=\arccos \frac{3}{5}$. Since the maximum possible value of $\cos (\varphi+\theta), \varphi \in[0 ; 2 \pi]$ is 1, then $(x-2 y)_{\max }=\frac{25}{6}$.

problem: Problem 2. Answer: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x=\frac{5 \pi}{2}(5-4 t) \\ y=12 \pi(t-1)\end{array}, t \in Z\right.$
solution:
Solution.

Since $|2 \sin (x+y)+3| \leq 5,|\cos (2 x-y)-1| \leq 2$, equality is possible only when $\left\{\begin{array}{c}\sin (x+y)=1 \\ \cos (2 x-y)=-1\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}x+y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2 \pi m, \\ 2 x-y=\pi+2 \pi n\end{array} \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}x=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{2 \pi}{3}(m+n) \\ y=\frac{2 \pi}{3}(2 m-n)\end{array}, m, n \in Z\right.\right.\right.$. Substituting the found $x$ and $y$ into the equation of the line, we get $3 \pi+4 \pi(m+n)+\frac{10 \pi}{3}(2 m-n)=15 \pi \rightarrow 32 m+2 n=36 \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}m=t \\ n=18-16 t\end{array}, t \in Z\right.$.

Then $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x=\frac{5 \pi}{2}(5-4 t) \\ y=12 \pi(t-1)\end{array}, t \in Z\right.$.

Problem 3 Answer: 1) $\left.k_{n}^{2}=C_{n+1}^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad k_{n}^{3}=C_{n+2}^{3}=\frac{n(n+1)(\mathrm{n}+2)}{6} \quad 2\right) n=10$

## Solution

1) Let $k_{n}^{m}$ denote the number of non-negative solutions to the equation $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}=m$. For $m=2$, the number of solutions where $x_{i}=2$ and $x_{j}=0, j \neq i$ is $C_{n}^{1}=n$. The number of solutions where $x_{i}=1, x_{j}=1, x_{k}=0, k \neq i, j$ is $C_{n}^{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Thus, $k_{n}^{2}=n+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=C_{n+1}^{2}$. For $m=3$, the number of solutions where $x_{i}=3$ and $x_{j}=0, j \neq i$ is $C_{n}^{1}=n$. The number of solutions where $x_{i}=2, x_{j}=1, x_{k}=0, k \neq i, j$ is $A_{n}^{2}=2!C_{n}^{2}=n(n-1)$. The number of solutions where $x_{i}=1, x_{j}=1, x_{k}=1, x_{r}=0, r \neq i, j, k$ is $C_{n}^{3}=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}$. Thus, $k_{n}^{3}=C_{n}^{1}+2 C_{n}^{2}+C_{n}^{3}=n+n(n-1)+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}=n+\frac{n(n-1)(n+4)}{6}=$ $=\frac{n}{6}\left(n^{2}+3 n+2\right)=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}=C_{n+2}^{3}$
2) The condition $k_{n}^{3}=4 k_{n}^{2}$ leads to the equation $\frac{n(n+1)(\mathrm{n}+2)}{6}=4 \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \rightarrow n+2=12 \rightarrow n=10$

If $\varphi_{1}(0)=\frac{v_{w}(n-1) \sqrt{2}}{n v_{c}}>1$, then the wolf's breakthrough on the boundary $[K ; C]$ is possible when $\frac{v_{c}}{v_{w}}1 \rightarrow \varphi_{2}(p)=\frac{t_{c}}{t_{w}}=\frac{v_{w} \sqrt{2}}{n v_{c}} \cdot \frac{p n+1}{\sqrt{1-2 p+2 p^{2}}}>1$.

Problem 3 Answer: $P(x)=\frac{1}{6}(x-1)\left(x^{2}-2 x+6\right)$

## Solution

Let $n$ be the degree of the polynomial $P(x)$. We will prove that $n \leq 3$. Substitution $t=x+1$. Then the identity will take the form: $P(t+1)+P(t-1)-2 P(t)=t-1$.

Let $P(t)=a_{n} t^{n}+a_{n-1} t^{n-1}+a_{n-2} t^{n-2}+\ldots+a_{1} t+a_{0}$. Then

$P(t+1)+P(t-1)-2 P(t)=a_{n}\left((t+1)^{n}+(t-1)^{n}-2 t^{n}\right)+a_{n-1}\left((t+1)^{n-1}+(t-1)^{n-1}-2 t^{n-1}\right)+\ldots+2 a_{0}$.

The highest degree of $t$ in the first bracket is $n-2$ with a coefficient of $n(n-1)$, in the second bracket $n-3$ with a coefficient of $(n-1)(n-2)$, and so on. If $n-2>1$, the identity in $t$ is impossible, so $n \leq 3$.

Case 1. $n=3$

$P(t+1)+P(t-1)-2 P(t)=a_{3}\left((t+1)^{3}+(t-1)^{3}-2 t^{3}\right)+2 a_{2}=6 a_{3} t+2 a_{2} \equiv t-1$

$\rightarrow a_{3}=\frac{1}{6}, a_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}$

in this case, the coefficients $a_{1}, a_{0}$ are arbitrary: $P(t)=\frac{1}{6} t^{3}-\frac{1}{2} t^{2}+a_{1} t+a_{0}$.

The condition that $P(x)$ is divisible by $x-1$ and $P(2)=1$ is equivalent to the system:

$\left\{\begin{array}{c}P(\mathrm{t})=a_{1}+a_{0}=1 / 3 \\ P(2)=2 a_{1}+a_{0}-2 / 3=1\end{array} \rightarrow a_{1}=\frac{4}{3}, a_{0}=-1\right.$

$P(x)=\frac{1}{6} x^{3}-\frac{1}{2} x^{2}+\frac{4}{3} x-1=\frac{1}{6}\left(x^{3}-3 x^{2}+8 x-6\right)=\frac{1}{6}(x-1)\left(x^{2}-2 x+6\right)$

Case 2. $n=2$

$P(t+1)+P(t-1)-2 P(t)=2 a_{2} \equiv t-1$, which is impossible.

Case 3. $n=1$

$P(t+1)+P(t-1)-2 P(t)=0 \equiv t-1$, which is impossible.

Problem 4 Answer: 9 pairs, $\left\{\begin{array}{l}x=23-3 t-t^{2} \\ y=23-2 t-t^{2}\end{array}, t=-5,-4, \ldots, 3\right.$

The integer values of $t$ are $t=-5,-4, \ldots, 3$, giving 9 pairs of solutions.

problem: 1. Find all $x$ that satisfy the inequality $n^{2} x^{2}-\left(2 n^{2}+n\right) x+n^{2}+n-6 \leq 0$ for any natural $n$.
solution:
Solution. The roots of the quadratic trinomial $n^{2} x^{2}-\left(2 n^{2}+n\right) x+n^{2}+n-6$ are

$$
x_{1}=1-\frac{2}{n}, x_{2}=1+\frac{3}{n}
$$

Factorize the left side of the inequality

$$
n^{2}\left(x-\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\right)\right)\left(x-\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)\right) \leq 0
$$

Solving the inequality using the interval method, we get $x \in\left[1-\frac{2}{n} ; 1+\frac{3}{n}\right]$. Only $x=1$ belongs to this interval for any $n$.

Answer: $x=1$

problem: 2. Solve the equation $\left(\cos \frac{2 x}{5}-\cos \frac{2 \pi}{15}\right)^{2}+\left(\sin \frac{2 x}{3}-\sin \frac{4 \pi}{9}\right)^{2}=0$.
solution:
Solution. The equation is equivalent to the system of equations $\left\{\begin{array}{l}\cos \frac{2 x}{5}-\cos \frac{2 \pi}{15}=0 \\ \sin \frac{2 x}{3}-\sin \frac{4 \pi}{9}=0\end{array}\right.$.

Solve the equation $\cos \frac{2 x}{5}=\cos \frac{2 \pi}{15}:\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{2 x}{5}=\frac{2 \pi}{15}+2 \pi k, \rightarrow x_{1}=\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi k, k \in Z \\ \frac{2 x}{5}=-\frac{2 \pi}{15}+2 \pi k \rightarrow x_{2}=-\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi n, n \in Z\end{array}\right.$.

Solve the equation $\sin \frac{2 x}{3}=\sin \frac{4 \pi}{9}:\left[\begin{array}{l}\frac{2 x}{3}=\frac{4 \pi}{9}+2 \pi m, \rightarrow x_{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}+3 \pi m, m \in Z \\ \frac{2 x}{3}=\frac{5 \pi}{9}+2 \pi s \rightarrow x_{4}=\frac{5 \pi}{6}+3 \pi s, s \in Z\end{array}\right.$.

The solutions to the original equation can be the intersections of the series $x_{1} \cap x_{3}, x_{1} \cap x_{4}, x_{2} \cap x_{3}, x_{2} \cap x_{4}$

Case 1. Intersection $x_{1} \cap x_{3}=\varnothing$. Indeed,

$$
x_{1}=\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi k=x_{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}+3 \pi m \rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=5 k-3 m .
$$

The equality is impossible, since the right side is an integer.

Case 2. Intersection $x_{1} \cap x_{4}=\varnothing$. Indeed,

$$
x_{1}=\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi k=x_{4}=\frac{5 \pi}{6}+3 \pi s \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}=5 k-3 s .
$$

The last equality is impossible, since $k$ and $s$ are integers.

Case 3. Intersection $x_{2} \cap x_{3} \neq \varnothing$. Indeed,

$$
x_{2}=-\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi n=x_{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}+3 \pi m \rightarrow 5 n-3 m=1 \rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}
n=2+3 t \\
m=3+5 t, t \in Z
\end{array}\right.
$$

Then $x=-\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi(2+3 t)=\frac{29 \pi}{3}+15 \pi t, t \in Z$

Case 4. Intersection $x_{2} \cap x_{4}=\varnothing$. Indeed,

$$
x_{2}=-\frac{\pi}{3}+5 \pi n=x_{4}=\frac{5 \pi}{6}+3 \pi s \rightarrow 5 n-3 s=\frac{7}{6} \text {, which is impossible. }
$$

Answer. $x=\frac{29 \pi}{3}+15 \pi t, t \in Z$

The system becomes: $\left\{\begin{array}{l}2[x]+[y]=2.5-4 u+3 v \\ {[x]-3[y]=12-4 u-4 v}\end{array}\right.$.

Express $[x]$ and $[y]$ in terms of $u$ and $v:\left\{\begin{array}{l}{[x]=\frac{19.5-16 u+5 v}{7}} \\ {[y]=\frac{-21.5+4 u+11 v}{7}}\end{array}\right.$.

Thus, for $[x]$ only three values are possible: $[x]=1 ; 2 ; 3$.

$$
16 u-5 v=12.5 \rightarrow u=\frac{12.5+5 v}{16} \in[0 ; 1) \rightarrow v \in[-2.5 ; 0.7) \rightarrow v \in[0 ; 0.7)
$$

Then $[y]=\frac{49 v-73.5}{28} \in(-2.625 ;-1.4)$ for $v \in[0 ; 0.7)$ and with the condition of integer $[y]$ we get $\quad[y]=-2 . \quad$ This $\quad$ value $\quad$ corresponds to $\quad v_{1}=\frac{5}{14}, u_{1}=\frac{25}{28} \quad$ and $x_{1}=1+\frac{25}{28}=\frac{53}{28}, y_{1}=-2+\frac{5}{14}=-\frac{23}{14}$.

Case 2. $[x]=2$. We have $\frac{19.5-16 u+5 v}{7}=2$. From this we get

$$

$$

Then $[y]=\frac{49 v-80.5}{28} \in[-2.875 ;-1.125)$ for $v \in[0 ; 1)$ and with the condition of integer $[y]$ we get $[y]=-2$. This value corresponds to $v_{2}=0.5, u_{2}=0.5$ and $x_{2}=2+0.5=2.5, y_{2}=-2+0.5=-1.5$.

Case 3. $[x]=3$. We have $\frac{19.5-16 u+5 v}{7}=3$. From this we get
