problem: 3. There are 195 different cards with numbers $1, 5, 7, 5^{2}, 7^{2}, \ldots, 5^{97}, 7^{97}$ (each card has exactly one number, and each number appears exactly once). In how many ways can 3 cards be chosen so that the product of the numbers on the chosen cards is a square of an integer divisible by 35?
solution:
Answer: 223488.

Solution. Consider the case when one of the selected cards has a one written on it. Then, on the other two cards, even powers of fives and sevens must be recorded. There are 48 ways to choose an even power of five and 48 ways to choose an even power of seven, and since this choice is made independently, the total number of ways in this case is $48^{2}=2304$.

Now let's move on to the case when the card with one is not used. There are two possibilities: to take two cards with powers of five and one with a power of seven, or vice versa.

Suppose we take two cards with powers of seven. Since the product of the selected numbers must contain seven in an even power, the powers of seven on the selected cards must have the same parity. We have a total of 49 cards with odd powers and 48 cards with even powers. Thus, there are $C_{49}^{2}=\frac{49 \cdot 48}{2}=1176$ ways to choose cards with odd powers and $C_{48}^{2}=\frac{48 \cdot 47}{2}=1128$ ways to choose two cards with even powers, totaling 2304 ways. After selecting the cards with powers of seven, we can choose any card with an even power of five (48 ways). Since the choice of the card with the power of five is independent of the previous choice, in total, we get $2304 \cdot 48=110592$ ways.

It is easy to see that if we take two cards with powers of five and one with a power of seven, the number of ways will be the same as in the previous case. Therefore, we get $2304+110592 \cdot 2=223488$ ways.

problem: 5. Solve the inequality $\log _{1+x^{2}}\left(1+8 x^{5}\right)+\log _{1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}}\left(1+x^{2}\right) \leqslant 1+\log _{1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}}\left(1+8 x^{5}\right)$. Answer: $x \in\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{8}} ;-\frac{1}{2}\right] \cup\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} ; 0\right) \cup\left(0 ; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) \cup\left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\}$.
solution:
Solution. Let $1+x^{2}=u, 1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}=v, 1+8 x^{5}=w$. Then the inequality takes the form $\log _{u} w+\log _{v} u-\log _{v} w-1 \leqslant 0$. It can be transformed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log _{u} w+\frac{1}{\log _{u} v}-\frac{\log _{u} w}{\log _{u} v}-1 \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{\log _{u} v \log _{u} w+1-\log _{u} w-\log _{u} v}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \Leftrightarrow \frac{\left(\log _{u} w-1\right)\left(\log _{u} v-1\right)}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{\left(\log _{u} w-\log _{u} u\right)\left(\log _{u} v-\log _{u} u\right)}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0
\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this inequality, we further apply the method of rationalization: the sign of the difference $\log _{a} b- \log _{a} c$ on the domain of admissible values coincides with the sign of the expression $\frac{b-c}{a-1}$; in particular (when $c=1$), the sign of the logarithm $\log _{a} b$ coincides with the sign of the expression $\frac{b-1}{a-1}$. Then from the last inequality we get

$$
\frac{(w-u)(v-u)}{(u-1)(v-1)} \leqslant 0
$$

The domain of admissible values (DAV) of the original inequality is defined by the conditions $u>0, v>0, w>0, u \neq 1, v \neq 1$. The last two restrictions are automatically satisfied for any solution (??), since at $u=1$ or $v=1$ the denominator of the fraction turns to zero. In addition, $u=1+x^{2}$ and $v=1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}$ are positive for all values of $x$. Therefore, the only restriction from the DAV that needs to be taken into account is the inequality $1+8 x^{5}>0$, from which $x>-\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{8}}$. We solve the inequality (??):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\left(8 x^{5}+1-x^{2}-1\right)\left(1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}-1-x^{2}\right)}{\left(1+x^{2}-1\right)\left(1-3 x^{2}+16 x^{4}-1\right)} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{4 x^{4}\left(8 x^{3}-1\right)\left(4 x^{2}-1\right)}{x^{4}\left(16 x^{2}-3\right)} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0, \\
\frac{(2 x-1)(4 x^{2}+2 x+1)(2 x+1)(2 x-1)}{(16 x^{2}-3)} \leqslant 0
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0, \\
\frac{(2 x+1)(2 x-1)^{2}}{\left(x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)\left(x+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)} \leqslant 0
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow\right.\right. \\
& \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0 \\
x \in\left(-\infty ;-\frac{1}{2}\right] \cup\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} ; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) \cup\left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\}
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking into account the DAV, we finally get $x \in\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{8}} ;-\frac{1}{2}\right] \cup\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} ; 0\right) \cup\left(0 ; \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) \bigcup\left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\}$.

problem:
6. Find all values of the parameter $a$, for each of which the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}+y^{2}=26(y \sin a-x \cos a) \\
x^{2}+y^{2}=26(y \cos 2 a-x \sin 2 a)
\end{array}\right.
$$

has two solutions $\left(x_{1} ; y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2} ; y_{2}\right)$ such that the distance between the points $P\left(x_{1} ; y_{1}\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{2} ; y_{2}\right)$ is 24.
solution:
Answer: $a=\frac{\pi}{6} \pm \frac{2}{3} \operatorname{arctg} \frac{5}{12}+\frac{2 \pi n}{3}, \frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2 \pi n}{3}$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Solution. By completing the squares, we rewrite the system as

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(x+13 \cos a)^{2}+(y-13 \sin a)^{2}=169 \\
(x+13 \sin 2 a)^{2}+(y-13 \cos 2 a)^{2}=169
\end{array}\right.
$$

Each of these equations represents a circle with radius 13; the center of the first circle is the point $A(-13 \cos a ; 13 \sin a)$, and the center of the second circle is the point $B(-13 \sin 2 a ; 13 \cos 2 a)$.

If these equations represent the same circle, then there will be points on this circle that are 24 units apart. The circles coincide if they have the same center. We get

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } a = \operatorname { s i n } 2 a , } \\
{ \operatorname { s i n } 2 a = \operatorname { c o s } a }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } 2 a + \operatorname { c o s } ( \frac { \pi } { 2 } + 2 a ) = 0 , } \\
{ \operatorname { c o s } 2 a + \operatorname { c o s } ( \frac { \pi } { 2 } + a ) = 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
2 \cos \frac{\pi+6 a}{4} \cos \frac{\pi+2 a}{4}=0 \\
2 \cos \frac{\pi+6 a}{4} \cos \frac{\pi-2 a}{4}=0
\end{array}\right.\right.\right.
$$

These equalities hold if either $\cos \frac{\pi+6 a}{4}=0$ or $\cos \frac{\pi+2 a}{4}=\cos \frac{\pi-2 a}{4}=0$. In the first case, we get $a=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2 k \pi}{3}, k \in \mathbb{Z}$. The second case clearly does not provide solutions.

Now suppose the circles are different and intersect at points $P$ and $Q$. Then the quadrilateral $A P B Q$ is a rhombus. It is known that in any parallelogram, the sum of the squares of the diagonals is equal to the sum of the squares of all four sides, so $A B^{2}+P Q^{2}=4 A P^{2}$. Since we want the points $P$ and $Q$ to be 24 units apart, $P Q=24$, therefore $A B^{2}+576=4 \cdot 169, A B=10$. Thus, it is necessary that the distance between the centers of the circles $A$ and $B$ be 10. From this,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{(-13 \sin 2 a+13 \cos a)^{2}+(13 \cos 2 a-13 \sin a)^{2}}=10 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow 338-338 \sin 2 a \cos a-338 \sin a \cos 2 a=100 \Leftrightarrow 338 \sin 3 a=238 \Leftrightarrow
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\Leftrightarrow a=\frac{(-1)^{k}}{3} \arcsin \frac{119}{169}+\frac{k \pi}{3}, k \in \mathbb{Z}
$$

problem:

Answer: a) $AB=\sqrt{21}$; b) $\angle\left(C_{1} C, A A_{1} B\right)=\arcsin \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}, A_{1} C_{1}=\frac{7-2 \sqrt{7}}{3}$.

Solution. a) Let $O$ be the center of the sphere $\Omega, Q$ be the center of the triangle $ABA_{1}, A_{1}X$ be its median. Then $O$ lies on the perpendicular $\ell$ to $(ABA_{1})$ passing through $Q$. On the other hand, $O$ lies in the plane $\alpha$ passing through $M$ and perpendicular to $CC_{1}$, which is parallel to $(ABC)$. Note that $Q$ lies in $\alpha$, since $XQ:QA_{1}=1:2=CM:MC_{1}$. But $Q$ also lies on $\ell$. If the plane $(ABB_{1}A_{1})$ were perpendicular to the plane $(ABC)$, then all three lateral faces would be perpendicular to the base, which is impossible in a truncated pyramid. b) Let $Y$ and $Z$ be the projections of points $A_{1}$ and $O$ onto the plane $(ABC)$; then $Z$ divides the segment $XY$ in the ratio $XZ:ZY=1:2$. Since $CC_{1} \perp (ABC)$, the point $Y$ lies on the line $AC$.

$$
\angle\left(CC_{1}, ABA_{1}\right)=\angle YA_{1}X=\arcsin \frac{YX}{A_{1}X}=\arcsin \left(\sqrt{\frac{21}{2}}:\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \sqrt{21}\right)\right)=\arcsin \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

In addition, $YZ=\frac{2}{3} YX=\sqrt{\frac{14}{3}}$.

Let $T$ be the projection of $Z$ onto $AC$. Then $ZT=YZ \cos \angle YZT=YZ \cos \angle BAC=\frac{\sqrt{14}}{3}$ and $YT=$ $YZ \sin \angle YZT=\frac{2 \sqrt{7}}{3}$. On the other hand, since $CZ=MO=\sqrt{7}$, we have $CT=\sqrt{CZ^{2}-ZT^{2}}=$ $\sqrt{7-\frac{14}{9}}=\frac{7}{3}$. Therefore, $A_{1}C_{1}=YC=CT-YT=\frac{7}{3}-\frac{2 \sqrt{7}}{3}$.

Solution. Let $f(x)=a x+b$. Then the abscissas of the points of intersection of the graphs in the first case are determined from the equation $x^{2}+2=a x+b$, and in the second case - from the equation $x^{2}-1=a x+b+1$. Consider the first case in more detail. The equation has the form $x^{2}-a x-(b-2)=0$, from which $x_{1,2}=$ $\frac{a \pm \sqrt{a^{2}+4 b-8}}{2},\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right|=\sqrt{a^{2}+4 b-8}$. Since the points of intersection of the graphs lie on a line with a slope of $a$, the distance between the points is $\sqrt{a^{2}+1}$ times greater than $\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right|$. Therefore, the distance between the points is $\sqrt{\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(a^{2}+4 b-8\right)}$. Similarly, we find that in the second case, the distance between the points is $\sqrt{\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(a^{2}+4 b-8\right)}$. From the condition, we obtain the system of equations $\left\{\begin{array}{l}\left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(a^{2}+4 b-8\right)=10, \\ \left(a^{2}+1\right)\left(a^{2}+4 b+8\right)=42,\end{array}\right.$ solving which, we find that $a^{2}=1, b=3$.

Let's find the required distance. The abscissas of the points of intersection are determined by the equation $x^{2}-a x-$ $b-1=0$, so $\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right|=\sqrt{a^{2}+4 b+4}=\sqrt{17}$, and the distance between the points of intersection is $\left|x_{2}-x_{1}\right| \sqrt{a^{2}+1}=\sqrt{17} \sqrt{2}=\sqrt{34}$.

problem: 2. It is known that $\frac{\cos 3 x}{(2 \cos 2 x-1) \cos 2 y}=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2}(x+2 y)$ and $\frac{\sin 3 x}{(2 \cos 2 x+1) \sin 2 y}=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2}(x+2 y)$. Find all possible values of the expression $\cos (x+6 y)$, given that there are at least two. Answer: -1 or $-\frac{2}{3}$.
solution:
Solution. Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos 3 x=\cos (2 x+x)=\cos 2 x \cos x-\sin 2 x \sin x=\cos 2 x \cos x-2 \sin ^{2} x \cos x= \\
& \quad=\cos 2 x \cos x-(1-\cos 2 x) \cos x=(2 \cos 2 x-1) \cos x \\
& \sin 3 x=\sin (2 x+x)=\sin 2 x \cos x+\sin x \cos 2 x= \\
& \quad=2 \sin x \cos ^{2} x+\sin x \cos 2 x=\sin x(1+\cos 2 x)+\sin x \cos 2 x=(2 \cos 2 x+1) \sin x
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking this into account, the given equalities take the form

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\cos x}{\cos 2 y}=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2}(x+2 y) \\
\frac{\sin x}{\sin 2 y}=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2}(x+2 y)
\end{array}\right.
$$

(it is also necessary to take into account that $\cos 2 x \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}$). Adding the equations (??) we get $\frac{\cos x}{\cos 2 y}+$ $\frac{\sin x}{\sin 2 y}=2$, from which $\cos 2 y \neq 0, \sin 2 y \neq 0$ and $\cos x \sin 2 y+\sin x \cos 2 y=2 \sin 2 y \cos 2 y$. The last equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\sin (x+2 y)=\sin 4 y \Leftrightarrow\left[\begin{array} { l } 
{ x + 2 y = 4 y + 2 \pi k } \\
{ x + 2 y = \pi - 4 y + 2 \pi k , k \in \mathbb { Z } }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
x=2 y+2 \pi k \\
x=\pi-6 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Let's consider these two possibilities separately.

If $x=2 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, then the system (??) takes the form $\left\{\begin{array}{l}1=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2} 4 y, \\ 1=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2} 4 y ;\end{array} \quad\right.$ from which $\sin ^{2} 4 y=\frac{5}{6}$, $\cos ^{2} 4 y=\frac{1}{6}$. It is easy to see that this system has solutions. In this case, $\cos (x+6 y)=\cos 8 y=$ $2 \cos ^{2} 4 y-1=2 \cdot \frac{1}{6}-1=-\frac{2}{3}$.

If $x=\pi-6 y+2 \pi k, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, then (??) takes the form

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - \frac { \operatorname { c o s } 6 y } { \operatorname { c o s } 2 y } = \frac { 1 } { 6 } + \operatorname { s i n } ^ { 2 } 4 y , } \\
{ \frac { \operatorname { s i n } 6 y } { \operatorname { s i n } 2 y } = \frac { 5 } { 6 } + \operatorname { c o s } ^ { 2 } 4 y }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
3-4 \cos ^{2} 2 y=\frac{1}{6}+\sin ^{2} 4 y \\
3-4 \sin ^{2} 2 y=\frac{5}{6}+\cos ^{2} 4 y
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Each of the equations in the last system reduces to the equation $\cos ^{2} 4 y-2 \cos 4 y-\frac{1}{6}=0$, which has solutions, since $\cos 4 y=1-\sqrt{\frac{7}{6}}$. Therefore, this case is also possible, and we get that $\cos (x+6 y)=\cos (\pi+2 \pi k)=-1$.

Thus, $\cos (x+6 y)$ can be equal to $-\frac{2}{3}$ or -1.

Note that in both cases all the restrictions that appeared in connection with the domain of definition $\left(\cos 2 x \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}\right.$, $\cos 2 y \neq 0, \sin 2 y \neq 0$) are satisfied.

Remark. Since the problem states that the expression $\cos (x+6 y)$ has at least two different values, checking the possibility of the cases is not mandatory.

problem: 3. There are 167 different cards with numbers $1, 3, 11, 3^{2}, 11^{2}, \ldots, 3^{83}, 11^{83}$ (each card has exactly one number, and each number appears exactly once). In how many ways can 3 cards be chosen so that the product of the numbers on the chosen cards is a square of an integer divisible by 33?
solution:
Answer: 139523.

Solution. Consider the case when one of the selected cards has the number one written on it. Then, on the other two cards, even powers of the numbers three and eleven must be recorded. There are 41 ways to choose an even power of three and 41 ways to choose an even power of eleven, and since this choice is made independently, the total number of ways in this case is $41^{2}=1681$.

Now let's move on to the case when the card with the number one is not used. There are two possibilities: to take two cards with powers of three and one with a power of eleven, or vice versa. Suppose we take two cards with powers of three. Since the number three must be present in an even power in the product of the selected numbers, the powers of three on the selected cards must have the same parity. We have a total of 42 cards with odd powers and 41 cards with even powers. Thus, there are $C_{42}^{2}=\frac{42 \cdot 41}{2}=861$ ways to choose cards with odd powers and $C_{41}^{2}=\frac{41 \cdot 40}{2}=820$ ways to choose two cards with even powers - in total, we get 1681 ways. After selecting the cards with powers of three, we can choose any card with an even power of eleven (41 ways). Since the choice of the card with the power of eleven is independent of the previous choice, in total, we get $1681 \cdot 41=68921$ ways.

It is easy to see that if we take two cards with powers of eleven and one with a power of three, the number of ways will be the same as in the previous case. Therefore, we get $1681+68921 \cdot 2=139523$ ways.

problem:
4. Chords $AB$ and $CD$ of circle $\Gamma$ with center $O$ have a length of 8. The extensions of segments $BA$ and $CD$ beyond points $A$ and $D$ respectively intersect at point $P$. Line $PO$ intersects segment $AC$ at point $L$, such that $AL: LC = 1: 5$.

a) Find $AP$.

b) Suppose additionally that the radius of circle $\Gamma$ is 5, and point $T$ is the center of the circle inscribed in triangle $ACP$. Find the length of segment $PT$ and the area of triangle $ACP$.
solution:
Answer: $A P=2, P T=3 \sqrt{5}-5, S_{\triangle A P C}=8$.

Solution. a) Drop perpendiculars $O H$ and $O N$ from point $O$ to the chords $C D$ and $A B$ respectively. Since these chords are equal, the distances from the center of the circle to them are also equal, so
$O H=O N$. Right triangles $O P N$ and $O P H$ are equal by the leg and hypotenuse ( $O P$ is common), so $P N=P H, \angle O P N=\angle O P H$ (the latter means that $P O$ is the bisector of angle $B P C$). Since a diameter perpendicular to a chord bisects it, points $H$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $C D$ and $A B$ respectively, so $A N=H D=4$; from this it follows that $A P=D P$. Let $A P=D P=y$. Since $P L$ is the bisector of triangle $A P C, \frac{P A}{P C}=\frac{A L}{L C}$, hence $\frac{y}{y+8}=\frac{1}{5}$, $y=2$.

b) Triangles $O P A$ and $O P D$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them ( $P O$ is common, $A P=D P, \angle A P O=\angle D P O)$, so $\angle A O P=\angle D O P$. This means that segment $O P$ bisects arc $A D$. Denote the intersection point of segment $O P$ with the circle as $J$. Then $C J$ is the bisector of angle $A C D$ (angles $A C J$ and $D C J$ are inscribed, subtending equal arcs). Moreover, $P J$ is the bisector of angle $A P C$, so $J$ is the intersection point of the bisectors of triangle $A P C$, i.e., the center of its inscribed circle. Thus, points $J$ and $T$ coincide.

By the Pythagorean theorem for triangle $D H O$ we get $O H^{2}=O D^{2}-D H^{2}=25-16=9$. By the Pythagorean theorem for triangle $P H O: P O^{2}=P H^{2}+O H^{2}=6^{2}+9=45$. Therefore, $P T=P O-O T=3 \sqrt{5}-5$.

Let $\angle C P O=\beta$. Then $\sin \beta=\frac{O H}{O P}=3: \sqrt{45}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \cos \beta=\sqrt{1-\sin ^{2} \beta}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}, \sin 2 \beta=$ $2 \cos \beta \sin \beta=\frac{4}{5}, S_{\triangle A P C}=\frac{1}{2} P A \cdot P C \sin 2 \beta=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot 10 \cdot \frac{4}{5}=8$.

problem: 5. Solve the inequality $\log _{1+x^{2}}\left(1-27 x^{5}\right)+\log _{1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}}\left(1+x^{2}\right) \leqslant 1+\log _{1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}}\left(1-27 x^{5}\right)$. Answer: $x \in\left\{-\frac{1}{3}\right\} \bigcup\left(-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}} ; 0\right) \cup\left(0 ; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right) \cup\left[\frac{1}{3} ; \frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{27}}\right)$.
solution:
Solution. Let $1+x^{2}=u, 1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}=v, 1-27 x^{5}=w$. Then the inequality takes the form $\log _{u} w+\log _{v} u-\log _{v} w-1 \leqslant 0$. It can be transformed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log _{u} w+\frac{1}{\log _{u} v}-\frac{\log _{u} w}{\log _{u} v}-1 \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{\log _{u} v \log _{u} w+1-\log _{u} w-\log _{u} v}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \Leftrightarrow \frac{\left(\log _{u} w-1\right)\left(\log _{u} v-1\right)}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{\left(\log _{u} w-\log _{u} u\right)\left(\log _{u} v-\log _{u} u\right)}{\log _{u} v} \leqslant 0
\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this inequality, we further apply the method of rationalization: the sign of the difference $\log _{a} b- \log _{a} c$ on the domain of admissible values coincides with the sign of the expression $\frac{b-c}{a-1}$; in particular (when $c=1$), the sign of the logarithm $\log _{a} b$ coincides with the sign of the expression $\frac{b-1}{a-1}$. Then from the last inequality we get

$$
\frac{(w-u)(v-u)}{(u-1)(v-1)} \leqslant 0
$$

The domain of admissible values (DAV) of the original inequality is defined by the conditions $u>0, v>0, w>0, u \neq 1, v \neq 1$. The last two restrictions are automatically satisfied for any solution (??), since at $u=1$ or $v=1$ the denominator of the fraction turns to zero. In addition, $u=1+x^{2}$ and $v=1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}$ are positive for all values of $x$. Therefore, the only restriction from the DAV that needs to be taken into account is the inequality $1-27 x^{5}>0$, from which $x<\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{27}}$. We solve the inequality $(?):$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\left(1-27 x^{5}-x^{2}-1\right)\left(1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}-1-x^{2}\right)}{\left(1+x^{2}-1\right)\left(1-3 x^{2}+36 x^{4}-1\right)} \leqslant 0 & \Leftrightarrow \frac{4 x^{4}\left(-27 x^{3}-1\right)\left(9 x^{2}-1\right)}{3 x^{4}\left(12 x^{2}-1\right)} \leqslant 0 \Leftrightarrow \\
\Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0, \\
\frac{(3 x+1)\left(9 x^{2}-3 x+1\right)(3 x+1)(3 x-1)}{\left(12 x^{2}-1\right)} \geqslant 0
\end{array}\right. & \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0, \\
\frac{(3 x-1)(3 x+1)^{2}}{\left(x-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right)\left(x+\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right)} \geqslant 0
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow\right. \\
& \Leftrightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x \neq 0, \\
x \in\left\{-\frac{1}{3}\right\} \bigcup\left(-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}} ; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right) \cup\left[\frac{1}{3} ;+\infty\right) . \\
\text { Taking into account the DAV, we finally get } x \in\left\{-\frac{1}{3}\right\} \bigcup\left(-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}} ; 0\right) \cup\left(0 ; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right) \bigcup\left[\frac{1}{3} ; \frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{27}}\right) .
\end{array}\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
6. Find all values of the parameter $a$, for each of which the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}+y^{2}=10(x \cos a+y \sin a) \\
x^{2}+y^{2}=10(x \sin 3 a+y \cos 3 a)
\end{array}\right.
$$

has two solutions $\left(x_{1} ; y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2} ; y_{2}\right)$ such that the distance between the points $P\left(x_{1} ; y_{1}\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{2} ; y_{2}\right)$ is 8.
solution:
Answer: $a=\frac{\pi}{8} \pm \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{arctg} \frac{3}{4}+\frac{\pi n}{2}, \frac{\pi}{8}+\frac{\pi n}{2}$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Solution. By completing the squares, we rewrite the system as

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(x-5 \cos a)^{2}+(y-5 \sin a)^{2}=25 \\
(x-5 \sin 3 a)^{2}+(y-5 \cos 3 a)^{2}=25
\end{array}\right.
$$

Each of these equations represents a circle of radius 5; the center of the first circle is the point $A(5 \cos a ; 5 \sin a)$, and the center of the second circle is the point $B(5 \sin 3 a ; 5 \cos 3 a)$.

If these equations represent the same circle, then there will be points on this circle that are 8 units apart. The circles coincide if they have the same center. We get

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } a = \operatorname { s i n } 3 a , } \\
{ \operatorname { s i n } 3 a = \operatorname { c o s } a }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ \operatorname { c o s } a + \operatorname { c o s } ( \frac { \pi } { 2 } + 3 a ) = 0 , } \\
{ \operatorname { c o s } 3 a + \operatorname { c o s } ( \frac { \pi } { 2 } + a ) = 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
2 \cos \frac{\pi+8 a}{4} \cos \frac{\pi+4 a}{4}=0 \\
2 \cos \frac{\pi+8 a}{4} \cos \frac{\pi-4 a}{4}=0
\end{array}\right.\right.\right.
$$

These equalities hold if either $\cos \frac{\pi+8 a}{4}=0$ or $\cos \frac{\pi-4 a}{4}=\cos \frac{\pi+4 a}{4}=0$. In the first case, we get $a=\frac{\pi}{8}+\frac{k \pi}{2}, k \in \mathbb{Z}$. The second case clearly does not provide solutions.

Now suppose the circles are different and intersect at points $P$ and $Q$. Then the quadrilateral $A P B Q$ is a rhombus. It is known that in any parallelogram, the sum of the squares of the diagonals is equal to the sum of the squares of all four sides, so $A B^{2}+P Q^{2}=4 A P^{2}$. Since we want the points $P$ and $Q$ to be 8 units apart, $P Q=8$, therefore $A B^{2}+64=4 \cdot 25, A B=6$. Thus, it is necessary that the distance between the centers of the circles $A$ and $B$ be 6. From this,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{(5 \sin 3 a-5 \cos a)^{2}+(5 \cos 3 a-5 \sin a)^{2}}=6 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \Leftrightarrow 50-50 \sin a \cos 3 a-50 \sin 3 a \cos a=36 \Leftrightarrow 50 \sin 4 a=14 \Leftrightarrow \\
& \Leftrightarrow a=\frac{(-1)^{k}}{4} \arcsin \frac{7}{25}+\frac{k \pi}{4}, k \in \mathbb{Z}
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
7. Given a truncated pyramid $A B C A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ with lateral edges $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}\left(A B C \| A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}\right)$, such that the triangle $B B_{1} C$ is equilateral. On the edge $A A_{1}$, perpendicular to the base $A B C$ of the pyramid, there is a point $N$ such that $A N: N A_{1}=1: 2$. The sphere $\Omega \mathrm{c}$ with radius $\sqrt{7}$ passes through the vertices of the triangle $B B_{1} C$ and is tangent to the segment $A A_{1}$ at point $N$.

a) Find the length of the edge $B B_{1}$.

b) Suppose additionally that $\angle A B C=\arccos \frac{2}{\sqrt{7}}$. Find the angle between the line $A A_{1}$ and the plane $B B_{1} C$, as well as the length of the edge $A_{1} B_{1}$.
solution:
Answer: a) $B B_{1}=\sqrt{21} ;$ b) $\angle\left(A A_{1}, B B_{1} C\right)=\pi / 6, A_{1} B_{1}=\sqrt{6}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Solution. a) Let $O$ be the center of the sphere $\Omega, Q$ be the center of the triangle $B C B_{1}, B_{1} X$ be its median. Then $O$ lies on the perpendicular $\ell$ to $\left(B C B_{1}\right)$ passing through $Q$. On the other hand, $O$ lies in the plane $\alpha$, passing through $N$ perpendicular to $A A_{1}$ - that is, parallel to ( $A B C$ ). Note that $Q$ lies in $\alpha$, since $X Q: Q B_{1}=1: 2=A N: N A_{1}$. But $Q$ lies on $\ell$ as well. If
the plane $\left(B C C_{1} B_{1}\right)$ were perpendicular to the plane $(A B C)$, then all three lateral faces would be perpendicular to the base, which is impossible in a truncated pyramid. Therefore, $\alpha$ and $\ell$ intersect at exactly one point - the point $Q$. Thus, $Q=O$.

Thus, the circle circumscribed around the triangle $B C B_{1}$ is a great circle on $\Omega$, and its radius is $\sqrt{7}$. Hence, $B C=R \sqrt{3}=\sqrt{21}$.

b) Let $Y$ and $Z$ be the projections of the points $B_{1}$ and $O$ onto the plane $(A B C)$; then $Z$ divides the segment $X Y$ in the ratio $X Z: Z Y=1: 2$. Since $A A_{1} \perp(A B C)$, the point $Y$ lies on the line $A B$.

Right triangles $B_{1} Y B$ and $B_{1} Y C$ are equal by leg and hypotenuse, so $Y C=Y B$. Therefore, the height $Y X$ of the triangle $C B Y$ is equal to $X B \operatorname{tg} \angle A B C=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{4}$. From the right triangle $A_{1} Y X$ we find

$$
\angle\left(A A_{1}, B C B_{1}\right)=\angle Y B_{1} X=\arcsin \frac{Y X}{B_{1} X}=\arcsin \left(\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{4}:\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \sqrt{21}\right)\right)=\arcsin \frac{1}{2}
$$

from which $\angle\left(A A_{1}, B C B_{1}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6}$. In addition, $Y Z=\frac{2}{3} Y X=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$.

Let $T$ be the projection of $Z$ onto $A B$. Then $Z T=Y Z \cos \angle Y Z T=Y Z \cos \angle A B C=1$ and $Y T=$ $Y Z \sin \angle Y Z T=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. On the other hand, since $A Z=N O=\sqrt{7}$, we have $A T=\sqrt{A Z^{2}-Z T^{2}}=$ $\sqrt{7-1}=\sqrt{6}$. Hence $A_{1} B_{1}=A Y=A T-Y T=\sqrt{6}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

problem: 1. Find all values of $x$, for each of which one of the three given numbers $\log _{x^{2}}\left(x^{2}-3 x+2\right)$, $\log _{x^{2}} \frac{x^{2}}{x-2}$, and $\log _{x^{2}} \frac{x^{2}}{x-1}$ is equal to the sum of the other two.
solution:
Answer: $x=3$.

Solution. Note that on the domain of definition, the sum of all three logarithms is

$$
\log _{x^{2}}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{x-2} \cdot \frac{x^{2}}{x-1}\left(x^{2}-3 x+2\right)\right)=\log _{x^{2}} x^{4}=2
$$

Let the number that is equal to the sum of the other two be denoted by $c$, and the two remaining numbers by $a$ and $b$. Then $c=a+b$ and $a+b+c=2$, from which it follows that $c=1$, i.e., one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1.

The converse is also true, namely, if one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1, then since the sum of all three logarithms is 2, the sum of the remaining two is 1, i.e., their sum is equal to the first logarithm.

Thus, the condition of the problem is satisfied if and only if one of the logarithms is equal to 1 (and all logarithms exist). A logarithm is equal to 1 when its base is equal to the logarithmic expression. We obtain the system

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-2}, \\
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-1}, \\
x^{2}=x^{2}-3 x+2
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
x=0 \\
x=3 \\
x=2 \\
x=\frac{2}{3}
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Of the found values of the variable, only $x=3$ satisfies the domain of definition.

problem: 2. Given two linear functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ such that the graphs $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are parallel lines, not parallel to the coordinate axes. Find the minimum value of the function $3(g(x))^{2}+$ $2 f(x)$, if the minimum value of the function $3(f(x))^{2}+2 g(x)$ is $-\frac{19}{6}$.
solution:
Answer: $\frac{5}{2}$.

Solution. Let $f(x)=a x+b, g(x)=a x+c$, where $a \neq 0$. Consider $h(x)=3(f(x))^{2}+$ $2 g(x)$. Expanding the brackets, we get $h(x)=3(a x+b)^{2}+2(a x+c)=3 a^{2} x^{2}+2 a(3 b+1) x+3 b^{2}+$ 2c. The graph of $y=h(x)$ is a parabola opening upwards, and the minimum value is attained at the vertex. The x-coordinate of the vertex is $x_{\mathrm{v}}=-\frac{3 b+1}{3 a}$; the y-coordinate of the vertex is $h\left(x_{\mathrm{v}}\right)=-2 b-$ $\frac{1}{3}+2 c$.

Similarly, we obtain that the minimum value of the expression $3(g(x))^{2}+2 f(x)$ is $-2 c-\frac{1}{3}+2 b$. Note that the sum of these two minimum values is $-\frac{2}{3}$, therefore, if one of these minimum values is $-\frac{19}{6}$, then the other is $-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{19}{6}=\frac{5}{2}$.

problem: 3. On each of the lines $y=1$ and $y=6$, there are 200 points with abscissas $1,2,3, \ldots, 200$. In how many ways can three points be chosen from the 400 marked points so that they form the vertices of a right triangle?
solution:
Answer: $C_{200}^{2} \cdot 4 + 190 \cdot 2 + 174 \cdot 4 = 80676$.

Solution. There are two possibilities.

1) The hypotenuse of the triangle lies on one of the lines, and the vertex of the right angle lies on the other line. Let $A B C$ be the given triangle with a right angle at vertex $C$, and $C H$ be its height dropped to the hypotenuse. From the proportionality of segments of a right triangle, we get that $C H^{2} = A H \cdot B H$, i.e., $A H \cdot B H = 25$. Since $A H$ and $B H$ are integers, the following cases are possible: $A H = B H = 5, A H = 25$ and $B H = 1, A H = 1$ and $B H = 25$.

In the first of these cases, the hypotenuse $A B$, equal to 10, can be placed in $190 \cdot 2 = 380$ ways (200 - 10 ways of placement on each of the two given lines), and the position of vertex $C$ is uniquely determined.

In the second and third cases, the length of the hypotenuse is 26, and it can be placed in $2(200 - 26) = 348$ ways. For each position of the hypotenuse, there are two ways to place the vertex - resulting in $2 \cdot 348 = 696$ ways.

2) One of the legs of the triangle (let's call it $B C$) is perpendicular to the given lines, and the other leg ($A C$) lies on one of the given lines. Then the position of leg $B C$ can be chosen in 200 ways. For each variant of the placement of leg $B C$, vertex $A$ can be placed in 398 ways (all points except the already chosen $B$ and $C$ are suitable) - in total, we get $200 \cdot 398 = 79600$ ways.

In total, we get $380 + 696 + 79600 = 80676$ ways.

problem: 4. The numbers $x$ and $y$ are such that the equalities $\operatorname{ctg} x+\operatorname{ctg} y=3$ and $2 \sin (2 x+2 y)=\sin 2 x \sin 2 y$ hold. Find $\operatorname{ctg} x \operatorname{ctg} y$.
solution:
Answer: $\frac{3}{2}$.

Solution. On the domain of definition, the first equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\frac{\cos x \sin y+\cos y \sin x}{\sin x \sin y}=3 \Leftrightarrow \sin (x+y)=3 \sin x \sin y
$$

Transform the second equality:

$$
4 \sin (x+y) \cos (x+y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y
$$

Substitute $3 \sin x \sin y$ for $\sin (x+y)$ in the left part and transform the obtained equality (considering that $\sin x \sin y \neq 0$ due to the domain of definition):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 12 \sin x \sin y \cos (x+y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow 3 \cos (x+y)=\cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow 3 \cos x \cos y-3 \sin x \sin y=\cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow 2 \cos x \cos y=3 \sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{ctg} x \operatorname{ctg} y=\frac{3}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

problem: 5. Circle $\Omega$ with radius $\sqrt{3}$ touches sides $B C$ and $A C$ of triangle $A B C$ at points $K$ and $L$ respectively, and intersects side $A B$ at points $M$ and $N$ ( $M$ lies between $A$ and $N$ ) such that segment $M K$ is parallel to $A C$, $K C=1$, $A L=4$. Find $\angle A C B$, the lengths of segments $M K$, $A B$, and the area of triangle $C M N$.
solution:
Answer: $\angle A C B=\frac{2 \pi}{3}, M K=3, A B=\frac{5 \sqrt{7}}{2}, S_{\triangle C M N}=\frac{45 \sqrt{3}}{28}$.

Solution. Let the center of the circle be denoted as $O$, the foot of the altitude from vertex $C$ of the triangle as $H$, and the angle $B A C$ as $\alpha$.

Since the radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, $\operatorname{to} \operatorname{tg} \angle O C K=$ $\frac{O K}{C K}=\sqrt{3}$ and $\angle O C K=60^{\circ}$. The center of the circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of that angle, so $\angle A C B=2 \angle O C K=120^{\circ}$. Then, by the sum of the angles of the quadrilateral $O L C K$, we find that $\angle L O K=60^{\circ}$.

Since $O L \perp A C$ and $M K \| A C$, then $O L \perp M K$. Triangle $M O K$ is isosceles, the height in it is also the bisector, so $\angle M O K=2 \angle L O K=120^{\circ}$. Hence, $M K=2 \cdot M O \cdot \sin 60^{\circ}=3$. $\angle M O L=\frac{1}{2} \angle M O K=60^{\circ}, M O=L O$, therefore, triangle $M O L$ is equilateral, $\angle M L O=60^{\circ}, M L=\sqrt{3}$. Then $\angle A L M=\angle A L O-\angle M L O=30^{\circ}$.

Consider triangle $A L M$. By the cosine theorem, we get $A M^{2}=A L^{2}+L M^{2}-2$. $A L \cdot L M \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=7$. By the sine theorem, $\frac{A M}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{L M}{\sin \alpha}$, from which $\sin \alpha=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 \sqrt{7}}$. Since angle $\alpha$ lies opposite the smaller side of the triangle, it is acute. From triangle $A C H$, we get $C H=A C \sin \alpha=\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{2 \sqrt{7}}$.

By the tangent and secant theorem, $A L^{2}=A M \cdot A N$, from which $A N=\frac{16}{\sqrt{7}}, M N=A N-A M=\frac{9}{\sqrt{7}}$. Then the area of triangle $C M N$ is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot C H \cdot M N=\frac{45 \sqrt{3}}{28}$.

Since $K M \| A C$, triangles $B K M$ and $B C A$ are similar, with the similarity ratio being $K M: C A=3: 5$. Therefore, $\frac{B M}{B A}=\frac{3}{5}, \frac{B A-\sqrt{7}}{B A}=\frac{3}{5}, A B=\frac{5 \sqrt{7}}{2}$.

problem: 6. Let's call the distance between numbers the absolute value of their difference. It is known that the sum of the distances from seven consecutive natural numbers to some number $a$ is 609, and the sum of the distances from these same seven numbers to some number $b$ is 721. Find all possible values of $a$, given that $a+b=192$.
solution:
Answer: $a=104, a=191, a=1$.

Solution. Let the given consecutive natural numbers be denoted by $k, k+1, \ldots, k+6$. Notice that if some number lies on the interval $[k ; k+6]$, then the sum of the distances from it to the given seven numbers does not exceed $\frac{7}{2} \cdot 6=21$ (the sum of the distances to the two extreme numbers is exactly 6, the sum of the distances to $k+1$ and $k+5$ does not exceed 6, the sum of the distances to $k+2$ and $k+4$ also does not exceed 6, and the distance to $k+3$ does not exceed half the length of the interval between the extreme numbers, i.e., 3). Therefore, the numbers $a$ and $b$ lie outside the interval $[k ; k+6]$. Then the sum of the distances from the number $a$ to each of the given consecutive numbers is expressed by the formula $|7 a-k-(k+1)-\ldots-(k+6)|=7|a-k-3|$. Similarly, the sum of the distances from the number $b$ to each of the given numbers is $7|b-k-3|$. We obtain the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 7 | a - k - 3 | = 6 0 9 , } \\
{ 7 | b - k - 3 | = 7 2 1 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 9 2 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
|a-k-3|=87 \\
|b-k-3|=103 \\
a+b=192
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Consider four cases for the removal of the modulus.

1) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the right of the interval $[k ; k+6]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 3 = 8 7 , } \\
{ b - k - 3 = 1 0 3 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 9 2 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=88 \\
b=104 \\
k=-2
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Since $k$ must be a natural number, this case does not fit.

2) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the left of the interval $[k ; k+6]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 3 = 8 7 , } \\
{ - b + k + 3 = 1 0 3 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 9 2 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=104 \\
b=88 \\
k=188
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

3) The number $a$ lies to the right, and $b$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+6]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 3 = 8 7 , } \\
{ - b + k + 3 = 1 0 3 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 9 2 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=191 \\
b=1 \\
k=101
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

4) The number $b$ lies to the right, and $a$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+6]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 3 = 8 7 , } \\
{ b - k - 3 = 1 0 3 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 9 2 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=1 \\
b=191 \\
k=85
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Thus, there are three possible cases: $a=1, a=191, a=104$.

problem:
7. Edge $A_{1} A$ of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ is perpendicular to its face $A B C D$. Sphere $\Omega$ touches the edges $B B_{1}, B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} C, C B, C D$, and touches edge $C D$ at a point $K$ such that $C K=9, K D=1$.

a) Find the length of edge $A_{1} A$.

b) Suppose it is additionally known that sphere $\Omega$ touches edge $A_{1} D_{1}$. Find the volume of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ and the radius of sphere $\Omega$.
solution:
Answer: $A_{1} A=18, V=1944, R=3 \sqrt{10}$.

Solution. a) From the condition, it follows that $B B_{1} \perp A B C D$, therefore $B B_{1} \perp B C$ and the face $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a rectangle. A circle (the section of the sphere by the plane $B C C_{1} B_{1}$) can be inscribed in this rectangle, which means this face is a square. Let $F$ be the point of tangency of the given sphere with the edge $B C$. The segments $C K$ and $C F$ are equal as tangents to the sphere drawn from the same point. Moreover, a circle inscribed in a square touches its sides at their midpoints. Therefore, $F$ is the midpoint of $B C$ and $B C=2 \cdot C F=2 \cdot C K=18$. The lateral edges of the parallelepiped are equal to each other, and $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a square, so $A A_{1}=C C_{1}=B C=18$.

b) The center of the sphere is located on a line perpendicular to the plane of the square $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ and passing through its center, so it is equidistant from the lines $A D$ and $A_{1} D_{1}$. Therefore, if the sphere touches one of these edges, it touches the other as well. Let $M$ be the point of tangency of the sphere with the edge $A D$, and the circle obtained by the section of the sphere by the plane $A B C D$ be denoted as $\omega$. Let $O$ be the center of $\omega$.

The center of a circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of this angle, so $\angle O C D + \angle O D C = \frac{1}{2}(\angle F C D + \angle M D C) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 180^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$. Thus, triangle $O C D$ is a right triangle, and $O K = \sqrt{C K \cdot D K} = 3$.

The area of the parallelogram $A B C D$ is $B C \cdot F M = 2 \cdot C F \cdot 2 \cdot O K = 2 \cdot 9 \cdot 6 = 108$. The volume of the parallelepiped is $A A_{1} \cdot S_{A B C D} = 18 \cdot 108 = 1944$.

Let $Q$ be the center of the sphere. Then $Q K$ is its radius; and triangle $O K Q$ is a right triangle. Therefore, $Q K = \sqrt{O K^{2} + O Q^{2}} = \sqrt{O K^{2} + \frac{1}{4} A A_{1}^{2}} = 3 \sqrt{10}$.

problem: 1. Find all values of $x$, for each of which one of the three given numbers $\log _{x^{2}}\left(x^{2}-7 x+12\right)$, $\log _{x^{2}} \frac{x^{2}}{x-3}$, and $\log _{x^{2}} \frac{x^{2}}{x-4}$ is equal to the sum of the other two.
solution:
Answer: $x=5$.

Solution. Note that on the domain of definition, the sum of all three logarithms is

$$
\log _{x^{2}}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{x-3} \cdot \frac{x^{2}}{x-4}\left(x^{2}-7 x+12\right)\right)=\log _{x^{2}} x^{4}=2
$$

Let the number that is equal to the sum of the other two be denoted by $c$, and the two remaining numbers by $a$ and $b$. Then $c=a+b$ and $a+b+c=2$, from which it follows that $c=1$, i.e., one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1.

The converse is also true, namely, if one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1, then since the sum of all three logarithms is 2, the sum of the remaining two is 1, i.e., their sum is equal to the first logarithm.

Thus, the requirement of the problem is satisfied if and only if one of the logarithms is equal to 1 (and all logarithms exist). A logarithm is equal to 1 when its base is equal to the logarithmic expression. We obtain the system

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-3}, \\
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-4}, \\
x^{2}=x^{2}-7 x+12
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}
x=0 \\
x=4 \\
x=5 \\
x=\frac{12}{7}
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Of the found values of the variable, only $x=5$ satisfies the domain of definition.

problem: 2. Given two linear functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ such that the graphs $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are parallel lines, not parallel to the coordinate axes. Find the minimum value of the function $2(g(x))^{2}-$ $f(x)$, if the minimum value of the function $2(f(x))^{2}-g(x)$ is $\frac{7}{2}$.
solution:
Answer: $-\frac{15}{4}$.

Solution. Let $f(x)=a x+b, g(x)=a x+c$, where $a \neq 0$. Consider $h(x)=2(f(x))^{2}-g(x)$. Expanding the brackets, we get $h(x)=2(a x+b)^{2}-(a x+c)=2 a^{2} x^{2}+a(4 b-1) x+2 b^{2}-c$. The graph of $y=$ $h(x)$ is a parabola opening upwards, and the minimum value is attained at the vertex. The x-coordinate of the vertex is $x_{\mathrm{B}}=-\frac{4 b-1}{4 a}$; the y-coordinate of the vertex is $h\left(x_{\mathrm{B}}\right)=b-\frac{1}{8}-c$.

Similarly, we obtain that the minimum value of the expression $2(g(x))^{2}-f(x)$ is $c-\frac{1}{8}-b$. Notice that the sum of these two minimum values is $-\frac{1}{4}$, therefore, if one of these minimum values is $\frac{7}{2}$, then the other is $-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{7}{2}=-\frac{15}{4}$.

problem: 3. On each of the lines $x=2$ and $x=9$, there are 400 points with ordinates $1,2,3, \ldots, 400$. In how many ways can three points be chosen from the 800 marked points so that they form the vertices of a right triangle?
solution:
Answer: 321372.

Solution. There are two possibilities.

1) The hypotenuse of the triangle lies on one of the lines, and the vertex of the right angle is on the second line. Let $ABC$ be the given triangle with a right angle at vertex $C$, and $CH$ be its height dropped to the hypotenuse. From the proportionality of the segments of the right triangle, we get that $CH^2 = AH \cdot BH$, i.e., $AH \cdot BH = 49$. Since $AH$ and $BH$ are integers, the following cases are possible: $AH = BH = 7$, $AH = 49$ and $BH = 1$, $AH = 1$ and $BH = 49$.

In the first of these cases, the hypotenuse $AB$, equal to 14, can be placed in $386 \cdot 2 = 772$ ways (400 - 14 ways of placement on each of the two given lines), and the position of vertex $C$ is uniquely determined.

In the second and third cases, the length of the hypotenuse is 50, and it can be placed in $2(400 - 50) = 700$ ways. For each position of the hypotenuse, there are two ways to place the vertex - resulting in $2 \cdot 700 = 1400$ ways.

2) One of the legs of the triangle (let's call it $BC$) is perpendicular to the given lines, and the second leg ($AC$) lies on one of the given lines. Then the position of the leg $BC$ can be chosen in 400 ways. For each variant of the placement of the leg $BC$, the vertex $A$ can be placed in 798 ways (all points except the already chosen $B$ and $C$ are suitable) - in total, we get $400 \cdot 798 = 319200$ ways.

In total, we get $772 + 1400 + 319200 = 321372$ ways.

problem: 4. The numbers $x$ and $y$ are such that the equalities $\operatorname{tg} x - \operatorname{tg} y = 7$ and $2 \sin (2 x - 2 y) = \sin 2 x \sin 2 y$ hold. Find $\operatorname{tg} x \operatorname{tg} y$.
solution:
Answer: $-\frac{7}{6}$.

Solution. On the domain of definition, the first equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\frac{\sin x \cos y-\sin y \cos x}{\cos x \cos y}=3 \Leftrightarrow \sin (x-y)=7 \cos x \cos y
$$

Transform the second equality:

$$
4 \sin (x-y) \cos (x-y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y
$$

Substitute $7 \cos x \cos y$ for $\sin (x-y)$ in the left part and transform the obtained equality (considering that due to the domain of definition $\cos x \cos y \neq 0$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 7 \cos x \cos y \cos (x-y)=\sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow 7 \cos (x-y)=\sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow \\
& \quad \Leftrightarrow 7 \cos x \cos y+7 \sin x \sin y=\sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow 7 \cos x \cos y=-6 \sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{tg} x \operatorname{tg} y=-\frac{7}{6}
\end{aligned}
$$

problem: 5. Circle G with radius $2 \sqrt{3}$ touches sides $B C$ and $A C$ of triangle $A B C$ at points $K$ and $L$ respectively and intersects side $A B$ at points $M$ and $N$ ( $M$ lies between $A$ and $N$ ) such that segment $M K$ is parallel to $A C, C L=2, B K=3$. Find $\angle A C B$, the lengths of segments $M K, A B$ and the area of triangle $B K N$.
solution:
Answer: $\angle A C B=\frac{2 \pi}{3}, M K=6, A B=5 \sqrt{7}, S_{\triangle B K N}=\frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{14}$.

Solution. Let the center of the circle be denoted as $O$, and the angle $C B A$ as $\beta$.

Since the radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, $\operatorname{to} \operatorname{tg} \angle O C K=$ $\frac{O K}{C K}=\sqrt{3}$ and $\angle O C K=60^{\circ}$. The center of the circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of that angle, so $\angle A C B=2 \angle O C K=120^{\circ}$. Then, by the sum of the angles of the quadrilateral $O L C K$, we find that $\angle L O K=60^{\circ}$.

Since $O L \perp A C$ and $M K \| A C$, then $O L \perp M K$. Triangle $M O K$ is isosceles, and the height in it is also the bisector, so $\angle M O K=2 \angle L O K=120^{\circ}$. Hence, $M K=2 \cdot M O \cdot \sin 60^{\circ}=6$. Due to the parallelism of the lines $M K$ and $A C$, we get that $\angle M K B=120^{\circ}$. Consider triangle $M K B$. By the cosine theorem, $B M^{2}=B K^{2}+K M^{2}-2 \cdot B K \cdot K M \cdot \cos 120^{\circ}=63, B M=3 \sqrt{7}$. By the sine theorem, $\frac{M K}{\sin \beta}=\frac{B M}{\sin 120^{\circ}}$, from which $\sin \beta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{7}}$.

By the tangent-secant theorem, $B K^{2}=B M \cdot B N$, from which $B N=\frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}$. Then the area of triangle $B K N$ is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot B K \cdot B N \cdot \sin \beta=\frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{14}$.

Since $K M \| A C$, triangles $B K M$ and $B C A$ are similar, with the similarity ratio being $B K: B C=3: 5$. From this, it follows that $\frac{B M}{B A}=\frac{3}{5}, \frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{B A}=\frac{3}{5}, A B=5 \sqrt{7}$.

problem: 6. Let's call the distance between numbers the absolute value of their difference. It is known that the sum of the distances from thirty-three consecutive natural numbers to some number $a$ is 3168, and the sum of the distances from these same thirty-three numbers to some number $b$ is 924. Find all possible values of $a$, given that $a+b=120$.
solution:
Answer: $a=26, a=-2, a=122$.

Solution. Let the given sequence of consecutive natural numbers be denoted as $k, k+1, \ldots, k+32$. Note that if some number lies on the interval $[k ; k+32]$, then the sum of the distances from it to these thirty-three numbers does not exceed $\frac{33}{2} \cdot 32=528$ (the sum of the distances to the two extreme numbers is exactly 32, the sum of the distances to $k+1$ and $k+31$ does not exceed 32, the sum of the distances to $k+2$ and $k+30$ also does not exceed 32, and so on; the distance to $k+16$ does not exceed half the length of the interval between the extreme numbers, i.e., 16). Therefore, the numbers $a$ and $b$ lie outside the interval $[k ; k+32]$. Then the sum of the distances from the number $a$ to each of the given consecutive numbers is expressed by the formula $|33 a-k-(k+1)-\ldots-(k+32)|=33|a-k-16|$. Similarly, the sum of the distances from the number $b$ to each of the given numbers is $33|b-k-16|$. We obtain the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 3 3 | a - k - 1 6 | = 3 1 6 8 , } \\
{ 3 3 | b - k - 1 6 | = 9 2 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 2 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
|a-k-16|=96 \\
|b-k-16|=28 \\
a+b=120
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Consider four cases for the removal of the modulus.

1) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the right of the interval $[k ; k+32]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 1 6 = 9 6 , } \\
{ b - k - 1 6 = 2 8 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 2 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=94 \\
b=26 \\
k=-18
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Since $k$ must be a natural number, this case does not fit.

2) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the left of the interval $[k ; k+32]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 1 6 = 9 6 , } \\
{ - b + k + 1 6 = 2 8 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 2 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=26 \\
b=94 \\
k=106
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

3) The number $a$ lies to the right, and $b$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+32]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 1 6 = 9 6 , } \\
{ - b + k + 1 6 = 2 8 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 2 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=122 \\
b=-2 \\
k=10
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

4) The number $b$ lies to the right, and $a$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+32]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 1 6 = 9 6 , } \\
{ b - k - 1 6 = 2 8 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 2 0 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=-2 \\
b=122 \\
k=78
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Thus, there are three possible cases: $a=26, a=122, a=-2$.

problem:
7. Edge $A_{1} A$ of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ is perpendicular to its face $A B C D$. Sphere $\Omega$ touches the edges $B B_{1}, B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} C, C B, C_{1} D_{1}$, and touches the edge $C_{1} D_{1}$ at a point $K$ such that $C_{1} K=9, K D_{1}=4$.

a) Find the length of edge $A_{1} A$.

b) Suppose it is additionally known that sphere $\Omega$ touches the edge $A D$. Find the volume of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ and the radius of sphere $\Omega$.
solution:
Answer: $A_{1} A=18, V=3888, R=3 \sqrt{13}$.

Solution. a) From the condition, it follows that $B B_{1} \perp A B C D$, therefore $B B_{1} \perp B C$ and the face $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a rectangle. A circle (the section of the sphere by the plane $B C C_{1} B_{1}$) can be inscribed in this rectangle, which means this face is a square. Let $F$ be the point of tangency of the given sphere with the edge $B_{1} C_{1}$. The segments $C_{1} K$ and $C_{1} F$ are equal as tangents to the sphere drawn from the same point. Moreover, a circle inscribed in a square touches its sides at their midpoints. Therefore, $F$ is the midpoint of $B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B_{1} C_{1}=2 \cdot C_{1} F=2 \cdot C_{1} K=18$. The lateral edges of the parallelepiped are equal to each other, and $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a square, so $A A_{1}=C C_{1}=B_{1} C_{1}=18$.

b) The center of the sphere is located on a line perpendicular to the plane of the square $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ and passing through its center, so it is equidistant from the lines $A D$ and $A_{1} D_{1}$. Therefore, if the sphere touches one of these edges, it touches the other as well. Let $M$ be the point of tangency of the sphere with the edge $A_{1} D_{1}$, and the circle obtained by the section of the sphere by the plane $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ be denoted as $\omega$. Let $O$ be the center of $\omega$.

The center of a circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of this angle, so $\angle O C_{1} D_{1} + \angle O D_{1} C_{1} = \frac{1}{2} (\angle F C_{1} D_{1} + \angle M D_{1} C_{1}) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 180^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$. Thus, the triangle $O C_{1} D_{1}$ is a right triangle, and $O K = \sqrt{C_{1} K \cdot D_{1} K} = 6$.

The area of the parallelogram $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ is $B_{1} C_{1} \cdot F M = 2 \cdot C_{1} F \cdot 2 \cdot O K = 2 \cdot 9 \cdot 12 = 216$. The volume of the parallelepiped is $A A_{1} \cdot S_{A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}} = 18 \cdot 216 = 3888$.

Let $Q$ be the center of the sphere. Then $Q K$ is its radius; and the triangle $O K Q$ is a right triangle. Therefore, $Q K = \sqrt{O K^{2} + O Q^{2}} = \sqrt{O K^{2} + \frac{1}{4} A A_{1}^{2}} = 3 \sqrt{13}$.

problem: 2. Given two linear functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ such that the graphs $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are parallel lines, not parallel to the coordinate axes. Find the minimum value of the function $(g(x))^{2}+$ $5 f(x)$, if the minimum value of the function $(f(x))^{2}+5 g(x)$ is -17.
solution:
Answer: $\frac{9}{2}$.

Solution. Let $f(x)=a x+b, g(x)=a x+c$, where $a \neq 0$. Consider $h(x)=(f(x))^{2}+5 g(x)$. Expanding the brackets, we get $h(x)=(a x+b)^{2}+5(a x+c)=a^{2} x^{2}+a(2 b+5) x+b^{2}+5 c$. The graph of $y=$ $h(x)$ is a parabola opening upwards, and the minimum value is attained at the vertex. The x-coordinate of the vertex is $x_{\mathrm{B}}=-\frac{2 b+5}{2 a}$; the y-coordinate of the vertex is $h\left(x_{\mathrm{B}}\right)=-5 b-\frac{25}{4}+5 c$.

Similarly, we obtain that the minimum value of the expression $(g(x))^{2}+5 f(x)$ is $-5 c-\frac{25}{4}+5 b$. Note that the sum of these two minimum values is $-\frac{25}{2}$, therefore, if one of these minimum values is -17, then the other is $-\frac{25}{2}+17=\frac{9}{2}$.

problem: 3. On each of the lines $y=1$ and $y=12$, there are 200 points with abscissas $1,2,3, \ldots, 200$. In how many ways can three points be chosen from the 400 marked points so that they form the vertices of a right triangle?
solution:
Answer: 80268.

Solution. There are two possibilities.

1) The hypotenuse of the triangle lies on one of the lines, and the vertex of the right angle is on the second line. Let $ABC$ be the given triangle with a right angle at vertex $C$, and $CH$ be its height dropped to the hypotenuse. From the proportionality of the segments of the right triangle, we get that $CH^2 = AH \cdot BH$, i.e., $AH \cdot BH = 121$. Since $AH$ and $BH$ are integers, the following cases are possible: $AH = BH = 11$, $AH = 121$ and $BH = 1$, $AH = 1$ and $BH = 121$.

In the first of these cases, the hypotenuse $AB$, equal to 22, can be placed in $178 \cdot 2 = 356$ ways (200 - 22 ways of placement on each of the two given lines), and the position of vertex $C$ is uniquely determined.

In the second and third cases, the length of the hypotenuse is 122, and it can be placed in $2(200 - 122) = 156$ ways. For each position of the hypotenuse, there are two ways to place the vertex - resulting in $2 \cdot 156 = 312$ ways.

2) One of the legs of the triangle (let's call it $BC$) is perpendicular to the given lines, and the second leg ($AC$) lies on one of the given lines. Then the position of the leg $BC$ can be chosen in 200 ways. For each variant of the placement of the leg $BC$, the vertex $A$ can be placed in 398 ways (all points except the already chosen $B$ and $C$ are suitable) - in total, we get $200 \cdot 398 = 79600$ ways.

In total, we get $356 + 312 + 79600 = 80268$ ways.

problem: 4. The numbers $x$ and $y$ are such that the equalities $\operatorname{ctg} x - \operatorname{ctg} y = 2$ and $5 \sin (2 x - 2 y) = \sin 2 x \sin 2 y$ hold. Find $\operatorname{tg} x \operatorname{tg} y$.
solution:
Answer: $-\frac{6}{5}$.

Solution. On the domain of definition, the first equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\frac{\cos x \sin y-\cos y \sin x}{\sin x \sin y}=3 \Leftrightarrow-\sin (x-y)=2 \sin x \sin y
$$

Transform the second equality:

$$
10 \sin (x-y) \cos (x-y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y
$$

Substitute $-2 \sin x \sin y$ for $\sin (x-y)$ in the left part and transform the obtained equality (considering that $\sin x \sin y \neq 0$ due to the domain of definition):

$$
\begin{aligned}
-20 \sin x \sin y \cos (x-y) & =4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow-5 \cos (x-y)=\cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow \\
\Leftrightarrow 5 \cos x \cos y+5 \sin x \sin y & =-\cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow 6 \cos x \cos y=-5 \sin x \sin y
\end{aligned}
$$

From the last equality, it follows that $\cos x \cos y \neq 0$, so the expression $\operatorname{tg} x \operatorname{tg} y$ exists and $\operatorname{tg} x \operatorname{tg} y=-\frac{6}{5}$.

problem: 6. Let's call the distance between numbers the absolute value of their difference. It is known that the sum of the distances from eleven consecutive natural numbers to some number $a$ is 902, and the sum of the distances from these same eleven numbers to some number $b$ is 374. Find all possible values of $a$, given that $a+b=98$.
solution:
Answer: $a=107, a=-9, a=25$.

Solution. Let the given sequence of natural numbers be denoted as $k, k+1, \ldots, k+10$. Notice that if some number lies on the interval $[k ; k+10]$, then the sum of the distances from it to these eleven numbers does not exceed $\frac{11}{2} \cdot 10=55$ (the sum of the distances to the two extreme numbers is exactly 10, the sum of the distances to $k+1$ and $k+9$ does not exceed 10, the sum of the distances to $k+2$ and $k+8$ also does not exceed 6, and so on; the distance to $k+5$ does not exceed half the length of the interval between the extreme numbers, i.e., 5). Therefore, the numbers $a$ and $b$ lie outside the interval $[k ; k+10]$. Then the sum of the distances from the number $a$ to each of the given consecutive numbers is expressed by the formula $|11 a-k-(k+1)-\ldots-(k+10)|=11|a-k-5|$. Similarly, the sum of the distances from the number $b$ to each of the given numbers is $11|b-k-5|$. We obtain the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 1 1 | a - k - 5 | = 9 0 2 , } \\
{ 1 1 | b - k - 5 | = 3 7 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 9 8 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
|a-k-5|=82 \\
|b-k-5|=34 \\
a+b=98
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Consider four cases for the removal of the modulus.

1) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the right of the interval $[k ; k+10]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 5 = 8 2 , } \\
{ b - k - 5 = 3 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 9 8 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=73 \\
b=25 \\
k=-14
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Since $k$ must be a natural number, this case does not fit.

2) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the left of the interval $[k ; k+10]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 5 = 8 2 , } \\
{ - b + k + 5 = 3 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 9 8 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=25 \\
b=73 \\
k=102
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

3) The number $a$ lies to the right, and $b$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+10]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 5 = 8 2 , } \\
{ - b + k + 5 = 3 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 9 8 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=107 \\
b=-9 \\
k=20
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

4) The number $b$ lies to the right, and $a$ to the left of the interval $[k ; k+10]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 5 = 8 2 , } \\
{ b - k - 5 = 3 4 , } \\
{ a + b = 9 8 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=-9 \\
b=107 \\
k=68
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Thus, there are three possible cases: $a=25, a=107, a=-9$.

problem:
7. Edge $A_{1} A$ of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ is perpendicular to its face $A B C D$. Sphere $\Omega$ touches the edges $B B_{1}, B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} C, C B, C D$, and touches edge $C D$ at a point $K$ such that $C K=4, K D=1$.

a) Find the length of edge $A_{1} A$.

b) Suppose it is additionally known that sphere $\Omega$ touches edge $A_{1} D_{1}$. Find the volume of the parallelepiped $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ and the radius of sphere $\Omega$.
solution:
Answer: $A_{1} A=8, V=256, R=2 \sqrt{5}$.

Solution. a) From the condition, it follows that $B B_{1} \perp A B C D$, therefore $B B_{1} \perp B C$ and the face $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a rectangle. A circle can be inscribed in this rectangle (the section of the sphere by the plane $B C C_{1} B_{1}$), which means this face is a square. Let $F$ be the point of tangency of the given sphere with the edge $B C$. The segments $C K$ and $C F$ are equal as tangents to the sphere drawn from the same point. Moreover, a circle inscribed in a square touches its sides at their midpoints. Therefore, $F$ is the midpoint of $B C$ and $B C=2 \cdot C F=2 \cdot C K=4$. The lateral edges of the parallelepiped are equal to each other, and $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ is a square, so $A A_{1}=C C_{1}=B C=4$.

b) The center of the sphere is located on a line perpendicular to the plane of the square $B C C_{1} B_{1}$ and passing through its center, so it is equidistant from the lines $A D$ and $A_{1} D_{1}$. Therefore, if the sphere touches one of these edges, it touches the other as well. Let $M$ be the point of tangency of the sphere with the edge $A D$, and the circle obtained by the section of the sphere by the plane $A B C D$ be denoted as $\omega$. Let $O$ be the center of $\omega$.

The center of a circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of this angle, so $\angle O C D + \angle O D C = \frac{1}{2}(\angle F C D + \angle M D C) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 180^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$. Thus, triangle $O C D$ is a right triangle, and $O K = \sqrt{C K \cdot D K} = 2$.

The area of the parallelogram $A B C D$ is $B C \cdot F M = 2 \cdot C F \cdot 2 \cdot O K = 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 32$. The volume of the parallelepiped is $A A_{1} \cdot S_{A B C D} = 8 \cdot 32 = 256$.

Let $Q$ be the center of the sphere. Then $Q K$ is its radius; and triangle $O K Q$ is a right triangle. Therefore, $Q K = \sqrt{O K^{2} + O Q^{2}} = \sqrt{O K^{2} + \frac{1}{4} A A_{1}^{2}} = 2 \sqrt{5}$.

$$
\log _{x^{2}}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{x-2} \cdot \frac{x^{2}}{x-5}\left(x^{2}-7 x+10\right)\right)=\log _{x^{2}} x^{4}=2
$$

Let the number that is equal to the sum of the other two be denoted by $c$, and the two remaining numbers by $a$ and $b$. Then $c=a+b$ and $a+b+c=2$, from which it follows that $c=1$, i.e., one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1.

The converse is also true, namely, if one of the three given logarithms is equal to 1, then since the sum of all three logarithms is 2, the sum of the remaining two is 1, i.e., their sum is equal to the first logarithm.

Thus, the requirement of the problem is satisfied if and only if one of the logarithms is equal to 1 (and all logarithms exist). A logarithm is equal to 1 when its base is equal to the logarithmic expression. We obtain the system

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l}
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-2}, \\
x^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{x-5}, \\
x^{2}=x^{2}-7 x+10
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left[\begin{array}{l}

problem: 2. Given two linear functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ such that the graphs $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are parallel lines, not parallel to the coordinate axes. Find the minimum value of the function $(g(x))^{2}-$ $3 f(x)$, if the minimum value of the function $(f(x))^{2}-3 g(x)$ is $\frac{11}{2}$.
solution:
Answer: -10.

Solution. Let $f(x)=a x+b, g(x)=a x+c$, where $a \neq 0$. Consider $h(x)=(f(x))^{2}-3 g(x)$. Expanding the brackets, we get $h(x)=(a x+b)^{2}-3(a x+c)=a^{2} x^{2}+a(2 b-3) x+b^{2}-3 c$. The graph of $y=$ $h(x)$ is a parabola opening upwards, and the minimum value is attained at the vertex. The x-coordinate of the vertex is $x_{\mathrm{B}}=-\frac{2 b-3}{2 a}$; the y-coordinate of the vertex is $h\left(x_{\mathrm{B}}\right)=3 b-\frac{9}{4}-3 c$.

Similarly, we find that the minimum value of the expression $(g(x))^{2}-3 f(x)$ is $3 c-\frac{9}{4}-3 b$. Note that the sum of these two minimum values is $-\frac{9}{2}$, therefore, if one of these minimum values is $\frac{11}{2}$, then the other is $-\frac{9}{2}-\frac{11}{2}=-10$.

problem: 3. On each of the lines $x=2$ and $x=15$, there are 400 points with ordinates $1,2,3, \ldots, 400$. In how many ways can three points be chosen from the 800 marked points so that they form the vertices of a right triangle?
solution:
Answer: 320868.

Solution. There are two possibilities.

1) The hypotenuse of the triangle lies on one of the lines, and the vertex of the right angle is on the second line. Let $ABC$ be the given triangle with a right angle at vertex $C$, and $CH$ be its height dropped to the hypotenuse. From the proportionality of segments of a right triangle, we get that $CH^2 = AH \cdot BH$, i.e., $AH \cdot BH = 169$. Since $AH$ and $BH$ are integers, the following cases are possible: $AH = BH = 13$, $AH = 169$ and $BH = 1$, $AH = 1$ and $BH = 169$.

In the first of these cases, the hypotenuse $AB$, equal to 26, can be placed in $374 \cdot 2 = 748$ ways (400 - 26 ways of placement on each of the two given lines), and the position of vertex $C$ is uniquely determined.

In the second and third cases, the length of the hypotenuse is 170, and it can be placed in $2(400 - 170) = 460$ ways. For each position of the hypotenuse, there are two ways to place the vertex - resulting in $2 \cdot 460 = 920$ ways.

2) One of the legs of the triangle (let's call it $BC$) is perpendicular to the given lines, and the second leg ($AC$) lies on one of the given lines. For each variant of the placement of the leg $BC$, the vertex $A$ can be placed in 798 ways (all points except the already chosen $B$ and $C$ are suitable) - in total, we get $400 \cdot 798 = 319200$ ways.

problem: 4. The numbers $x$ and $y$ are such that the equalities $\operatorname{tg} x+\operatorname{tg} y=4$ and $3 \sin (2 x+2 y)=\sin 2 x \sin 2 y$ hold. Find $\operatorname{ctg} x \operatorname{ctg} y$.
solution:
Answer: $\frac{7}{6}$.

Solution. On the domain of definition, the first equality is equivalent to the following:

$$
\frac{\sin x \cos y+\sin y \cos x}{\cos x \cos y}=4 \Leftrightarrow \sin (x+y)=4 \cos x \cos y
$$

Transform the second equality:

$$
6 \sin (x+y) \cos (x+y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y
$$

Substitute $4 \cos x \cos y$ for $\sin (x+y)$ in the left part and transform the obtained equality (considering that $\cos x \cos y \neq 0$ due to the domain of definition):

$24 \cos x \cos y \cos (x+y)=4 \sin x \sin y \cos x \cos y \Leftrightarrow 6 \cos (x+y)=\sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow$

$$
\Leftrightarrow 6 \cos x \cos y-6 \sin x \sin y=\sin x \sin y \Leftrightarrow 6 \cos x \cos y=7 \sin x \sin y
$$

From the last equality, it follows that $\sin x \sin y \neq 0$, so the expression $\operatorname{ctg} x \operatorname{ctg} y$ exists and $\operatorname{ctg} x \operatorname{ctg} y=\frac{7}{6}$.

Solution. Let the center of the circle be denoted as $O$, and the angle $C B A$ as $\beta$.

Since the radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, $\operatorname{to} \operatorname{tg} \angle O C K=$ $\frac{O K}{C K}=\sqrt{3}$ and $\angle O C K=60^{\circ}$. The center of the circle inscribed in an angle lies on the bisector of that angle, so $\angle A C B=2 \angle O C K=120^{\circ}$. Then, by the sum of the angles of the quadrilateral $O L C K$, we find that $\angle L O K=60^{\circ}$.

Since $O L \perp A C$ and $M K \| A C$, then $O L \perp M K$. Triangle $M O K$ is isosceles, the height in it is also the bisector, hence, $\angle M O K=2 \angle L O K=120^{\circ}$. From this, $M K=2 \cdot M O \cdot \sin 60^{\circ}=$ 12.

Due to the parallelism of the lines $M K$ and $A C$, we get that $\angle M K B=120^{\circ}$. Consider triangle $M K B$. By the cosine theorem, $B M^{2}=B K^{2}+K M^{2}-2 \cdot B K \cdot K M \cdot \cos 120^{\circ}=189$, $B M=3 \sqrt{21}$. problem: 6. Let's call the distance between numbers the absolute value of their difference. It is known that the sum of the distances from twenty-nine consecutive natural numbers to some number $a$ is 1624, and the sum of the distances from these same twenty-nine numbers to some number $b$ is 1305. Find all possible values of $a$, given that $a+b=115$.
solution:
Answer: $a=52, a=108, a=7$.

Solution. Let the given sequence of natural numbers be denoted as $k, k+1, \ldots, k+28$. Notice that if some number lies on the interval $[k ; k+28]$, then the sum of the distances from it to the given twenty-nine numbers does not exceed $\frac{29}{2} \cdot 28=406$ (the sum of the distances to the two extreme numbers is exactly 28, the sum of the distances to $k+1$ and $k+27$ does not exceed 28, the sum of the distances to $k+2$ and $k+26$ also does not exceed 28, and so on; the distance to $k+14$ does not exceed half the length of the interval between the extreme numbers, i.e., 14). Therefore, the numbers $a$ and $b$ lie outside the interval $[k ; k+28]$. Then the sum of the distances from the number $a$ to each of the given consecutive numbers is expressed by the formula $|29 a-k-(k+1)-\ldots-(k+28)|=29|a-k-14|$. Similarly, the sum of the distances from the number $b$ to each of the given numbers is $29|b-k-14|$. We obtain the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 2 9 | a - k - 1 4 | = 1 6 2 4 , } \\
{ 2 9 | b - k - 1 4 | = 1 3 0 5 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 1 5 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
|a-k-14|=56 \\
|b-k-14|=45 \\
a+b=115
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Consider four cases for the removal of the modulus.

1) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the right of the interval $[k ; k+28]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 1 4 = 5 6 , } \\
{ b - k - 1 4 = 4 5 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 1 5 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=63 \\
b=52 \\
k=-7
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

Since $k$ must be a natural number, this case does not fit.

2) Both numbers $a$ and $b$ lie to the left of the interval $[k ; k+28]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ - a + k + 1 4 = 5 6 , } \\
{ - b + k + 1 4 = 4 5 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 1 5 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=52 \\
b=63 \\
k=94
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

3) The number $a$ lies to the right, and $b$ - to the left of the interval $[k ; k+28]$. Then

$$
\left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ a - k - 1 4 = 5 6 , } \\
{ - b + k + 1 4 = 4 5 , } \\
{ a + b = 1 1 5 }
\end{array} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{l}
a=108 \\
b=7 \\
k=38
\end{array}\right.\right.
$$

4) The number $b$ lies to the right, and $a$ - to the left of the interval $[k ; k+28]$. Then

$$
